Reply to Return of Habeas Corpus
 COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS

 Reply to Return of Habeas Corpus (MA)

[COUNTY], ss. [COURT NAME]

 OF THE TRIAL COURT

COMMONWEALTH; )

 )

 )

v. ) Docket No. [number]

 )

[Petitioner name] )

 )

Petitioner. )

 Reply to Return of Habeas Corpus (MA)

 REPLY TO RETURN OF HABEAS CORPUS

NOW COMES the Petitioner, [petitioner name], replying to the Return to the writ of habeas corpus herein
and respectfully alleges:
 1.

 [He/She/They] [denies/deny] that [he/she/they] [is/are] being detained by a lawful judgment or mandate
 of a Court as set forth in Paragraph [paragraph in the Return to Writ of Habeas Corpus template
 detailing the judgment or mandate] of the said Return.
 2.

 [He/She/They] [denies/deny] each and every allegation contained in paragraphs of the said Return.
 3.

 That as shown by the said Return, the Petitioner was convicted of the [crime/crimes] of [offense
 name(s)] by the [court] Court of [county] County on the [day] day of [month], [year], and was sentenced
 to serve a term of [sentence, in years] years in [name of prison where petitioner was sentenced] at
 [location of prison] [state].
 4.

 That at the time of the entry of the judgment of conviction, the Petitioner had already been confined in
 the County Jail of the County of [county] awaiting trial for a period of [pretrial detention period, in days]
 days, which time [he was/she was/they were] entitled to have deducted from the sentence so imposed
 upon [him/her/them].
 5.

 That on the [day] day of [month], [year], after the Petitioner had served [number of years served] years,
 [number of months served] months, and [number of days served] days of [his/her/their] sentence,
 including the jail time aforementioned, the Petitioner was released from custody on parole.
 6.

 That the Petitioner's sentence expired on the [day] day of [month], [year].
 7.

 That from the date of the Petitioner's release until the [day] day of [month], [year], the Petitioner fulfilled
 all the conditions of the agreement under which [he was/she was/they were] so paroled, made all the
 reports required of [him/her/them], and conducted [himself/herself/themself] in the manner required of
 [him/her/them].
 8.

 That thereafter the Petitioner was arrested under a warrant issued by the Board of Parole of the
 Commonwealth of Massachusetts charging that [he/she/they] had violated the conditions of
 [his/her/their] parole on the [day] day of [month], [year], and directing that [he/she/they] be returned to
 [prison name].
 9.

 That such alleged violation of parole, if in fact any act of the Petitioner was such a violation, was
 committed after the expiration of the Petitioner's sentence and after [his/her/their] discharge from
 custody.

 Reply to Return of Habeas Corpus (MA)

WHEREFORE, the Petitioner prays that the writ of habeas corpus granted herein be sustained and that
[he/she/they] be discharged forthwith from imprisonment.

 Reply to Return of Habeas Corpus (MA)

Date: ____________________
Respectfully submitted,
____________________
(Signature of Defendant's attorney)
[Petitioner attorney name], Attorney for Petitioner
[Office Street Address]
[OPTIONAL LANGUAGE: P.O. Box address]
[city], [state] [zip code]
Email: [Email address]
____________________
(Signature of Petitioner)

 Reply to Return of Habeas Corpus (MA)

 VERIFICATION

[Petitioner name], first being duly sworn, deposes and says that [he/she/they] [is/are] the Petitioner in this
action; that [he/she/they] [has/have] read the foregoing affirmation and knows the contents thereof; and that
the same are based on information and belief [he/she/they] [believe/believes] them to be true.

Date: ____________________
____________________
(Signature of Petitioner)

Sworn to and subscribed to before me this the [day] day of [month], [year].
____________________
Notary Public

 CERTIFICATE OF SERVICE

 I hereby certify that I have this date served [Commonwealth's attorney name], at [location], with a copy of
 the within and foregoing by [United States First Class Mail/hand-delivery].

 This [day] day of [month], [year].

Return to Writ of Habeas Corpus
 COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS

 Return to Writ of Habeas Corpus (MA)

[COUNTY], ss. [COURT NAME]

 OF THE TRIAL COURT

COMMONWEALTH; )

 )

 )

v. ) Docket No. [number]

 )

[Prisoner name] )

 )

Defendant. )

 Return to Writ of Habeas Corpus (MA)

 RETURN TO WRIT OF HABEAS CORPUS

[Deponent name], being duly sworn, deposes and says:

 I, [Deponent name], [Warden of [prison name],/Sheriff of the County of] [county] County,
 Massachusetts, as and for a return to the writ of habeas corpus granted herein on the [day] day of
 [month], [year], and requiring me to produce one [prisoner name] before this Court at a [court
 information], thereof, to be held in and for the County of [county] at the County Court House in the City
 of [city], on the [day] day of [month], [year]:
 1.

 That at the time the writ was served upon me on the [day] day of [month], [year], the said [prisoner
 name] was and still is in my custody.
 2.

 That the said [prisoner name] was duly indicted by a Grand Jury in this Court on the [day] day of
 [month], [year], for the [crime/crimes] of [name of crime(s) prisoner was indicted for], a copy of
 which indictment is hereto annexed.
 3.

 That I took the said [prisoner name] into my custody and now hold [him/her/them] in custody under
 and pursuant to a [bench warrant/commitment] issued by [[district attorney name], District
 Attorney/the Court /[name of the relevant authority that issued the warrant or commitment], [title of
 the relevant authority that issued the warrant or commitment]] of the County of [county], a copy of
 which is hereto annexed.
 4.

 That the originals of the said [bench warrant/commitment] will be produced and exhibited to the
 Court on the return of this writ.
 5.

 Pursuant to the command of the said writ I (will) have here before you on the day and place
 mentioned therein the body of the said [prisoner name].

 Return to Writ of Habeas Corpus (MA)

 ____________________
 [Warden of [prison name]/Sheriff of the County of [county]]

 Sworn to and subscribed to before me this the [day] day of [month], [year].
 ____________________
 Notary Public

§ 11.01 Scope
This chapter discusses how to deliver a successful opening statement during an OUI trial. Specifically, the chapter explains how to prepare an opening statement for an OUI trial, offers suggested content for opening statements for OUI trials, and provides practice tips on how to deliver your opening statement.

entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 11.02
LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 11 OPENING STATEMENTS > PART I: STRATEGY
§ 11.02 Objective and Strategy
The objective of this chapter is to provide guidance to the defense attorney on how to prepare and deliver effective opening statements. An opening statement is considered by many accomplished trial attorneys to be one of the most important parts of every criminal trial, because it is the first of only two times during the course of a trial that you are permitted to speak directly to the members of the jury or the judge about the facts and issues in the case. Unfortunately, there is no overnight solution, quick shortcut, or magic formula available to instantaneously become an expert at giving an opening statement. To become a trial-tested expert at giving opening statements, it is necessary to maintain a steadfast commitment during your career as a trial attorney to refining and eventually mastering your delivery of opening statements. Becoming adept at handling this part of a trial takes time and requires that you actually do trial work.
Like an athlete reviewing game tapes of a future opponent, you can learn new skills and techniques by taking the time to watch other attorneys give their opening statements during OUI trials. As you will quickly learn, there are very few hard-and-fast rules on how to deliver an opening statement. If you dedicate yourself to developing this skill, it will prove invaluable to your practice as a trial attorney and drastically increase the likelihood of obtaining a positive outcome after each one of your trials.
LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

entries.title: Factual Preparation
entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 11-14 Trial
entries.sourceFile: __11.04 Factual Preparation.docx
entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 11.04
LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 11 OPENING STATEMENTS > PART II: PREPARING YOUR OPENING STATEMENT
§ 11.04 Factual Preparation
The one constant key to delivering a successful opening statement is that you must devote ample time to be thoroughly prepared. Sufficient preparation for your opening cannot be completed the night before the trial. Before you can construct your opening statement, you must have already determined the details and nuances of your general trial strategy and have anticipated what evidence the Commonwealth will present as part of its case-in-chief and what legal theories it will attempt to develop at trial. Once you have garnered a firm grasp of your client’s OUI case and have competently completed your trial preparation, you can begin to prepare your opening remarks to the jury or the judge. This preparation will fall into three steps: factual preparation; legal preparation; and personal preparation.
Factual preparation is a seemingly obvious step, but attorneys sometimes fail to set aside the necessary time and attention to thoroughly learn the facts of the client’s particular OUI case before preparing an opening statement. Without exception, you must know the background and facts of the case better than everyone else in the courtroom. Knowing the facts inside and out-such as the public ways where the police officer followed your client, names of witnesses, the chronological order of events, and other details of the case on trial-will give you much needed confidence and improve the natural flow of your opening statement. You do not want to find yourself in a situation where you are undermining a defensible OUI case because your ability to deliver a cohesive statement is compromised due to repeated difficulties recalling various details of the case.
A thorough understanding of the facts of the OUI case will also help you anticipate the various facts that the Commonwealth may find objectionable. You cannot mention facts in your opening statement that you will not be able to introduce at trial. If there are facts that you believe the Commonwealth will object to during your opening statement, it is advisable that you prepare pretrial motions in limine related to those issues. Such potentially problematic pieces of evidence include, but are not limited to, mentioning 911/turret tapes, your client’s medical records, and anticipated expert testimony. You must vet these issues ahead of time and know the facts that the judge will permit you to discuss. Nothing will disrupt you more than a successful objection by the Commonwealth to a factual remark you make during your opening statement. It is therefore of critical importance to identify these issues and address them so that your delivery goes as smoothly as possible.
You should consider preparing a one-page outline with only the key details of the case. This outline will be useful to help you quickly recall a fact if you suffer a memory lapse during your opening statement. A suggested outline would be:
Date of offense.
Time of offense.
Location of offense: Include all of the roadways involved in the case and list them in the order that your client drove on them according the incident reports written by the police officers that you anticipate will testify.
List of anticipated witnesses.
Brief statement of reason the police officers made contact with your client.
Major roadside observations.
List of field sobriety tests your client attempted to complete.
Major booking observations.
Result of the breath test, if any.
If you do not take the time to address the first step of factual preparation, you will not be able to properly prepare the legal issues that you will need to address during your opening statement. A trial is like a puzzle; you cannot put the whole picture together if you are missing a piece, and the members of the jury will quickly notice that there is a gap in your defense.
LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

Strategic Point:
Although you should create an outline of the facts, it is always best to deliver your opening statement without the use of notes. This approach will improve your natural oral flow, make you more relatable to the members of the jury, and prevent you from sounding like you are reciting a memorized speech. The outline should be kept nearby in the event of an emergency so that you can find the forgotten detail without rummaging through your file and quickly get back on track.
Warning:
Be careful with the amount of factual detail from the defense that you present. Saying too much may reveal for the prosecution a defense the prosecution might not otherwise anticipate.

1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 11.05
LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 11 OPENING STATEMENTS > PART II: PREPARING YOUR OPENING STATEMENT
§ 11.05 Legal Preparation
The second step that is necessary to take during the preparation of your opening statement is to meticulously identify and evaluate the legal issues raised by the specific facts of your case in regard to the various areas of the relevant Massachusetts OUI statutes. The facts of every trial are unique and will give rise to different situations during the course of your OUI trial that can be finessed to support a defense or to undermine the Commonwealth’s case. You must have a working knowledge of the relevant definitions from the OUI statutes, any evidentiary standards that will arise during the trial, and the Commonwealth’s burden of proof in regard to the three elements of proving an OUI. This knowledge will help you identify the facts that will become evidence at trial and that must be discussed during your opening statement.
LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

entries.title: Personal Preparation
entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 11-14 Trial
entries.sourceFile: __11.06 Personal Preparation.docx
entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 11.06
LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 11 OPENING STATEMENTS > PART II: PREPARING YOUR OPENING STATEMENT
§ 11.06 Personal Preparation
Equally important to diligently learning the facts of your OUI case and vetting the relevant legal issues, you must consider that a trial is largely a presentation of many moving parts. While only so many of these parts are within your control, it is imperative that you strive to positively influence as many of them as is realistically possible.
Take the time to plan your first impression with the members of the jury, as it will impact how they receive your case and judge your client.
LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

Example:
It is the date of your OUI jury trial, and the judge has decided to hear your case. You are going through some last-minute preparations while sitting at the defense table with your client when a court officer says, “Everyone rise; jurors entering.” You stand as the people in the jury pool begin to file into the room and sit in the gallery. Your client’s fate and a positive verdict for the defense rest with each one of these people, as they alone will decide the outcome of the case. You must appreciate that these jurors are simply ordinary people that have been notified that they must step away from their families, their friends, and their jobs to fulfill their obligation of serving jury duty. Research shows that people make a series of snap judgments within seconds of first seeing another person. As soon as they enter the courtroom, the jurors will quickly evaluate the prosecutor, the judge, your client, and you. Because of the immense role these jurors will play during the trial, the tremendous importance of making a strong first impression with them simply cannot be overstated. A juror’s perception of you will always be attributed to your client. The good news is that with a small amount of planning, you can positively influence the jurors’ impression of you and begin constructing a solid foundation to deliver your opening statement upon and ultimately your entire OUI defense. The first impression will already be made by the time you stand to deliver your opening statement, and it will be much more difficult to connect with the jurors if they perceive you poorly before you even start talking.
Practice Tip:
Consider the following practice tips to help obtain a strong first impression:
Choose appropriate attire for the trial and request that your client dress appropriately as well. Make sure that you appear orderly and not disheveled.
Make sure that your table is organized. Jurors will think that you are ill prepared if your files and documents are in disarray. Having an organized table will also help you access reports and your evidentiary exhibits during the course of the trial.
Instruct your client to turn and face the jurors as they enter the courtroom, and you do the same. Do not sit down or turn away from the jury pool until instructed to do so by the trial clerk. When the jurors are in the courtroom, they always deserve your full attention.
Attempt to make brief eye contact with each juror as they enter the courtroom. This simple act will convey honesty and positive energy.
Be aware of your attitude and the corresponding facial expressions that you make. If you just lost an important pretrial motion in limine or suffered some other setback in your case, you must move on quickly. The jurors will adversely judge you if you appear hostile or angry.
When you stand to introduce yourself, make a succinct statement that is appropriately audible for the size of the courtroom. Again, make eye contact with the jurors and speak directly to them.

entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 11-14 Trial

entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 11.07
LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 11 OPENING STATEMENTS > PART II: PREPARING YOUR OPENING STATEMENT
§ 11.07 Exhibits and Demonstrative Aids
The use of exhibits and demonstrative aids during your opening can tremendously buttress your defense and assist in effectively organizing the evidence so that the members of the jury or judge will easily be able to comprehend your positions. When you plan to use any materials during your opening statement that you believe will later be entered into evidence, provide the materials to the prosecutor at least 10 days prior to trial so that he or she will have the time to inspect them.
On the day of trial, address the materials with the judge and inform him or her that you have a good faith basis to believe that the materials will be entered into evidence. With proper notice to both the Commonwealth and the court before trial, judges will often permit you to use the materials during your opening statement.
You should follow a similar procedure with demonstrative aids. It is not as imperative to give 10 days advance notice to the Commonwealth, but it is still preferred practice. Consider creating diagrams or flowcharts as you deliver your opening. A simple map of a roadway or checklist of the OUI elements can be useful when describing a series of events or highlighting anticipated problems with the testimony from a Commonwealth witness.
LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

entries.title: General Considerations on Opening Statements
entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 11-14 Trial
entries.sourceFile: __11.09 General Considerations on Opening Statements.docx
entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 11.09
LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 11 OPENING STATEMENTS > PART III: CONTENT OF OPENING STATEMENTS
§ 11.09 General Considerations on Opening Statements
The most effective opening statements are organized like a road map. An opening statement should be a concise layout of exactly what you anticipate the members of the jury can expect to see and hear during the course of the OUI trial. Many attorneys often incorrectly refer to opening statements as opening arguments. The judge will not permit you to argue the facts during your opening statement and, accordingly, you should not plan to make any arguments until your closing argument. There are only two times during your OUI trial that you will be permitted to directly address the members of the jury or the judge in regard to your case, and you will have few additional opportunities to present your strongest facts. Because these opportunities are at such a premium, you must be prepared to deliver a concentrated opening statement that offers an encompassing outline of your position and how you will counter the Commonwealth’s evidence.
LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

Strategic Point:
Use the words “we” and “us,” instead of “you,” when telling the jurors what they saw or heard during the trial. This technique will organically encourage the members of the jury to align with the defense.
Example 1: “The arresting officer told us that he stopped my client because …”
Example 2: “When we saw the photographs of the scene …”

entries.title: Commonwealth s Opening Statement
entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 11-14 Trial
entries.sourceFile: __11.10 Commonwealth_s Opening Statement.docx
entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 11.10
LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 11 OPENING STATEMENTS > PART III: CONTENT OF OPENING STATEMENTS
§ 11.10 Commonwealth’s Opening Statement
Defense Counsel’s Reaction
Because the Commonwealth has the burden of proof, the prosecutor will be given the opportunity to deliver his or her opening statement first. Unfortunately, this order means that the prosecutor will be the first attorney to appear before the jury, and this gives the prosecutor the ability to take the lead and potentially set the tone for the entire case. Not all is lost, however, because in cases, like life, there are always two sides to every story, and you will have your turn to address the members of the jury or the judge.
Make sure to be stoic while listening to the prosecutor’s opening statement and be especially careful not to adversely react to remarks about incriminating pieces of evidence or testimony. The members of the jury will be sure to notice your negative reaction and that evidence or anticipated testimony will stand out in their minds. During your preparation for the trial, you should have already anticipated what issues the prosecutor would address during his or her opening statement, and you should be ready to counter those remarks when the judge gives you the opportunity to address the jury. A standard outline for the Commonwealth’s opening is set forth below.
Introduction/Theme/Analogy/Story
The prosecutor will take one of two approaches-either put forward a theme of the case-in-chief or move right into the facts that he or she will seek to introduce during the trial. Themes range significantly between prosecutors, but they may be related to a defendant not taking responsibility for his or her actions or serve to encourage the members of the jury to evaluate all the evidence.
Narrative
Prosecutors will almost always present the facts in the order that they occurred on the date of the incident. The prosecutor will simply start with the date of the incident, transition into the events that led the arresting police officer to come into contact with your client, and then finish with a summary of the observations that the police officer(s) made after making contact with your client.
Witnesses/Parties
Shortly after setting out his or her theme, the prosecutor typically will begin to introduce the relevant people. He or she will identify the police officers involved, any civilian witnesses the Commonwealth summonsed to testify for the prosecution, and any experts who will offer their opinions during the trial. The prosecutor will typically introduce these parties in the chronological order that they appeared during the narrative of events surrounding the incident. The following is an example of the usual roster and order of Commonwealth witnesses in an OUI trial:
Civilian witness(es) who allegedly observed and reported your client for driving erratically.
Police officer who made the initial motor vehicle stop of your client.
Police officer who arrived to back up the first police officer while your client did field sobriety tests.
Police officer who performed the booking procedures at the arresting police department after your client was taken into custody and transported.
Police officer who administered the Breathalyzer test to your client.
Police officer responsible for keeping the records for the arresting police department’s Breathalyzer machine.
Request Guilty Verdict
The prosecutor will finish his or her opening statement by requesting that the members of the jury find your client guilty based on the evidence and testimony that is anticipated to be seen and heard during the trial.
LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

Strategic Point:
Be sure to listen carefully to the prosecutor during the part of the opening statement where he or she recites what the prosecution considers to be the relevant facts. There may be grounds to move for a directed verdict if the evidence to be presented is insufficient to warrant a finding of guilty. Commonwealth v. Lowder, 432 Mass. 92, 731 N.E.2d 510 (2000). For example, if the prosecutor fails to mention the results of your client’s Breathalyzer test, you can move for a directed verdict on the per se theory of prosecution. Winning a case before even addressing the jury is an opportunity that you cannot afford to ignore.
Warning:
District court prosecutors often neglect or intentionally ignore facts that damage the case-in-chief. You must be ready to seize this opportunity during your opening statement by pointing out that the Commonwealth did not want to present a full picture of the incident that led to the OUI charge against your client, because the full picture shows that it is a weak case for the prosecution.
Warning:
You should be attentive to any potentially objectionable statements the prosecutor makes during his or her opening statement, as you will need to make a timely objection to preserve your client’s rights if he or she later decides to appeal an issue from your OUI trial. It is a rare occasion when you will need to object in the middle of the prosecutor’s opening statement. Such an action should be reserved for only the most egregious of statements and almost always should be addressed at a sidebar with the judge and out of the earshot of the jury.

entries.title: Defense s Opening Statement
entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 11-14 Trial
entries.sourceFile: __11.11 Defense_s Opening Statement.docx
entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 11.11
LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 11 OPENING STATEMENTS > PART III: CONTENT OF OPENING STATEMENTS
§ 11.11 Defense’s Opening Statement
Timing and Strategy
After the Commonwealth presents its opening statement, you will have the opportunity to immediately give an opening statement or to wait until after the close of the Commonwealth’s evidence. It is slightly uncommon for a defense attorney to elect to wait and open after the close of the Commonwealth’s case. Waiting allows the prosecutor to completely dominate the course of the trial and leaves the members of the jury with only one side of the case for a lengthy period of time. Despite these issues, it may make sense to wait until the close of the Commonwealth’s evidence to do your opening statement, for example, if your trial strategy entails offering a relatively complicated defense or calling a large number of witnesses and you are concerned that the jury will forget key parts of your opening statement by the time you can call your first witness.
Regardless of when you elect to give your opening statement, do not bury the lead. In other words, always put great emphasis on the strongest parts of your defense or the weakest parts of the Commonwealth’s case. If it is available, an early opportunity to put the Commonwealth into a defensive posture and to raise questions about the strength of its case before the prosecutor even has the chance to present evidence should be capitalized on during your opening statement.
This discrepancy is an example of a factual issue that you would be best served raising during your opening statement as a means to undermine the credibility of the police officers before they even take the stand and testify. If you know before the trial that there will be factual issues with the Commonwealth’s case similar to the one discussed in the scenario above, you should bring them up as early and often as possible. In the same regard, if you have facts that support a not guilty finding, you should bring those up during your opening statement as well. Below is a general outline for an opening statement for an OUI trial.
Introduction
Like the prosecutor, the opening statement is your opportunity to tell the members of the jury or the judge about the case that you believe they are about to hear. Attorneys have traditionally started their opening statements with a brief introduction of themselves and their clients. Attorneys also often thank the members of the jury for their time and patience. While both approaches are polite, it is now more common and best practice to simply move into your case. You already introduced yourself during the juror selection process. At this point of the trial, the jurors have an understanding that the case is about an OUI and are eager to hear the evidence so that they can return to their regular lives. The most polite gesture is to not waste their time with superfluous ceremony.
Presumption of Innocence/Burden of Proof
Remind the members of the jury or the judge that your client is presumed to be innocent unless, and until, the Commonwealth is able to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that your client operated a motor vehicle on a public way while under the influence of intoxicating liquor or with a blood-alcohol content of 0.08 or greater. Reinforcing these maxims is of paramount importance to ensure that the members of the jury or the judge always apply them to the evidence that they will see and hear.
Theme/Analogy/Story
A good technique for a jury trial is to tell the jurors a theme, analogy, or story that relates to your particular case, because it will capture their attention and help you construct a consistent thread through your presentation at the trial. Many attorneys who regularly handle OUI cases have a canned theme, analogy, or story that they use at almost every trial. Many of these approaches can be boiled down to a creative method of encouraging the jury to keep an open mind during the trial and to avoid jumping to conclusions too early.
Narrative
Your trial strategy will dictate whether or not you should present a fact pattern during your opening statement. If you believe the Commonwealth has a weak case that it cannot win based on its evidence, then you may not choose to contest the facts at all. Instead, you may decide to spend time reminding the members of the jury that under the law, your client is presumed to be innocent unless, and until, the Commonwealth has proven his or her guilt, and that it is the Commonwealth’s burden to prove each and every element of an OUI before the jury can find your client guilty. Do not ignore potentially damaging evidence. If you address it, you can stifle its impact. This approach is a judgment call, because there will be times when a prosecutor does not intend to raise an issue until you draw attention to it.
If you intend to develop a fact pattern during the trial, you may deliver a clear and vivid description of what you believe happened. Most of the members of the jury or the judge will not be personally familiar with the scene of the incident or how police officers handle OUI arrests. A powerful depiction of the events and places involved in the case will help the members of the jury or the judge visualize exactly what happened. You should deliver a summarized preview of what they will see and hear, including the names of any witness you intend to call at trial, their roles in the facts of the case, and any evidence you will submit. Emphasize the particular facts that differ from the prosecutor’s narrative, and be careful not to mention any facts that you will not be able to enter into evidence during the course of the trial. Be cautious not to overstate the strength of your evidence, as testimony will never go as you anticipate. You may lose trust with members of the jury or the judge if you come on too strong about a particular point.
Legal Positions
If you plan to attack the Commonwealth’s case on more technical legal grounds, such as an inability to prove operation or that a road is a public way within the meaning of the OUI statute, you should plant the seeds of doubt with the members of the jury during your opening statement. Tell the jurors when they should listen during the trial to help draw their attention to the issue. Too often, attorneys fail to sufficiently highlight their main points, and jurors miss them, as they often quickly come and go during a trial.
Request Not Guilty Verdict
Tell the members of the jury or the judge that after the close of the evidence, you will appear before them again during closing arguments and ask that they find your client not guilty of OUI.
LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

Example:
Two police officers are involved in your client’s motor vehicle stop and subsequent field sobriety tests. Each police officer writes a separate incident report, and both incident reports set forth seemingly overwhelming facts and observations that portray your client as being severely intoxicated at the time of the arrest. When the two incident reports are compared, however, there are a number of inconsistencies regarding your client’s performance on the field sobriety tests.
Warning:
Do not tell the members of the jury what the prosecutor or the Commonwealth’s witnesses will say or do. Unfortunately, no matter how confident you are that something will happen with the Commonwealth’s case during the course of the trial, there is always the possibility that it will not occur and you will look like you did not know what you were talking about in front of the jury. You should also paraphrase the anticipated testimony from your own witnesses, because they too will often testify differently at trial from the statements they made to you during your pretrial preparation meeting.
Warning:
Do not state personal opinions about the evidence or the case in general. The judge will not permit you to offer your own thoughts, because they are irrelevant, as it is the jury or the judge that has the responsibility to weigh the evidence. Offering your personal thoughts on the case will also dilute your argument. Simply tell the fact finders what they should think about the evidence or testimony. The following are several examples of phrases to avoid when prefacing a statement and several phrases that are appropriate:
“The witness was clearly not credible because …”; not “I believe that the witness was not credible because …”
“The evidence points you to one possible verdict …”; not “I think that the evidence points you to one possible verdict …”
“The photographs show that the parking lot is not a public way …”; not “In my opinion, the photographs show that the parking lot is not a public way …”
Strategic Point:
Because you cannot argue during an opening statement, consider the following phrases to preface your remarks:
“You will hear …”
“The witness will testify …”
“You will have the chance to see …”

1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 12.02
LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 12 CLOSING ARGUMENTS > PART I: STRATEGY
§ 12.02 Objective and Strategy
The object of this chapter is to provide guidance to the defense attorney on how to prepare and deliver effective closing arguments. The closing argument has the potential to save a lost case or to lose a case that you should have won. It is the last chance you will have to communicate directly to the members of the jury or to the judge about the case, and thus you must be prepared to efficiently and persuasively break the case down and convince the fact finders that your client is not guilty of OUI. During a jury trial, the prosecutor must convince each member of the jury beyond a reasonable doubt that your client is guilty, but you need to only raise reasonable doubt in the mind of one member. You can increase the odds of successfully planting seeds of reasonable doubt amongst the members of the jury by delivering a well-executed closing argument.
Like opening statements, there are no set rules that must be followed to give a successful closing argument, but there are a number of necessary fundamental skills that you need to be mindful of when preparing for your closing argument. Despite your greatest intentions or best-laid plans, closing arguments can never be as rigidly structured as opening statements because of the inherent uncertainty that comes with every trial. Witnesses, for both the Commonwealth and the defense, will occasionally testify differently from what you anticipated they would say during your preparations prior to the trial. The judge may not permit certain pieces of evidence to be presented that you either wished to enter or believed would be entered by the Commonwealth. There are many other issues that arise during OUI trials that will require that your closing arguments be more fluid than your opening statement and force you to be able to adapt the outline of your closing argument to the various wrinkles that will inevitably arise.

entries.title: Importance of Jury Instructions
entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 11-14 Trial
entries.sourceFile: __12.04 Importance of Jury Instructions.docx
entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 12.04
LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 12 CLOSING ARGUMENTS > PART II: PREPARING YOUR CLOSING ARGUMENT
§ 12.04 Importance of Jury Instructions
Before you can begin to draft the outline of your closing argument, you must have a working knowledge of the jury instructions that you anticipate the judge will utilize at your trial. Most judges in Massachusetts rely on the model jury instructions for OUI, so it is not difficult to accomplish this step in the trial preparation process. You will find that anticipating the jury instructions will assist you while structuring your closing argument, because aside from the facts of the case, the jury instructions dictate the playing field in which you will be operating. The particular facts of your case will enable you to determine the correct jury instructions. The elements of “operation” and “public way” must be proven at every OUI trial, but the Commonwealth may not attempt to prove both theories of “under the influence.” You should also be thoughtful of other jury instructions that may be relevant and beneficial for your trial strategy, such as absent witness, expert witness, or omissions in police investigations.
LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

Warning:
Judges typically do not give additional instructions, like the three listed above, unless facts supporting the instructions are raised during evidence and one of the parties specifically requests them during your jury instruction conference at the close of evidence.

entries.title: Laying Foundation for Your Closing Argument
entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 11-14 Trial
entries.sourceFile: __12.05 Laying Foundation for Your Closing Argument.docx
entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 12.05
LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 12 CLOSING ARGUMENTS > PART II: PREPARING YOUR CLOSING ARGUMENT
§ 12.05 Laying Foundation for Your Closing Argument
As you prepare for trial and delve into the facts of your particular OUI case, you will begin to formulate the trial strategies that you will attempt to employ to defend your client. Ultimately, the end goal of your trial strategy is to find a way to answer only one question in the minds of the members of the jury or the judge: Why is your client not guilty of OUI?
Maybe you believe that the credibility of one of the Commonwealth’s witnesses is questionable, or you think there will be insufficient evidence for the Commonwealth to prove that your client was the driver of a motor vehicle involved in a single-car motor vehicle accident. Your answers, whatever they may be (there may be more than one), are the crux of your closing argument. However, before you can offer the reasons why your client is not guilty of OUI during your closing argument and convince the members of the jury or the judge to deliver a verdict for the defense, you must offer evidence and elicit testimony during the course of your trial to support your positions. Simply stated, if you do not produce a certain fact during the trial, you cannot refer to or rely on that fact during your closing argument.
A closing argument, in effect, is an outline of what you will need to accomplish before the close of evidence. To this end, you should consider drafting the outline for your closing argument before you prepare any other parts of the trial, such as questions for witnesses, your opening statement, and exhibits, as this will act as a trial guide.
In this scenario, your closing argument, in sum, would be that, based on the evidence presented during the trial through the testimony of the responding police officers, the Commonwealth failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that your client was driving at the time of the accident. Therefore, he is not guilty. The development of this argument becomes the outline of your trial strategy and requires that you craft a line of cross-examination questions for the responding police officers that show that the keys to the crashed motor vehicle were not found on your client and the motor vehicle was registered to a female who lived nearby the scene of the crash. By working backwards from the outline of your closing argument, you will create a list of goals to be accomplished during the trial and ensure that you will have the facts to support your positions during the closing arguments.
LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

Example:
Police officers from Anywhere, Massachusetts, respond to a report of a single-car motor vehicle accident on Main Street, a public way in a well-populated residential neighborhood. Upon arrival, the police officers find your client sitting on the sidewalk approximately 50 feet from a motor vehicle that is off the roadway and up on its side on the front lawn of a residence. According to the police incident reports, your client is highly intoxicated. He shows no visible signs of injury and denies driving. The keys to the motor vehicle are not in the ignition and the responding police officers do not locate them on your client. Additionally, the car is registered to a female who lives three blocks from the scene of the accident. Your client is arrested for OUI and transported to the police station.
Practice Tip:
If evidence is excluded from trial, defense counsel cannot refer to the “lack” of that evidence to the jury in closing. Commonwealth v. O’Rourke, 178 N.E.3d 908 (Mass. App. Ct. 2021) (unpublished) (quoting Commonwealth v. Carroll, 439 Mass. 547, 555, 789 N.E.2d 1062 (2003)). (“Counsel may not, in closing, exploit the absence of evidence that had been excluded at his request … . Such exploitation of absent, excluded evidence is fundamentally unfair and reprehensible”).

entries.title: Delivery of Your Closing Argument
entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 11-14 Trial
entries.sourceFile: __12.06 Delivery of Your Closing Argument.docx
entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 12.06
LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 12 CLOSING ARGUMENTS > PART II: PREPARING YOUR CLOSING ARGUMENT
§ 12.06 Delivery of Your Closing Argument
Generally
Unlike your opening statement, the closing argument requires a more forceful presentation. Every attorney embraces a different style while speaking before the members of a jury or a judge. When developing your own courtroom personality, it is important to remain true to your natural presence and to take an approach to delivering your closing argument that is not fabricated. The following fundamentals are important to consider, no matter the approach you take while speaking during an OUI trial.
Volume
Speak at a volume appropriate for the size of the courtroom. The dimensions of courtrooms across the Commonwealth of Massachusetts vary greatly. Many of the courthouses are older and have acoustic problems. You also need to remember that some members of your jury or your judge may have difficulty hearing. Remain cognizant of these issues and adjust your delivery accordingly.
Tone
Use an appropriate tone. The facts of your case will dictate what tone you use during your closing argument. If your defense is that the police officer lied in the police report, then you may be more indignant, but if your defense is that the police officer was mistaken that your client was driving, your tone can be more soft-spoken.
Position
Find an appropriate position to stand in the courtroom while delivering your closing argument. This spot will be different depending on whether you tried the case to a jury or a judge. In a jury trial, your position should be a comfortable distance from and directly in front of the jury box. Respect the personal space of the members of the jury. Getting too close may make the jurors feel uncomfortable and cause them to negatively view you and, indirectly, your client. In the case of a bench trial, you will most often deliver your closing argument from a standing position at the defense table.
Notes
If at all possible, do not use notes. The ability to deliver a closing argument without notes may be something that you will need to eventually work up to, but it is a skill worth possessing. You will be less encumbered without notes, and your delivery will seem less scripted.
Podium
Do not use a podium during a jury trial. Standing behind a table or podium creates a barrier between the members of the jury and you and impedes your ability to connect with them. This point is less important during a bench trial because the nature of the proceeding is generally less theatrical.
Eye Contact
You should attempt to look directly at each member of the jury or the judge several times during your closing argument. Making eye contact with the fact finders will help you establish a stronger connection with them and indirectly convey to them that you respect their opinion and position at trial. If you do use notes, do not simply read from them without looking up from the page.
LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

entries.title: Communicating with Jury
entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 11-14 Trial
entries.sourceFile: __12.07 Communicating with Jury.docx
entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 12.07
LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 12 CLOSING ARGUMENTS > PART II: PREPARING YOUR CLOSING ARGUMENT
§ 12.07 Communicating with Jury
Delivering a great closing argument during a jury trial can convert those members of the jury who are still undecided about the verdict and solidify the positions of the jurors who have already taken your client’s side. Keep in mind that at the point of the trial where you will deliver your closing argument, the jury or judge has been sitting and listening to the case for at least the greater part of a day, and sometimes even longer. They are emotionally and physically tired, and they are feeling anxious to finish the trial.
OUI cases are typically straightforward and do not consist of a great deal of evidence or complicated material. To maintain the attention of the members of the jury or the judge, make sure that you start strong and that your closing is no longer than absolutely necessary. To achieve this end, try to deliver succinct, concentrated statements. The members of the jury have already heard all the evidence. Do not mince words; get to the point of your arguments. A closing argument that is too long will be counterproductive. You will lose the attention of the jurors and water down the important facts if you bombard them with too much information.
The members of a jury are more likely to come to the same conclusion regarding a verdict if they all begin their deliberations with the same basis of information. A failure to deliver a highly concentrated list of your strongest arguments will require the jurors to put forth greater effort during their deliberation to arrive at a decision in favor of your client. The harder a juror has to work to understand your position and accept your arguments, the less likely they will return a not guilty verdict. Try to break your arguments into simple, small points, so it is as easy as possible for the jurors to unite and reach a verdict for the defense.
LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

Warning:
Do not state personal opinions about the evidence or the case in general. The judge will not permit you to offer your own thoughts because they are irrelevant, as it is the jury or the judge that has the responsibility to weigh the evidence. Offering your personal thoughts on the case will also dilute your argument. Simply tell the fact finders what they should think about the evidence or testimony. The following are several examples of phrases to avoid when prefacing a statement and several phrases that are appropriate:
“The witness was clearly not credible because …”; not “I believe that the witness was not credible because …”
“The evidence points you to one possible verdict …”; not “I think that the evidence points you to one possible verdict …”
“The photographs show that the parking lot is not a public way …”; not “In my opinion, the photographs show that the parking lot is not a public way …”
Strategic Point:
Use the words “we” and “us,” instead of “you,” when telling the jurors what they saw or heard during the trial. This technique will organically encourage the members of the jury to align with the defense.
Example 1: “The arresting officer told us that he stopped my client because …”
Example 2: “When we saw the photographs of the scene …”
Do not forget that the members of the jury are lay people. Use common language and avoid technical words and phrases that are frequently used by members of law enforcement, because jurors may have difficulty relating to this jargon and may not fully understand it. Below are several examples:
“You stopped the car”; not “You initiated a motor vehicle stop”
“You told my client to get out of the car”; not “You issued an exit order”
“You arrested my client”; not “You took my client into custody”

entries.title: Influential Language
entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 11-14 Trial
entries.sourceFile: __12.08 Influential Language.docx
entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 12.08
LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 12 CLOSING ARGUMENTS > PART II: PREPARING YOUR CLOSING ARGUMENT
§ 12.08 Influential Language
Another valuable skill that will assist you in delivering persuasive closing arguments is the ability to incorporate the words and phrases that witnesses used while testifying during trial and the language contained in the model jury instructions for OUI. Listen to what the witnesses specifically say during the trial and take notes so that you can quote them during your closing argument. Witnesses will commonly make statements that are quite graphic and unique. Repeating a witness’s manner of describing a person or event creates consistency, highlights the testimony, and helps the members of the jury or the judge remember it.
In this scenario, the witness’s answer arms you with a colorful phrase to incorporate into your closing argument, and one that the jury or judge will easily remember.
In addition to quoting witness testimony, develop a working knowledge of the language contained in the OUI jury instructions and subtly track it during your closing arguments. Most judges will not permit you to directly instruct the members of the jury about the instructions, but will allow you to paraphrase them. This skill will help you show the jury that the facts of the Commonwealth’s case are insufficient to meet its burden of proof.
The above example demonstrates how to use language from the model jury instructions in a conversational manner, while avoiding the need to directly reference the instructions themselves.
LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

Example:
You represent John for his OUI case. At trial, you present testimony from John’s friend, who bailed him out from the police department after John’s arrest. You engage in the following line of questions:
Q: Did you make any observations of John after you picked him up from the police department?
A: Yeah, he was stone-cold sober.
Example:
The police officer who arrested your client, John, testifies on cross-examination that when he turned on his emergency lights, John promptly responded by putting on his turn signal and pulling into the breakdown lane without incident. John later admitted to the police officer that he had consumed two beers prior to driving. The model jury instructions for OUI state, in part: “A person is under the influence of alcohol if he (she) has consumed enough alcohol to reduce his (her) ability to operate a motor vehicle safely, by decreasing his (her) alertness, judgment and ability to respond promptly.” In your closing argument, you would argue the following:
“You heard the officer testify that when he flipped on his blue lights, John responded promptly by turning on his blinker and safely pulling into the breakdown lane exactly as he should have done. Ladies and gentlemen, John’s appropriate and timely reaction to the officer’s signal to pull over clearly demonstrates that John was alert and not under the influence after drinking two beers.”

§ 12.09 Exhibits and Demonstrative Aids
The use of exhibits and demonstrative aids during your closing argument can tremendously buttress your defense and assist in effectively organizing the evidence so that the members of the jury or judge will easily be able to comprehend your positions. Use the materials that have been entered into evidence and consider creating diagrams or flowcharts either before your closing argument or as you deliver it. A simple map of a roadway or checklist of the OUI elements can be useful when describing a series of events or highlighting problems with the testimony from a Commonwealth witness.

entries.title: Commonwealth s Closing Argument
entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 11-14 Trial
entries.sourceFile: __12.11 Commonwealth_s Closing Argument.docx
entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 12.11
LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 12 CLOSING ARGUMENTS > PART III: CONTENT OF CLOSING ARGUMENT
§ 12.11 Commonwealth’s Closing Argument
Prosecutor Speaks Last
The Commonwealth has the burden of proof, and thus the prosecutor will deliver his or her closing argument after you. Unfortunately, this order means that the prosecutor will have the last words in the trial, so you need to deliver a closing argument that resonates with the members of the jury or the judge. Having the burden of proof means that the Commonwealth will have presented the lion’s share of the evidence, and its witnesses will have testified extensively during the course of the trial. Prosecutors typically consider proving an OUI charge to be a numbers game; to win, they will attempt to generate as many facts and observations they can to show that your client was under the influence of alcohol on the date he or she was arrested for OUI. Operating with this premise, the prosecutor will devote a great deal of his or her closing argument to carefully listing every single helpful piece of evidence and simply point to all of it for the jurors as the reason why your client is guilty. Below is an outline of the typical approach prosecutors take when delivering a closing argument at an OUI trial.
Introduction/Theme/Analogy/Story
If the prosecutor offered a theme, analogy, or story during his or her opening statement, he or she will almost certainly briefly revisit it during the closing argument. This approach will generally consist of encouraging the members of the jury to look at all the evidence as a full picture, and not evaluate each piece of evidence individually.
Defense’s Case
The prosecutor will next attack any evidence that you entered as a defense and attempt to undermine any testimony you offered. The prosecutor will also seek to address any weaknesses you exposed while cross-examining the Commonwealth’s witnesses.
Commonwealth’s Case
During this section, the prosecutor will run through an almost exhaustive list of every piece of evidence and every part of the testimony that would arguably prove that your client was under the influence of alcohol on the date of the incident. The prosecutor will try to buttress the incriminating evidence by showing that it is corroborated by other sources.
Request Guilty Verdict
The prosecutor will ask the members of the jury or the judge to find your client guilty of OUI based on the overwhelming amount of evidence.
LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

Warning:
If the Commonwealth misstates the facts or the law or makes an inappropriate argument, make sure to object. If you do not make a timely objection, the issue may be waived. Commonwealth v. Cautela, 87 Mass. App. Ct. 1103, 24 N.E.3d 1060 (2015) (unpublished) (finding that incorrect statement by prosecutor was harmless because it was not significant enough to make an objection).
Warning:
Do not react adversely when the prosecutor discusses damaging evidence. The members of the jury or the judge will notice your reaction, and that particular piece of evidence will stand out in their minds.

entries.title: Defense s Closing Argument
entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 11-14 Trial
entries.sourceFile: __12.12 Defense_s Closing Argument.docx
entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 12.12
LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 12 CLOSING ARGUMENTS > PART III: CONTENT OF CLOSING ARGUMENT
§ 12.12 Defense’s Closing Argument
Delivering a Forceful Argument
Closing arguments are not the time to merely repeat your opening statement or to summarize what occurred over the course of the trial, because the members of the jury or the judge have already heard all the evidence. The closing argument is the opportunity to go on the offensive by delivering your legal theories and arguing to the members of the jury or the judge that the evidence supports them. Outlines for closing arguments vary greatly, as they are dependent on the evidence in a particular case, the number of witnesses presented, the types of witnesses presented, the introduction of a breath test reading, and whether evidence was offered as part of a defense. Below is a general outline for a closing argument for an OUI trial.
Introduction/Theme/Analogy/Story
If you told the members of the jury or the judge an analogy or story during your opening statement or that there was a theme of your case, you should address it again during your closing argument. By revisiting the theme, analogy, or story you can bring the entire trial around full circle, maintain consistency, and avoid the appearance of being disjointed. A failure to revisit the matter during your closing argument may cause the members of the jury or the judge to forget the theme, analogy, or story altogether. Alternatively, they might think that you did not successfully demonstrate why it was applicable and discount you and your evidence.
Presumption of Innocence/Burden of Proof
Remind the members of the jury or the judge that your client is presumed to be innocent unless, and until, the Commonwealth is able to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that your client operated a motor vehicle on a public way while under the influence of intoxicating liquor or with a blood-alcohol content of 0.08 or greater. Expressly tell the members of the jury or the judge that the Commonwealth has not met this standard and your client is not guilty.
Issues at Trial
This section of the outline is only applicable if you stipulated to certain elements or if the state of the evidence makes it obvious that you are only contesting one or two of the OUI elements. Many defense attorneys frequently decline to offer a significant challenge to the elements of “operation” and “public way” because they are often straightforward and factually indefensible. If you decide to narrow your defense to one of the elements or to just a few particular points, draw the attention of the members of the jury or the judge to your position. By framing the issues, you will decrease the time that the fact finders waste analyzing the other parts of the trial.
Commonwealth’s Case
Your trial strategy for the majority of OUI trials that you handle will be to simply question and undermine the evidence the prosecutor presents through his or her witnesses. This strategy generally consists of attacking the strengths of the Commonwealth’s case and emphasizing its weaknesses. It is important to first address the Commonwealth’s case, and specifically its strengths, because you want the last arguments that the fact finders hear to be about the problems with the prosecution’s evidence. This order will give you the best chance to leave the members of the jury or judge with a perception of the evidence that is favorable to the defense. The standard argument used to attack the Commonwealth’s case is essentially that the facts do not support the elements of OUI-specifically, the facts the Commonwealth is relying on to prove its case are either incorrect or they are undermined by other evidence, and even if they are true, the facts do not meet the Commonwealth’s lofty burden of proof.
Some attacks on the Commonwealth’s case are more indirect and not factually based. With this type of issue, remember to draw the attention of the members of the jury or the judge to the less obvious points that you developed during trial. Some of the issues that you will raise during a trial are quite subtle and may be overlooked by some members of the jury.
In a situation like the above example, you should remember to tell the members of the jury or the judge that the police officer did not appear forthcoming during his cross-examination. Inform them that they can consider the credibility of the police officer’s testimony based on his appearance and composure during the trial. These indirect attacks on the Commonwealth’s case can be as effective as more straightforward factual arguments and should not be forgotten during your closing argument.
Defense’s Case
If you elected to present evidence in defense of your client, you should address the weaknesses of your case before you emphasize the strengths. By reversing the order that you dealt with the Commonwealth’s case, you can quickly neutralize your weak points and leave the jury on a high note with your strongest points.
Brief Summary of Arguments
This section of the closing argument outline sets up your requested verdict and leaves the jurors with a quick sound bite summarizing the exact reason why your client is not guilty of OUI. This statement is the last substantive message that you will deliver to the jury, so be thoughtful about its contents and deliver it with emphasis. Several examples are listed below:
Presumption of Innocence/Burden of Proof
Quickly remind the jury one final time that your client is presumed innocent and that the Commonwealth has failed to meet its burden of proof.
Request Not Guilty Verdict
Ask the members of the jury or the judge to find your client not guilty. This part of the trial is quite simple but important.
LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

Example:
The prosecutor finishes his direct examination of the police officer who conducted the booking procedure for your client, and you begin your cross-examination. You quickly notice that while the police officer provided a detailed answer to each of the prosecutor’s questions, he paused significantly after the majority of your questions before claiming that he could not remember the answers.
Example:
You offer testimony from your client’s friend who was the last person to see your client at a birthday party before he was arrested for OUI. You client’s friend testifies that he saw your client drink two beers at the party and that he appeared to be perfectly fine before leaving. The friend admits on cross-examination that he was not with your client during the entire party. In this example, the prosecution will likely argue that because your client’s friend was not with your client for the whole party, he has no idea how much your client really drank before being arrested. You make the following argument:
“Sure, my client’s friend wasn’t with him the entire time at the party so he can’t tell you every single thing that my client did while he was there. What he did tell you, however, is that my client was perfectly fine before he left that night.”
By making these remarks, you acknowledge the prosecutor’s impending argument, neutralize it, and leave the jury with the key fact that this witness supplied to your case: your client was not under the influence of alcohol when he was arrested for OUI.
Example 1:
“Ladies and gentlemen, due to the conflicting testimony by the two police officers that we heard from today, we really have no idea what to believe regarding what really happened after my client was stopped.”
Example 2:
“As the doctor told you during his testimony, the results of the breath test machine were not accurate because of my client’s medical condition.”
Example 3:
“This case comes down to the simple fact that the gated parking lot where my client was stopped was not a public way, because it belonged to a private fishing club and was not accessible to the public in general.”
Example:
Ladies and gentlemen, at this time, due to the insufficiency of the evidence that you have seen and heard, I ask you to find my client not guilty of operating a motor vehicle while under the influence of alcohol.

§ 13.01 Scope
This chapter deals with the different evidentiary issues you will encounter when trying to introduce expert testimony. There are multiple factual issues you will encounter when deciding to introduce a witness. These include: the reliability of field sobriety tests; whether field tests were done correctly; whether blood was drawn and stored correctly; medical conditions that may affect the breath test reading; whether the victim’s injuries were “serious bodily” injuries; and whether a medical condition of your client caused the conduct that led to the arrest.

1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 13.02
LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 13 EXPERT TESTIMONY > PART I: STRATEGY
§ 13.02 Objective and Strategy
The objective of this chapter is to establish an understanding of the different issues that may require expert testimony and how to get that expert testimony introduced at trial. If you have questions about the qualifications or reliability of proposed expert testimony from the Commonwealth, defense counsel can ask to voir dire the expert outside of the presence of the jury. This request should be made pretrial with enough time for the Court to rule on it and hold the voir dire prior to trial. “The judge is not required to hold a voir dire before qualifying an expert, and the judge's determination may be inferred from the record.” Commonwealth v. White, 105 Mass. App. Ct. 1143, 265 N.E.3d 619 (2025), review denied, 497 Mass. 1102 (2026) (quoting Commonwealth v. Calderon, 65 Mass. App. Ct. 590, 593 (2006)).

Expert testimony is only allowed in certain circumstances.
The expert must be qualified to render the opinion.
The expert testimony must be reliable.
Common scenarios for expert testimony are to challenge the Commonwealth’s case and to establish an important fact for the defendant’s case-in-chief.
Retrograde extrapolation is no longer required when introducing the results of a breath test given within a reasonable time after operating.
