entries.title: Subject Must Require Expert Testimony
entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 11-14 Trial
entries.sourceFile: __13.04 Subject Must Require Expert Testimony.docx
entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 13.04
LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 13 EXPERT TESTIMONY > PART II: INTRODUCING EXPERT TESTIMONY
§ 13.04 Subject Must Require Expert Testimony
Normally, expert testimony by the prosecution will not be necessary. Testimony by a police officer or a civilian witness that a person was under the influence of alcohol is admissible as lay opinion. The reason for this is that citizens in the normal life experience encounter individuals who are intoxicated and in their regular experience are able to identify someone who is intoxicated. Expert testimony is allowed only if the proffered testimony is beyond the common knowledge or common experience of the jury. Commonwealth v. Richardson, 423 Mass. 180, 667 N.E.2d 257 (1996). Moreover, expert testimony is admissible whenever it will aid the jury in reaching its decision, even if the expert’s opinion touches on ultimate issues that the jury must decide. See Commonwealth v. Federico, 425 Mass. 844, 683 N.E.2d 1035 (1997). The ultimate decision to admit or exclude particular expert testimony depends on the circumstances of the case. See Commonwealth v. Francis, 390 Mass. 89, 453 N.E.2d 1204 (1983).
LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

entries.title: Expert Must Be Qualified to Render Opinion
entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 11-14 Trial
entries.sourceFile: __13.05 Expert Must Be Qualified to Render Opinion.docx
entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 13.05
LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 13 EXPERT TESTIMONY > PART II: INTRODUCING EXPERT TESTIMONY
§ 13.05 Expert Must Be Qualified to Render Opinion
Once it is determined that the testimony is beyond the common experience of the jury, it must then be shown that the witness has “sufficient skill, knowledge, and experience in this area of his training to aid the jury.” See Commonwealth v. Simmons, 419 Mass. 426, 646 N.E.2d 97 (1995). For the most part, the admission of expert testimony is within the sound discretion of the trial judge and does not even have to be on the record. See Commonwealth v. Ruiz, 442 Mass. 826, 833, 817 N.E.2d 771 (2004).
First, the party that is moving to have the expert recognized as a witness needs to make a showing that the reasoning and/or methodology underlying the testimony is scientifically valid and can be applied to the contested facts. However, even if this showing is made, the party opposing the introduction of the expert testimony may still object. See Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharms., Inc., 509 U.S. 579, 592–593, 113 S. Ct. 2786, 125 L. Ed. 2d 469 (1993). At the end of the day, the judge will make the decision, and that decision can only be challenged on appeal if it is shown that the judge committed an “abuse of discretion [or if the decision is] otherwise tainted with error of law.” Commonwealth v. Richardson, 423 Mass. 180, 182, 667 N.E.2d 257 (1996); see Commonwealth v. Guinan, 86 Mass. App. Ct. 445, 17 N.E.3d 439 (2014) (reversing conviction because of admission of expert testimony of trooper who was unqualified to testify regarding computer software and electronic power steering even though he was qualified to testify regarding mechanical integrity of the vehicle). “In the absence of evidence suggesting that the reliability of the witness’s testimony is in doubt or that the witness is under an actual conflict of interest, the remedy for the defendant’s concerns is in forceful cross-examination and argument, not in exclusion.” Commonwealth v. Baxter, 94 Mass. App. Ct. 587, 592, 116 N.E.3d 54, 59 (2018), review denied, 481 Mass. 1108, 123 N.E.3d 186 (2019).
LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

Practice Tip:
Make sure that the expertise of the witness matches the testimony. The Commonwealth’s expert witness may be precluded from testifying if the specific testimony (or part of the testimony) is beyond the witness’s expertise. Commonwealth v. Guinan, 86 Mass. App. Ct. 445, 17 N.E.3d 439 (2014) (reversing guilty finding because expert testified regarding subject beyond area of expertise). The Court may also exclude the testimony when the expertise is not tied specifically to the opinion rendered. Commonwealth v. Burden, 97 Mass. App. Ct. 1118, 145 N.E.3d 908, review denied, 485 Mass. 1103, 150 N.E.3d 1122 (2020) (“there was no evidence that she was qualified at that time to give any specific testimony about how anxiety can impact a person’s performance on field sobriety tests.”)

entries.title: Proffered Testimony Must Be Reliable
entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 11-14 Trial
entries.sourceFile: __13.06 Proffered Testimony Must Be Reliable.docx
entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 13.06
LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 13 EXPERT TESTIMONY > PART II: INTRODUCING EXPERT TESTIMONY
§ 13.06 Proffered Testimony Must Be Reliable
In order to have an expert’s testimony admitted at trial, the party seeking to admit the testimony must lay a foundation: (1) “by showing that the underlying scientific theory is generally accepted within the relevant scientific community”; or (2) “by showing that the theory is reliable or valid through other means.” See Commonwealth v. Sands, 424 Mass. 184, 185–186, 675 N.E.2d 370 (1997).
Beware of the expert who opines on issues in areas where he or she is not truly an expert. Expert testimony is improper to the extent that the witness testifies to matters beyond his or her area of expertise or competence. See Commonwealth v. Frangipane, 433 Mass. 527, 744 N.E.2d 25 (2001). Also, be on the lookout for testimony that is not explanatory in nature. Sometimes, when determining whether particular expert testimony is lawful, the better practice may be to focus the analysis on whether the evidence is explanatory. See Commonwealth v. Bienvenu, 63 Mass. App. Ct. 632, 828 N.E.2d 543 (2005).
LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

Practice Tip:
The Court must make the determinations regarding the need for expert testimony, the qualifications of the expert, and the reliability of the testimony outside the presence of the jury prior to the jury hearing any expert testimony. Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharms., Inc., 509 U.S. 579, 589, 113 S. Ct. 2786, 125 L. Ed. 2d 469 (1993). Some courts have held that, “[w]here a trial judge conducts a bench trial, the judge need not conduct a Daubert (or Rule 702) analysis before presentation of the evidence, even though he must determine admissibility at some point.” Kansas City S. Ry. Co. v. Sny Island Levee Drainage Dist., 831 F.3d 892, 900 (7th Cir. 2016).

entries.title: Common Scenarios Where Expert Defense Testimony Is Needed
entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 11-14 Trial
entries.sourceFile: __13.07 Common Scenarios Where Expert Defense Testimony Is Needed.docx
entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 13.07
LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 13 EXPERT TESTIMONY > PART II: INTRODUCING EXPERT TESTIMONY
§ 13.07 Common Scenarios Where Expert Defense Testimony Is Needed
There are two scenarios in which you may want to use an expert. They are: (1) to challenge the Commonwealth’s case; and (2) to establish an important fact for the defendant’s case in chief.
Prior to trial, you should file a discovery motion to find out if the Commonwealth will call an expert at trial. If the Commonwealth plans to call an expert at trial, you will need to review the expert’s field of expertise, as well as his or her training and experience. Being armed with this information will be instructive as to whether or not you will need an expert to rebut and challenge the Commonwealth’s expert. There will be many times when you will need to consider retaining the services of your own expert to review and challenge the opposing expert’s opinion.
Other times, you may need an expert to prove your own case. For instance, if your client says that he or she only had one beer and the police officer claims that your client was acting very intoxicated, you may need a witness to prove that one beer in combination with some legal activity (prescription medication, dehydration, etc.) caused the erratic behavior. You can also show that your client’s medication led to an incorrect breath test reading.
Normally, the issue of an expert arises in OUI cases when the Commonwealth tries to introduce evidence related to the prosecution for OUI-drugs, there is a blood test that requires conversion, or an accident reconstruction is needed. Importantly, it has been noted by Massachusetts courts that when possible, the practice of permitting police witnesses to provide expert testimony should be avoided, given that it is easy for specific observations and expert generalizations to become blurred. See Commonwealth v. Tanner, 45 Mass. App. Ct. 576, 700 N.E.2d 282 (1998).
As noted elsewhere, the Commonwealth can proceed on two theories of liability under the OUI statute. If the Commonwealth proceeds on a so-called “impaired ability” theory, but also intends to offer evidence of a breath test result of 0.08 or higher for that theory, it must present expert testimony on the significance of that level as it pertains to the defendant’s alleged impairment. See Commonwealth v. Colturi, 448 Mass. 809, 811, 864 N.E.2d 498, 500 (2007).
LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

Warning:
The failure to call an expert to rebut the Commonwealth’s expert may be ineffective assistance of counsel. Commonwealth v. Tompkins, 105 Mass. App. Ct. 1124, 257 N.E.3d 913 (2025) (affirming the allowance of a new trial motion based on ineffective assistance of counsel for failing to call or consult with a rebutal expert).

entries.title: Retrograde Extrapolation
entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 11-14 Trial
entries.sourceFile: __13.08 Retrograde Extrapolation.docx
entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 13.08
LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 13 EXPERT TESTIMONY > PART II: INTRODUCING EXPERT TESTIMONY
§ 13.08 Retrograde Extrapolation
The Commonwealth is not required to present evidence on the subject of retrograde extrapolation when a breath test is conducted within a reasonable time after the driver ceased operating his or her vehicle. The concept of retrograde extrapolation comes into play with older cases and the so-called “look-back rule.”
LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

Warning:
Make sure the expert testimony is explanatory, and not presented in conclusory form, in terms of whether the defendant did or did not commit a particular offense, to avoid infringing on the defendant’s right to a fair trial. See Commonwealth. v. Grissett, 66 Mass. App. Ct. 454, 848 N.E.2d 441 (2006). Indeed, qualified opinion testimony, properly admitted, informs jurors generally of the significance of evidence related to a fact-based issue, which ultimately must be decided by the jury alone. See Commonwealth v. Acosta, 81 Mass. App. Ct. 836, 969 N.E.2d 720 (2012).

entries.title: Lay Opinion Testimony
entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 11-14 Trial
entries.sourceFile: __13.09 Lay Opinion Testimony.docx
entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 13.09
LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 13 EXPERT TESTIMONY > PART II: INTRODUCING EXPERT TESTIMONY
§ 13.09 Lay Opinion Testimony
At times, lay people may also be permitted to give what amounts to “opinion” testimony on certain topics. For instance, one court noted that: “A layperson may provide an opinion, in summary form, about another person’s sobriety, provided there exists a basis for the opinion.” Commonwealth v. Orben, 53 Mass. App. Ct. 700, 703–704, 761 N.E.2d 991 (2002). This will almost always include whether the layperson thought the defendant was intoxicated by alcohol. Commonwealth v. Saulnier, 84 Mass. App. Ct. 603, 605, 999 N.E.2d 148, 151 (2013) (“the officer’s opinion about the defendant’s level of sobriety was admissible”).
Always be on the lookout for evidence introduced through other means that should be introduced through an expert. For instance, it has been found inappropriate for a prosecutor to provide a jury with an analysis of a mathematical probability, especially the mathematical probability that an eyewitness identification is accurate. This analysis must be offered through expert testimony, not the prosecutor’s closing argument. See Commonwealth v. Ferreira, 460 Mass. 781, 955 N.E.2d 898 (2011).
LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

Exception:
“In a prosecution for operating a motor vehicle while under the influence of alcohol, lay witnesses, including police officers, may not opine as to the ultimate question whether the defendant was operating while under the influence … .” Commonwealth v. Jones, 464 Mass. 16, 17 n.1, 979 N.E.2d 1088 (2012); Commonwealth v. Saulnier, 84 Mass. App. Ct. 603, 605–06, 999 N.E.2d 148, 151 (2013).
Exception:
“A police officer may testify to observed physical characteristics of the driver such as blood shot eyes, drowsiness, and lack of coordination [regarding marijuana use]. The officer is not permitted to offer an opinion that these characteristics mean that the driver is under the influence of marijuana.” Commonwealth v. Gerhardt, 477 Mass. 775, 787–88, 81 N.E.3d 751, 762 (2017).
Exception:
The prosecutor cannot try to bolster the lay opinions of officers with their training. Specifically, it is “improper for the prosecutor to frame the questioning in such a way that jurors might have ‘misunderstood [the answer] … as testimony based on scientific, technical, or other specialized knowledge … .’ ” Commonwealth v. Dow, 101 Mass. App. Ct. 1113, 193 N.E.3d 472, review denied, 490 Mass. 1107, 196 N.E.3d 749 (2022).
Strategic Point:
When asking a layperson about your client’s intoxication, be sure to cross-examine on the facts on which the witness is basing his or her opinion. For instance, you may want to ask if the witness smelled alcohol, watched your client drinking, noticed anything about your client’s demeanor, had ever met your client before, and had ever been with your client before when your client was drinking, and, if so, how your client behaved while intoxicated.

entries.title: Preparing Witnesses for Trial
entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 11-14 Trial
entries.sourceFile: __13.10 Preparing Witnesses for Trial.docx
entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 13.10
LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 13 EXPERT TESTIMONY > PART II: INTRODUCING EXPERT TESTIMONY
§ 13.10 Preparing Witnesses for Trial
In advance of trial, any expert witness needs to be very familiar with both the Commonwealth’s case and the defense case. There should not be any surprises during cross-examination. The expert should be provided with all the necessary information, including copies of: (1) breath test results; (2) police reports; (3) photos; (4) witness lists; and (5) any videos that were made. Defendants must provide the district attorney with notice of the experts who will be called to testify. Notice should include the expert’s C.V. and name and address. Failure to give the Commonwealth notice can result in the witness’s testimony being excluded, a potentially fatal blow to your defense. Mass. R. Crim. P. 14.
LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

Warning:
If you decide to retain an expert at the last minute, you must immediately notify the prosecutor and file a motion in limine to allow the testimony. Also attach an affidavit identifying the reasons for the late request.

§ 14.01 Scope
This chapter sets forth the various jury instructions a practitioner should consider requesting-when defending a client charged with OUI-and/or opposing-when the instruction is requested by the Commonwealth-depending on the factual circumstances of the case. Criminal jury instructions for use in the Massachusetts District Court are set forth in the Criminal District Court Model Jury Instructions (“Model Jury Instructions”).

entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 11-14 Trial
entries.sourceFile: __14.02 Objective and Strategy.docx
entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 14.02
LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 14 JURY INSTRUCTIONS > PART I: STRATEGY
§ 14.02 Objective and Strategy
The objective of this chapter is to provide practitioners with a list of potential jury instructions that may be used at the close of the OUI trial. A practitioner defending a client charged with OUI should consider requesting the following jury instructions: (1) presumption of innocence; (2) burden of proof; (3) proof beyond a reasonable doubt; (4) operation of a motor vehicle; (5) definition of “public way”; (6) definition of “OUI-alcohol”; (7) operating with a blood-alcohol content of 0.08% or greater; (8) definition of “OUI-drugs”; (9) credibility of a witness; and (10) absent witnesses.
LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law

entries.title: Timely Submission of Jury Instructions
entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 11-14 Trial
entries.sourceFile: __14.04 Timely Submission of Jury Instructions.docx
entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 14.04
LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 14 JURY INSTRUCTIONS > PART II: TIMING OF SUBMISSION
§ 14.04 Timely Submission of Jury Instructions
Massachusetts Rule of Civil Procedure 24(b) provides that: “At the close of the evidence or at such earlier time during the trial as the judge reasonably directs, any party may file written requests that the judge instruct the jury on the law as set forth in the requests.” After submission of each side’s jury instructions, the judge “shall inform counsel of his proposed action” as to specific jury instructions prior to closing. Mass. R. Crim. P. 24(b). Importantly, in order to preserve any appeal rights with respect to the judge’s refusal to use a proposed jury instruction, the practitioner must object on the record prior to the start of jury deliberations.
LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

Practice Tip:
Pay close attention to the instructions the court reads to the jury. Sometimes, judges will add extra, personalized instructions in addition to the instructions worked out between the parties and judge prior to trial. Improper instructions are grounds for a mistrial, and defense counsel needs to be prepared to object to them. Commonwealth v. Firmin, 89 Mass. App. Ct. 62, 65–66, 46 N.E.3d 558 (2016) (reversing conviction for inappropriate instruction judge made for the jury to reach a verdict).

entries.title: Presumption of Innocence; Burden of Proof; Unanimity
entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 11-14 Trial
entries.sourceFile: __14.06 Presumption of Innocence; Burden of Proof; Unanimity.docx
entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 14.06
LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 14 JURY INSTRUCTIONS > PART III: SPECIFIC INSTRUCTIONS
§ 14.06 Presumption of Innocence; Burden of Proof; Unanimity
Under the law, your client is entitled to a presumption of innocence. You should request an instruction on the presumption of innocence to make this point clear and crystallize it in the minds of your jurors. Indeed, the purpose of the instruction is to instruct the jurors to focus on and only consider the actual evidence admitted at trial-not any suspicions they may have based on the facts and/or charge. Bell v. Wolfish, 441 U.S. 520, 99 S. Ct. 1861, 60 L. Ed. 2d 447 (1979). Equally as important as the “presumption of innocence instruction,” you should request that the jury be instructed that it is solely and exclusively the Commonwealth’s burden to establish your client’s guilt and that your client has no responsibility to establish his or her innocence. Lastly, you should request that the judge instruct the jury that its verdict-whether guilty or innocent-must be unanimous. To that end, Mass. Crim. Model Jury Instr. 2.160 provides:
The complaint against the defendant is only an accusation. It is not evidence. The defendant has denied that he (she) is guilty of the crime(s) charged in this complaint.
The law presumes the defendant to be innocent of (the charge) (all the charges) against him (her). This presumption of innocence is a rule of law that compels you to find the defendant not guilty unless and until the Commonwealth produces evidence, from whatever source, that proves that the defendant is guilty beyond a reasonable doubt. This burden of proof never shifts. The defendant is not required to call any witnesses or produce any evidence, since he (she) is presumed to be innocent.
The presumption of innocence stays with the defendant unless and until the evidence convinces you unanimously as a jury that the defendant is guilty beyond a reasonable doubt. It requires you to find the defendant not guilty unless his (her) guilt has been proved beyond a reasonable doubt.
Your verdict, whether it is guilty or not guilty, must be unanimous.
Commonwealth v. Boyd, 367 Mass. 169, 189, 326 N.E.2d 320, 332 (1975); Commonwealth v. Devlin; 335 Mass. 555, 569, 141 N.E.2d 269, 276–277 (1957); Commonwealth v. DeFrancesco, 248 Mass. 9, 142 N.E. 749 (1924).
LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

Timing:
You should request that the judge give the jury the presumption of innocence charge at the start of the trial so it is clear to each juror that your client has not been proven guilty of any crime.
Practice Tip:
If the judge provides an improper instruction, make sure to object. If you do not, and the jury renders a guilty verdict, your client will only succeed on appeal if the instruction created “a substantial risk of a miscarriage of justice.” Commonwealth v. Firmin, 89 Mass. App. Ct. 62, 63, 46 N.E.3d 558 (2016) (reversing conviction for improper instruction) (quoting Commonwealth v. Scanlon, 412 Mass. 664, 678, 592 N.E.2d 1279 (1992)).

entries.title: Proof Beyond Reasonable Doubt The  Webster Instruction
entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 11-14 Trial
entries.sourceFile: __14.07 Proof Beyond Reasonable Doubt_The _Webster Instruction_.docx
entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 14.07
LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 14 JURY INSTRUCTIONS > PART III: SPECIFIC INSTRUCTIONS
§ 14.07 Proof Beyond Reasonable Doubt-The “Webster Instruction”
The Commonwealth must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that your client committed that crime with which he or she is charged. This fact is critical. Mass. Crim. Model Jury Instr. 2.180 provides:
The burden is on the Commonwealth to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant is guilty of the charge(s) made against him (her).
What is proof beyond a reasonable doubt? The term is often used and probably pretty well understood, though it is not easily defined. Proof beyond a reasonable doubt does not mean proof beyond all possible doubt, for everything in the lives of human beings is open to some possible or imaginary doubt. A charge is proved beyond a reasonable doubt if, after you have compared and considered all of the evidence, you have in your minds an abiding conviction, to a moral certainty, that the charge is true. When we refer to moral certainty, we mean the highest degree of certainty possible in matters relating to human affairs-based solely on the evidence that has been put before you in this case.
I have told you that every person is presumed to be innocent until he is proved guilty, and that the burden of proof is on the prosecutor. If you evaluate all the evidence and you still have a reasonable doubt remaining, the defendant is entitled to the benefit of that doubt and must be acquitted.
It is not enough for the Commonwealth to establish a probability, even a strong probability, that the defendant is more likely to be guilty than not guilty. That is not enough. Instead, the evidence must convince you of defendant’s guilt to a reasonable and moral certainty; a certainty that convinces your understanding and satisfies your reason and judgment as jurors who are sworn to act conscientiously on the evidence.
This is what we mean by proof beyond a reasonable doubt.
Commonwealth v. Webster, 55 Mass. (5 Cush.) 295, 320 (1850).
LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

entries.title: Operation of Motor Vehicle Instruction
entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 11-14 Trial
entries.sourceFile: __14.08 Operation of Motor Vehicle Instruction.docx
entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 14.08
LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 14 JURY INSTRUCTIONS > PART III: SPECIFIC INSTRUCTIONS
§ 14.08 Operation of Motor Vehicle Instruction
It is important that the jury understand what the Commonwealth must prove to establish that your client was “operating” under the influence of alcohol and/or drugs. Mass. Crim. Model Jury Instr. 3.200 defines operation in the following manner:
A person “operates” a motor vehicle not only while doing all of the well-known things that drivers do as they travel on a street or highway, but also when doing any act which directly tends to set the vehicle in motion. The law is that a person is “operating” a motor vehicle whenever he or she is in the vehicle and intentionally manipulates some mechanical or electrical part of the vehicle-like the gear shift or the ignition-which, alone or in sequence, will set the vehicle in motion.
Commonwealth v. Ginnetti, 400 Mass. 181, 184, 508 N.E.2d 603, 605 (1987); Commonwealth v. Uski, 263 Mass. 22, 24, 160 N.E. 305, 306 (1928).
Notably, your client need not actually be driving the motor vehicle to be convicted of operating under the influence of alcohol and/or drugs. Indeed, even with a “stopped engine,” your client may be convicted of operating. Mass. Crim. Model Jury Instr. 3.200 provides:
To “operate” a motor vehicle within the meaning of the law, it is not necessary that the engine be running. A driver continues to operate his or her motor vehicle when it is stopped in the ordinary course of its operation for some reason that is fairly incidental to the vehicle’s operation. A person is also considered to be “operating” a stationary vehicle when he or she manipulates some part of it, like the gear shift, so that it moves forward of its own weight.
Commonwealth v. McGillivary, 78 Mass. App. Ct. 644, 940 N.E.2d 506 (2011), rev. denied 459 Mass. 1107, 944 N.E.2d 1043 (2011); Commonwealth v. Clarke, 254 Mass. 566, 568, 150 N.E. 829, 830 (1926); Commonwealth v. Henry, 229 Mass. 19, 22, 118 N.E. 224, 225 (1918); Commonwealth v. Cavallaro, 25 Mass. App. Ct. 605, 607–611, 521 N.E.2d 420, 421–424 (1988).
Additionally, there need be no witness to your client’s “operation” in order for a conviction to occur. The Commonwealth may use circumstantial evidence in proving its case. Mass. Crim. Model Jury Instr. 2.240 provides the following, in pertinent part, about circumstantial evidence:
… You have circumstantial evidence where the witness cannot testify directly about the fact that is to be proved, but you are presented with evidence of other facts and you are then asked to draw reasonable inferences from them about the fact which is to be proved.
… .
… There are two things to keep in mind about circumstantial evidence:
The first one is that you may draw inferences and conclusions only from facts that have been proved to you.
The second rule is that any inferences or conclusions which you draw must be reasonable and natural, based on your common sense and experience of life. In a chain of circumstantial evidence, it is not required that every one of your inferences and conclusions be inevitable, but it is required that each of them be reasonable, that they all be consistent with one another, and that together they establish the defendant’s guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.
If the Commonwealth’s case is based solely on circumstantial evidence, you may find the defendant guilty only if those circumstances are conclusive enough to leave you with a moral certainty, a clear and settled belief, that the defendant is guilty and that there is no other reasonable explanation of the facts as proven. The evidence must not only be consistent with the defendant’s guilt, it must be inconsistent with his (her) innocence.
With that in mind, and in the context of a trial for OUI, Mass. Crim. Model Jury Instr. 3.200 provides:
You may find that the defendant was the operator of the motor vehicle even if no witness saw him (her) driving the vehicle, if there is enough circumstantial evidence to prove to you beyond a reasonable doubt that the vehicle was operated and that the defendant, and no one else, was the operator of that vehicle.
LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

Practice Tip:
Make sure that your client was driving a “motor vehicle.” The instruction for that is found in Mass. Crim. Model Jury Instr. 3.210. Mopeds are the most common vehicle not to fall under the definition of “motor vehicle” in Mass. G.L. c. 90, § 1. Specifically, the definition of “motor vehicle” excludes a “electric bicycle”-i.e., “a bicycle or tricycle equipped with fully operable pedals and an electric motor of 750 watts or less that meets the requirements of a class 1 electric bicycle or a class 2 electric bicycle.” Mass. G.L. c. 90, § 1. Larger mopeds that do not fit under this exception do count as “motor vehicles.”

entries.title: Definition of  Public Way
entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 11-14 Trial
entries.sourceFile: __14.09 Definition of _Public Way_.docx
entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 14.09
LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 14 JURY INSTRUCTIONS > PART III: SPECIFIC INSTRUCTIONS
§ 14.09 Definition of “Public Way”
In order to convict your client of OUI, the Commonwealth must prove that your client was operating a motor vehicle upon a public way. Mass. Crim. Model Jury Instr. 3.280 provides:
The Commonwealth must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant operated a motor vehicle in one of three places: on a public way, or in a place to which the public has a right of access, or in a place to which members of the public have access as invitees or licensees.
You will note that the statute treats these three types of places as alternatives. If any one of the alternatives is proved, then this element of the offense is satisfied. Let me discuss the three alternatives one at a time.
Our law defines a public “way” as:
“any public highway,
[or a] private way [that is] laid out under authority of [a] statute,
[or a] way dedicated to public use,
or [a] way [that is] under [the] control
of park commissioners or [a] body having [similar] powers.”
G.L. c. 90, § 1
Interstate and state highways, as well as municipal streets and roads, would all be included in this definition. In determining whether a road is a public way, you may consider whether it has some of the usual indications of a public way-for example, whether it is paved, whether it has street lights, street signs, traffic signals, curbing and fire hydrants, whether there are abutting houses or businesses, whether it has any crossroads intersecting it, whether it is publicly maintained, and whether there is an absence of signs prohibiting public access.
LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

entries.title: OUI-Alcohol Instructions
entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 11-14 Trial
entries.sourceFile: __14.10 OUI-Alcohol Instructions.docx
entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 14.10
LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 14 JURY INSTRUCTIONS > PART III: SPECIFIC INSTRUCTIONS
§ 14.10 OUI-Alcohol Instructions
Whether your client was operating a motor vehicle under the influence of intoxicating alcohol (i.e., was “impaired”) is the ultimate question that the jury must answer. As noted above, the Commonwealth must prove this beyond a reasonable doubt. As such, the jury instruction on the definition of “OUI-alcohol” is of utmost importance. Mass. Crim. Model Jury Instr. 5.310 provides:
The defendant is charged with operating a motor vehicle while under the influence of intoxicating liquor … .
In order to prove the defendant guilty of this offense, the Commonwealth must prove three things beyond a reasonable doubt:
First: That the defendant operated a motor vehicle;
Second: That the defendant did so (on a public way) (or) (in a place where the public has a right of access) (or) (in a place where members of the public have access as invitees or licensees); and
Third: That while operating the vehicle, the defendant was under the influence of intoxicating liquor.
… .
The third element which the Commonwealth must prove beyond a reasonable doubt is that the defendant was under the influence of intoxicating liquor while operating a motor vehicle. What does it mean be “under the influence” of alcohol? It is not illegal to drive after consuming alcohol as long as the operator is not under the influence of alcohol. However, neither does someone have to be drunk to be under the influence of alcohol. A person is under the influence of alcohol if he (she) has consumed enough alcohol to reduce his (her) ability to operate a motor vehicle safely, by decreasing his (her) alertness, judgment and ability to respond promptly. It means that a person has consumed enough alcohol to reduce his (her) mental clarity, self-control and reflexes, and thereby left him (her) with a reduced ability to drive safely.
So there are three things that the Commonwealth must prove beyond a reasonable doubt:
First: That the defendant operated a motor vehicle;
Second: That the defendant did so (on a public way) (or) (in a place where the public has a right of access) (or) (in a place where members of the public have access as invitees or licensees); and
Third: That while the defendant was operating the vehicle, he (she) was under the influence of intoxicating liquor.
If the Commonwealth has proven all three elements beyond a reasonable doubt, you should return a verdict of guilty. If the Commonwealth has failed to prove one or more of these elements beyond a reasonable doubt, you must return a verdict of not guilty.
Because Massachusetts is a per se state, the Commonwealth need not prove impairment to convict your client of an OUI. Rather, the Commonwealth may convict your client of operating with a blood-alcohol content of 0.08% or greater. Mass. Crim. Model Jury Instr. 5.300 provides:
The defendant is charged with operating a motor vehicle while having a blood alcohol level of .08 percent or greater (and with operating a motor vehicle while under the influence of alcohol).
In order to prove the defendant guilty of operating a motor vehicle while having a blood alcohol level of .08 percent or greater, the Commonwealth must prove three things beyond a reasonable doubt:
First: That the defendant operated a motor vehicle;
Second: That the defendant did so (on a public way) (or) (in a place where the public has a right of access) (or) (in a place where members of the public have access as invitees or licensees); and
Third: That at the time of operation, the percent of alcohol in the defendant’s blood was .08 or greater.
… .
The third element that the Commonwealth must prove beyond a reasonable doubt is that at the time of operation the percent of alcohol in the defendant’s (breath) (blood) was .08 or greater. The law allows defendant’s blood alcohol level to be shown by a chemical test or analysis of his (her) breath or blood.
… .
So there are three things that the Commonwealth must prove beyond a reasonable doubt:
First: That the defendant operated a motor vehicle;
Second: That the defendant did so (on a public way) (or) (in a place where the public has a right of access) (or) (in a place where members the public have access as invitees or licensees); and
Third: That at the time he (she) operated the vehicle, the percent of alcohol in the defendant’s blood was .08 or greater.
If the Commonwealth has proven all three elements beyond a reasonable doubt, you should return a verdict of guilty. If the Commonwealth has failed to prove one or more of these elements beyond a reasonable doubt, you must return a verdict of not guilty.
LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

Strategic Point:
If there is no breath test evidence, typically defense attorneys will not want to bring that fact to the attention of the jurors with an instruction regarding the absence. Commonwealth v. Downs, 53 Mass. App. Ct. 195, 198, 758 N.E.2d 1062, 1064 (2001), abrogated by Commonwealth v. Wolfe, 478 Mass. 142, 83 N.E.3d 811 (2017) (“You are not to mention or consider in anyway whatsoever, either for or against either side, that there is no evidence of a breathalyzer. Do not consider that in any way. Do not mention it. And put it completely out of your mind.”). The trial court may ask the defendant to elect to instruct the jury or not prior to finalizing jury instructions. Commonwealth v. Wolfe, 478 Mass. 142, 149, 83 N.E.3d 811, 817 (2017). If the jury asks about the absence of such evidence during deliberations, the defendant again has the option for a specific instruction on the absence of the breath test or a general instruction that the jury is to only consider the evidence presented. Commonwealth v. Snow, 100 Mass. App. Ct. 1125, 182 N.E.3d 345, review denied, 490 Mass. 1102, 192 N.E.3d 260 (2022).

entries.title: Definition of  OUI-Drugs
entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 11-14 Trial
entries.sourceFile: __14.11 Definition of _OUI-Drugs_.docx
entries.text:
LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 14.11
LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 14 JURY INSTRUCTIONS > PART III: SPECIFIC INSTRUCTIONS
§ 14.11 Definition of “OUI-Drugs”
The Commonwealth must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that your client was operating under the influence of drugs. As such, the jury instruction on the definition of “OUI-drugs” is of critical importance to any defense. Mass. Crim. Model Jury Instr. 5.400 provides:
The defendant is charged with operating a motor vehicle while under the influence of (marihuana) (narcotic drugs) (depressants) (stimulant substances) (the vapors of glue).
In order to prove the defendant guilty of this offense, the Commonwealth must prove three things beyond a reasonable doubt:
First: That the defendant operated a motor vehicle;
Second: That he (she) operated it (on a way) (or) (in a place where the public has a right of access) (or) (in a place where members of the public have access as invitees or licensees); and
Third: That while the defendant was operating the vehicle, he (she) was under the influence of (marihuana) (a narcotic drug, as I will define it for you in a moment) (a depressant, as I will define it for you in a moment) (a stimulant substance, as I will define it for your in a moment) (the vapors of glue).
… .
What does it mean to be “under the influence” of (marihuana) (narcotic drugs) (depressants) (stimulant substances) (the vapors of glue)? Someone is “under the influence” of such a drug whenever he (she) has consumed enough of it to reduce his (her) ability to operate a motor vehicle safely by diminishing (his) (her) alertness, judgment, and ability to respond promptly.
This would include anyone who has consumed enough (marihuana) (narcotic drugs) (depressants) (stimulant substances) (the vapors of glue) to reduce his (her) mental clarity, self-control and reflexes, and thereby left him (her) with a reduced ability to drive safely.
The Commonwealth is not required to prove that the defendant actually drove in an unsafe or erratic manner, but it must prove that the defendant had a diminished capacity or ability to drive safely.
You are to decide this from all the believable evidence in this case, together with any reasonable inferences that you draw from the evidence. You may consider evidence about the defendant’s appearance, condition and behavior at the time, in order to determine whether the defendant’s ability to drive safely was impaired.
So there are three things the Commonwealth must prove beyond a reasonable doubt: First, that the defendant operated a motor vehicle; Second, that he (she) operated it (on a way) (in a place where the public has a right of access) (in a place where members of the public have access as invitees or licensees); and Third, that he (she) operated it while under the influence of (marihuana) (narcotic drugs) (depressants) (stimulant substances) (the vapors of glue).
… .
If any one of those three things has not been proved beyond a reasonable doubt, then you must find the defendant not guilty.
LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

Practice Tip:
When the prosecution proceeds with charges of OUI-alcohol and OUI-drugs, “field sobriety tests” should not be mentioned. Instead, the jury instructions should use the term “roadside assessments.” Commonwealth v. Gerhardt, 477 Mass. 775, 785 (2017).

entries.title: Related Crimes
entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 11-14 Trial
entries.sourceFile: __14.12 Related Crimes.docx
entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 14.12
LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 14 JURY INSTRUCTIONS > PART III: SPECIFIC INSTRUCTIONS
§ 14.12 Related Crimes
In many instances, a client arrested for OUI will be charged with additional related charges emanating from the same incident. Such crimes include operating negligently so as to endanger, operating recklessly, and leaving the scene of an accident involving personal injury not resulting in death. The elements of each of these related crimes-which the Commonwealth must prove beyond a reasonable doubt-are set forth in the applicable jury instructions below.
Negligent operation is covered by Mass. Crim. Model Jury Instr. 5.240, which provides:
The defendant is charged with operating a motor vehicle negligently in a manner that might endanger the public. Section 24(2)(a) of chapter 90 of our General Laws provides as follows:
“Whoever, upon any way
or in any place to which the public has a right of access,
or [in] any place to which members of the public have access as invitees
or licensees,
operates a motor vehicle … negligently so that the lives or safety of the public might be endangered … shall be punished … .”
In order to prove the defendant guilty of this offense, the Commonwealth must prove three things beyond a reasonable doubt:
First: That the defendant operated a motor vehicle;
Second: That he (she) did so (on a way) (or) (in a place where the public has a right of access) (or) (in a place where members of the public have access as invitees or licensees); and
Third: That he (she) did so in a negligent manner so that the lives or safety of the public might have been endangered.
The third thing the Commonwealth must prove beyond a reasonable doubt is that the defendant drove negligently in a manner that might have endangered the lives or safety of other people.
A person acts negligently when he fails to use due care, that is, when he acts in a way that a reasonable person would not act. This can happen either by doing something that a reasonably prudent person would not do under those circumstances, or by failing to do something that a reasonably prudent person would do. The defendant acted negligently if he (she) drove in a way that a reasonable person would not have, and by doing so created an unnecessary danger to other people, a danger that he (she) could have avoided by driving more carefully.
A. If there was no accident. A person can be found to have driven negligently even if no accident resulted, and even if there was no one else actually on the road to be put in danger. A person is negligent if he drives in a way that has the potential to cause an accident or to endanger anyone who might be on the road.
B. If there was an accident. The fact that an accident occurred is not by itself evidence that the defendant was negligent. You must examine all the evidence about how the accident happened in order to determine whether any negligence was involved, and if so, whether that negligence was the defendant’s.
In determining whether the defendant drove negligently in a manner that might have endangered the public, you should take into account all the facts of the situation: the defendant’s rate of speed and manner of operation, the defendant’s physical condition and how well the defendant could see and could control the vehicle, the condition of the defendant’s vehicle, what kind of a road it was and who else was on the road, what the time of day, the weather and the condition of the road were, what any other vehicles or pedestrians were doing, and any other factors that you think are relevant. If you find that the defendant acted negligently, the defendant’s intent is not relevant. You are not required to find that the defendant intended to act negligently or unlawfully. This is in that category of situations where public safety requires each driver to determine and to adhere to an objective standard of reasonable behavior. Therefore, the defendant’s subjective intent is irrelevant; the issue is whether or not the defendant drove as a reasonable person would have under the circumstances.
In determining whether the defendant drove negligently in a manner that might have endangered the public, you should take into account all the facts of the situation: the defendant’s rate of speed and manner of operation, the defendant’s physical condition and how well he (she) could see and could control his (her) vehicle, the condition of the defendant’s vehicle, what kind of a road it was and who else was on the road, what the time of day, the weather and the condition of the road were, what any other vehicles or pedestrians were doing, and any other factors that you think are relevant.
If you find that the defendant acted negligently, the defendant’s intent is not relevant. You are not required to find that the defendant intended to act negligently or unlawfully. This is in that category of situations where public safety requires each driver to determine and to adhere to an objective standard of reasonable behavior. Therefore the defendant’s subjective intent is irrelevant; the issue is whether or not he (she) drove as a reasonable person would have under the circumstances.
Operating recklessly is covered by Mass. Crim. Model Jury Instr. 5.260, which provides:
The defendant is charged with operating a motor vehicle recklessly. Section 24(2)(a) of chapter 90 of our General Laws provides as follows:
“Whoever, upon any way
or in any place to which the public has a right of access,
or [in] any place to which members of the public have access as invitees
or licensees,
operates a motor vehicle recklessly … shall be punished … .”
In order to prove the defendant guilty of this offense, the Commonwealth must prove three things beyond a reasonable doubt:
First: That the defendant operated a motor vehicle;
Second: That he (she) did so (on a way) (or) (in a place where the public has a right of access) (or) (in a place where members of the public have access as invitees or licensees); and
Third: That he (she) did so in a reckless manner.
… .
The third thing the Commonwealth must prove beyond a reasonable doubt is that the defendant drove recklessly. A person drives recklessly when he ignores the fact that his manner of driving is very likely to result in death or serious injury to someone, or he is indifferent to whether someone is killed or seriously injured.
It is not enough for the Commonwealth to prove that the defendant acted negligently-that is, acted in a way that a reasonably careful person would not. It must be shown that the defendant’s actions went beyond mere negligence and amounted to recklessness. The defendant was reckless if he (she) knew, or should have known, that such actions would pose a grave danger of death or serious injury to others, but he (she) chose, nevertheless, to run the risk and go ahead.
A. If there was no accident. A person can be found to have driven recklessly even if no accident resulted, and even if there was no one else actually on the road near him. A person is reckless if he consciously disregards, or is indifferent to, a significant possibility of serious injury to anyone else who might be on the road.
B. If there was an accident. The fact that an accident occurred is not by itself evidence that the defendant was reckless. You must examine all the evidence about how the accident happened in order to determine whether the defendant was at fault, and if so, whether the defendant’s actions rose to the level of recklessness.
In determining whether the defendant drove recklessly, you should take into account all the facts of the situation: the defendant’s rate of speed and manner of operation, the defendant’s physical condition and how well he (she) could see and could control his (her) vehicle, the condition of the defendant’s vehicle, what kind of a road it was and who else was on the road, what the time of day, the weather and the condition of the road were, what any other vehicles or pedestrians were doing, and any other factors that you think are relevant.
The defendant must have intended his (her) acts, in the sense that they were not accidental. But it is not necessary that the defendant. intended or foresaw the consequences of those acts, as long as a reasonable person would know that they were so dangerous that death or serious injury would probably result. This is in that category of cases where public safety requires each driver, once he knows what the situation is, to determine and to adhere to an objective standard of behavior.
Leaving the scene of an accident involving personal injury not resulting in death is covered by Mass. Crim. Model Jury Instr. 5.190, which provides:
The defendant is charged with knowingly leaving the scene of an accident involving personal injury. In order to prove the defendant guilty of this offense, the Commonwealth must prove four things beyond a reasonable doubt:
First: That the defendant operated a motor vehicle;
Second: That (he) (she) operated it (on a way) (or) (in a place where the public has a right of access) (or) (upon a way or in a place where members of the public have access as invitees or licensees);
Third: That the defendant knowingly collided with or otherwise injured another person;
Fourth: That after such collision or injury, the defendant did not stop and make known (his) (her) name, home address, and the registration number of (his) (her) motor vehicle.
LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

Practice Tip:
The jury may consider evidence of intoxication with respect to determining if the defendant acted negligently. Commonwealth v. Roach, 94 Mass. App. Ct. 1109, 113 N.E.3d 934 (2018), review denied, 481 Mass. 1104 (2019).
Practice Tip:
Previously, there were separate misdemeanor offenses for negligently driving and causing the death of an individual and recklessly driving and causing the death of an individual. The penalty for each offense was exactly the same. In 2018, Section 37 of S.2371 created separate, different penalties for the two offenses. 2018 Acts c. 69, § 37. Negligent operation causing death remains a misdemeanor. Reckless operation causing death is now a felony offense with a state prison sentence as a possible penalty.

entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 11-14 Trial

entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 14.13
LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 14 JURY INSTRUCTIONS > PART III: SPECIFIC INSTRUCTIONS
§ 14.13 Related Instructions
If the Commonwealth has introduced opinion evidence concerning your client’s sobriety, you can request an instruction on this issue. Mass. Crim. Model Jury Instr. 5.310 contains the following supplemental jury instruction:
You have heard testimony of (an opinion) (opinions) about the defendant’s sobriety. Ultimately, it is for you as the jury to determine whether the defendant was under the influence of alcohol according to the definition I have provided. You may consider any opinion you have heard and accept it or reject it. In the end, you and you alone must decide whether the defendant was under the influence of intoxicating liquor.
If the Commonwealth has submitted evidence concerning any field sobriety test given to your client, you should consider requesting the following supplemental jury instruction contained within Mass. Crim. Model Jury Instr. 5.310:
You have heard evidence in this case that the defendant performed “field sobriety tests.” It is for you to decide if those tests demonstrate the defendant’s ability to operate a motor vehicle safely was diminished. It is for you to determine whether to rely on this evidence. You may accept it or reject it and you may give it such weight as you think it deserves. In making your assessment, you may consider the nature of the tests, the circumstances under which they were given and performed, and all of the other evidence in this case.
If the Commonwealth failed to conduct a field sobriety test on your client, you should consider requesting the following supplemental jury instruction contained within Mass. Crim. Model Jury Instr. 5.310:
There is evidence that there were no field sobriety tests. This is a factor you may consider in evaluating the evidence presented in this case. With respect to this factor, you should consider three questions:
First: Whether the omitted tests were standard procedure or steps that would otherwise normally be taken under the circumstances;
Second: Whether the omitted tests could reasonably have been expected to lead to significant evidence of the defendant’s guilt or innocence; and
Third: Whether the evidence provides a reasonable and adequate explanation for the omission of the tests or other actions.
If you find that any omissions in the investigation were significant and not adequately explained, you may consider whether the omissions tend to affect the quality, reliability, or credibility of the evidence presented by the Commonwealth.
All of these considerations involve factual determinations that are entirely up to you, and you are free to give this matter whatever weight, if any, you deem appropriate based on all the circumstances.
If you have challenged the Commonwealth’s administration of a breath test to your client, you should consider requesting the following supplemental jury instruction contained within Mass. Crim. Model Jury Instr. 5.300:
In deciding whether the Commonwealth has proved the defendant’s blood alcohol level beyond a reasonable doubt, you may consider evidence, if any, about:
when the test was given;
the qualifications of the person who gave the test, and your assessment of his (her) credibility;
the pre-test procedures that were employed;
whether the testing device was in good working order at the time the test was administered;
whether the test was administered properly;
and any other evidence pertaining to the administration of the test.
If the Commonwealth introduces evidence that your client’s blood-alcohol level was 0.05% or less, you should consider requesting the following supplemental jury instruction contained within Mass. Crim. Model Jury Instr. 5.310:
If the percentage of alcohol by weight in the defendant’s blood was .05 percent or less, that is evidence from which you may infer that the defendant was not under the influence of intoxicating liquor. You are not required to reach that conclusion. You may consider the test result along with all the other evidence in the case to determine whether the Commonwealth has met its burden of proving beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant was under the influence of intoxicating liquor.
LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law

entries.title: Instructions Concerning Witness Testimony
entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 11-14 Trial
entries.sourceFile: __14.14 Instructions Concerning Witness Testimony.docx
entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 14.14
LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 14 JURY INSTRUCTIONS > PART III: SPECIFIC INSTRUCTIONS
§ 14.14 Instructions Concerning Witness Testimony
In all trials, but particularly in OUI trials, the testimony of witnesses plays a central role. It is the jury’s job to determine which witnesses are credible and what weight should be given to their respective testimony. As such, you should request a jury instruction on credibility. Mass. Crim. Model Jury Instr. 2.120 provides the following guidance:
Your function as the jury is to determine the facts of this case. You alone determine what evidence you believe, how important any evidence is that you do believe, and what conclusions to draw from that evidence. In making these determinations, you are to use all of your common sense, life experience, and good judgment.
You are to decide what the facts are solely from the evidence admitted in this case. In evaluating the evidence and determining the facts, keep in mind that we all tend to perceive information and form opinions based on our own personal experience and background. This tendency may cause us to hold biases of which we may or may not be conscious. As I previously instructed you, you must not allow bias-whether held consciously or subconsciously-to interfere with your ability to fairly evaluate the evidence, apply the law as I instruct you, or render a fair and impartial verdict based on the evidence before you.
The evidence consists of the testimony of witnesses, as you recall it, (any documents or other things that were received into evidence as exhibits) (and any fact on which the lawyers have agreed or which I have told you that you may accept as proved).
…
You are the sole judges of the credibility of a witness. You may believe everything a witness says, or only part of it, or none of it. If there are any conflicts, discrepancies, or inconsistencies in the testimony, you should examine them carefully. You may consider whether a witness was candid or guarded, responsive or evasive, and whether the testimony is reasonable or unreasonable, probable or improbable. You may take into account how good an opportunity a witness had to observe the facts about which the witness testifies, and whether the testimony seems accurate. You may also consider evidence, if any, about a witness’s motive for testifying, whether a witness displays any bias in testifying, and whether or not a witness has any interest in the outcome of the case.
…
In conjunction with your credibility instruction, you should request an instruction that addresses the number of witnesses each side presents. A supplemental jury instruction contained in Mass. Crim. Model Jury Instr. 2.120 provides the following:
The weight of the evidence on each side does not necessarily depend on the number of witnesses testifying for one side or the other. You are going to have to determine the credibility of each witness who has testified, and then reach a verdict based on all the believable evidence in the case. You may come to the conclusion that the testimony of a smaller number of witnesses concerning some fact is more believable than the testimony of a larger number of witnesses to the contrary.
Commonwealth v. McCauley, 391 Mass. 697, 703 n.5, 464 N.E.2d 50 (1984); Committee on Pattern Jury Instructions, District Judges Ass’n of the Eleventh Circuit, Pattern Jury Instructions-Criminal Cases § 5 (1985 ed.).
If there are the discrepancies in the testimony of witnesses presented at trial, you should request the following supplemental jury instruction contained in Mass. Crim. Model Jury Instr. 2.120:
In evaluating testimony, you may find inconsistencies or discrepancies. They may or may not cause you to discredit such testimony. Consider whether they involve important facts or only minor details, and whether any inconsistencies or discrepancies result from innocent lapses of memory or intentional falsehoods.
If the Commonwealth has made a plea agreement with a witness in exchange for truthful testimony, you should request the following supplemental jury instruction contained in Mass. Crim. Model Jury Instr. 2.120:
In this case, you heard the testimony of [prosecution witness], and you heard that he (she) is testifying under an agreement. You should examine that witness’s testimony with particular care. In evaluating his (her) credibility, along with all of the other factors I have already mentioned, you may consider that agreement and any hopes that he (she) may have about receiving future benefits.
Lastly, if the Commonwealth fails to call a witness who was expected to provide testimony, you should request the “absent witness” instruction contained in Mass. Crim. Model Jury Instr. 3.500:
In this case, you have heard some reference to a potential witness who did not testify.
… .
If the Commonwealth did not call a potential witness to testify, and four conditions are met, you may infer that the witness’s testimony would not be favorable to the Commonwealth. The four conditions are:
First: that the Commonwealth’s case against the defendant is sufficiently weak that it would normally be expected to call that witness to testify;
Second: that the absent witness would be expected to offer important testimony that would support the Commonwealth’s case;
Third: that the absent witness is available to testify for the Commonwealth; and
Fourth: that the witness’s absence is not explained by any of the other circumstances in the case.
If any of these four conditions has not been met, then you may not draw any inference from the witness’s absence. If all four conditions have been met, you may infer that the witness’s testimony would not be favorable to the Commonwealth if that is a reasonable conclusion in the circumstances of this case.
This rule is based on common sense. First, you may not draw such an inference unless the Commonwealth’s case was sufficiently weak that it would be expected to bring in the absent witness.
Second, you may not draw such an inference unless the absent witness’s testimony would be relevant to the defendant’s guilt or innocence in some significant way. Normally the Commonwealth would have no reason to bring in a witness who would only testify about minor details, or who would only repeat what has already been said by other witnesses.
Third, you may not draw such an inference unless there is evidence that the Commonwealth was able to bring the absent witness into court.
And fourth, you may not draw such an inference if the evidence suggests another reasonable explanation for the witness’s absence.
LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law Form MOL 1.01

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Forms Appendix

Form MOL 1.01 Client Agreement

[1] Practice Tip

Clients, even returning clients, should always be asked to sign a client agreement that sets forth the terms of the
specific representation. Specifying the scope of the representation is important to avoid confusion later, especially if
the fee is a flat fee.

[2] Form

LAW FIRM NAME
LAW FIRM ADDRESS
DATE
CLIENT NAME
CLIENT ADDRESS
CLIENT PHONE NUMBER
CLIENT EMAIL ADDRESS

PERSONAL AND CONFIDENTIAL

Dear (CLIENT):

We appreciate the opportunity to act as your legal counsel. This letter sets forth the basic terms upon which you
have engaged our firm to represent you, including the anticipated scope of our services and the billing policies and
practices that will apply to the engagement.

Although we expect our normal method of communication will be less formal than a written statement such as this,
we believe it is important to set forth the terms of our engagement. We request that you review this letter carefully
and, if it is consistent with your understanding of our respective responsibilities, please return a signed copy of this
letter to us at your earliest convenience.

In order to avoid confusion in the future regarding the terms of my representation, I believe it will be helpful to set
forth in this letter the basic terms of my engagement. They are as follows:

1. Scope of Engagement. In general, you have requested advice and representation involving the charge of
Operating Under the Influence that you face in [name] District Court. Our services will include research and analysis
of legal and factual issues in the matter, preparation of any legal memoranda, any necessary motions, including
motions to suppress, and we will represent you at all hearings and trial, if necessary.

2. Billing Policies and Procedures. We generally charge for legal services based on the guideline hourly rates of our
lawyers and other professionals. We will be responsible for overall supervision of the legal services provided to you

 Rafael Faria

 Form MOL 1.01 Client Agreement

by the firm. Lawyer A’s guideline hourly rate is $150.00 and Lawyer B’s guideline hourly rate is $350. For this
matter, we will charge a flat fee of $[total] for the representation. Upon execution of this agreement, full payment will
be due.

I will also bill you for each cash disbursement in accordance with our normal practices, although I do not anticipate
any with respect to this matter. I will ask you to pay any substantial expenses directly to the vendor or provider of
the service, if any, unless you have advanced the payment to me. My firm will make advances for minor expenses
on your behalf and bill you for them. I generally bill for disbursements on a monthly basis. Any additional bills for
disbursements are due and payable within fifteen (15) days. Again, I do not anticipate any with respect to this
matter.

In the event our engagement is terminated, you will continue to be obliged to pay for charges based on my normal
hourly rate up to a maximum of $[total] for services plus any other charges incurred before the termination date. In
the event any disagreement arises between the firm and you as to any amounts owed for legal services performed
or expenses incurred by the firm, both you and the firm agree that we will submit any such disputes to the Fee
Arbitration Board of the Massachusetts Bar Association for resolution.

At the conclusion of your case, it is my firm’s usual practice to retain only certain portions of your file, returning
and/or destroying documents not typically retained in storage. We shall provide you with an opportunity to retain
these files at your discretion. If you choose not to retain said files, they will be destroyed pursuant to my firm’s
retention policy.

We look forward to working with you. Please do not hesitate to call me if you have any questions concerning these
matters.

Very truly yours,
[ATTORNEY NAME]
AS AGREED:
____________________________________________
[CLIENT NAME]
Date: ______________________

1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law Form MOL 1.05

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Forms Appendix

Form MOL 1.05 Letter to Police Requesting OUI Manual

[1] Practice Tip

The relevant training manual can be helpful at trial and should always be requested if your client performed field
sobriety tests. Officers often deviate from the training manual with respect to the field sobriety tests they ask the
defendant to perform. Cross-examining an officer regarding how he or she deviated from the “official” test can be
effective to undermine the reliability of the officer’s observations. The officer’s graduation year will let you know on
which version of the field sobriety tests the officer received training.

[2] Form
[Date]
Trooper [Name]
59 Horse Pond Road
Office of Alcohol Testing
Sudbury, MA 01076
RE: Commonwealth v. [Defendant’s Name]
Docket #:
Dear Trooper [Name]:

Please be advised that this office represents [defendant], whose case is pending in [town] District Court. According
to my files, Trooper [name] of the Massachusetts State Police, [badge #: ____], administered a number of Field
Sobriety Tests pursuant to my client’s arrest. Please provide me with a certified letter indicating the particular
manuals used in training these troopers for conducting Field Sobriety Tests.

Enclosed please find a copy of the Pre-trial Conference report in this matter directing that the identity and reference
number of the respective Field Sobriety Training Manuals for Troopers [name] be produced to this office.

If you have any questions please feel free to contact this office at [phone number].

Best regards,
____________________________________________
[ATTORNEY NAME]
Encl.

1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law Form MOL 10.01

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Forms Appendix

Form MOL 10.01 Defendant’s Motion to Clarify Charge

[1] Practice Tip

Understanding the prosecutor’s theory of the case is essential. Defendant’s motion to clarify charge forces the
prosecutor to state the theory under which he or she is proceeding on the record. This motion should be filed prior
to the start of trial and can be filed with motions in limine.

[2] Form

COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS
 [COUNTY], SS.: TRIAL COURT FOR
 THE
 COMMONWEALTH
 OF
 MASSACHUSETTS
 DOCKET NO.
 ____________

 COMMONWEALTH
 v.

 [DEFENDANT]

 MOTION TO CLARIFY CHARGE

Now comes the Defendant in the above-captioned matter and moves this Honorable Court to order the
Commonwealth to serve notice upon the defendant as to whether it intends to prosecute this complaint as a Per Se
OUI or an OUI, pursuant to G.L. c. 90, § 24 as amended by 2003 Mass. Acts c. 28, a so-called “under the influence”
charge.

The defendant further moves this Honorable Court to order the Commonwealth to serve such notice upon the
defendant no later than ___________. As grounds the defendant states that:
 1. He has been charged with violating M.G.L. c. 90, § 24 by operating a motor vehicle with a BAC of .08
 percent or higher (a per se OUI violation) or while under the influence of intoxicating liquor.
 2. The defendant in this complaint (did/did not) submit to a (breath/blood) test and (does/does not) expect the
 Commonwealth in the trial of this matter to introduce the results of the test into evidence.
 3. The defendant cannot fairly defend himself at trial without knowing which of the two alternative theories the
 Commonwealth will prosecute.

WHEREFORE, the motion should be granted as it is in the interest of justice.

 Rafael Faria

 Form MOL 10.01 Defendant’s Motion to Clarify Charge

Respectfully Submitted,
[DEFENDANT]
By his/her attorney,
____________________________________________
[ATTORNEY NAME]
[ATTORNEY ADDRESS]

entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law Form MOL 10.02

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Forms Appendix

Form MOL 10.02 Rule 17 Motion for Medical Records

[1] Practice Tip

Rule 17 motions can be used to request your client’s medical records in an admissible form prior to trial. Even if
your client has provided you with copies of his or her medical records and you have produced those records to the
prosecution, you may still need to file a Rule 17 motion to obtain the same records in an admissible form. Often,
prosecutors will stipulate to admissibility, in which case this motion may be unnecessary. Trial subpoenas may also
be used to request medical records that are produced in a form admissible at trial.

[2] Form

COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS
 [COUNTY], SS.: TRIAL COURT FOR
 THE
 COMMONWEALTH
 OF
 MASSACHUSETTS
 DOCKET NO.
 ____________

 COMMONWEALTH
 v.

 [DEFENDANT]

 MOTION AND AFFIDAVIT TO SUMMONS NON-PRIVILEGED DOCUMENTS PURSUANT TO MASS. R. CRIM.
 P. 17(a)(2)

Now comes the defendant [name] and moves pursuant to Mass. R. Crim. P. 17 (a)(2) and Commonwealth v.
Lampron, 441 Mass. 265, 269–270 (2004) (citing United States v. Nixon, 418 U.S. 683, 699–700 (1974)), that it be
permitted to summons a certified copy of medical records of [name and date of birth] on or about [relevant date] and
the days thereafter, from [hospital name] to the Criminal Clerk’s Office of the [name of court] located at [court’s
address] and a copy to the [your firm and address].

As grounds therefor, I, [your name], state that the defendant has “good cause,” Lampron, 441 Mass. at 269–270, to
summons this documentation because:
 1) The documents are evidentiary and relevant because they are likely to contain information that is relevant
 to the charges on the complaint regarding the [reason for relevance]. See Commonwealth v. Reed, 444
 Mass. 803, 808 (2005).
 2) The documents are not otherwise procurable reasonably in advance of trial by exercise of due diligence
 because they are not publicly available and the treating facility requires a court order.

 Rafael Faria

 Form MOL 10.02 Rule 17 Motion for Medical Records

 3) The defendant cannot properly prepare for trial without such production and inspection in advance of trial
 and the failure to obtain such inspection may tend unreasonably to delay the trial.
 4) This motion is made in good faith and is not intended as a general fishing expedition because the
 defendant has a good faith basis for believing that the patient was treated at this facility and that
 documents pertaining to this treatment would be relevant to the prosecution of this matter.
 5) Here, unlike in Commonwealth v. Dwyer, 448 Mass. 122, 123 (2006) (records statutorily protected by
 psychotherapist-patient privilege, G.L. c. 233, § 20B), the defendant is seeking information which is not
 privileged.

Signed under the pains and penalties of perjury this [date].

Respectfully Submitted,

For the Defendant
[Attorney Name and Firm Name]
____________________________________________
[Attorney Name]

1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law Form MOL 10.03

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Forms Appendix

Form MOL 10.03 Judicial Order Regarding Rule 17 Motion for Medical
Records

[1] Practice Tip

Rule 17 motions can be used to request your client’s medical records in an admissible form prior to trial. Even if
your client has provided you with copies of his or her medical records and you have produced those records to the
prosecution, you may still need to file a Rule 17 motion to obtain the same records in an admissible form. Often,
prosecutors will stipulate to admissibility, in which case this motion may be unnecessary. Trial subpoenas may also
be used to request medical records that are produced in a form admissible at trial.

[2] Form

COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS
 [COUNTY], SS.: TRIAL COURT FOR
 THE
 COMMONWEALTH
 OF
 MASSACHUSETTS
 DOCKET NO.
 ____________

 COMMONWEALTH
 v.

 [DEFENDANT]

 JUDICIAL ORDER TO PRODUCE MEDICAL RECORDS

This Court, ____________________________________________, J., presiding, orders the Keeper of the Records
for [hospital name] to produce all* records, books, papers, correspondence, and all other written or printed
documentation in its custody and control relating, referring, or in any way pertaining to the diagnosis and treatment
[patient name], D.O.B. [date] on or about [incident date] and the days thereafter, and to deliver said records, to the
from [hospital name] to the Criminal Clerk’s Office of the [name of court] located at [court’s address] and a copy to
the [your firm and address] within ______________________ days of receipt of this Order.

*The following specific sensitive or privileged information is NOT included in this order:
 1. Documentation of any statutorily privileged communication between a patient and a psychiatrist,
 psychologist, psychiatric nurse, social worker, sexual assault counselor, domestic violence counselor, or
 allied mental health professional;
 2. Blood analysis pertaining to HIV and/or AIDS;

 Rafael Faria

 Form MOL 10.03 Judicial Order Regarding Rule 17 Motion for Medical Records

 3. Records containing information about venereal diseases, sexually transmitted diseases, abortion consents
 or record, family planning services and/or genetic testing;
 4. Information pertaining to drug or alcohol abuse or treatment for substance abuse prior to January 11, 2008;
 5. Mammography records and/or film.

____________________________________________
Honorable Justice
Dated: ______________________

Form MOL 10.04 Defendant’s Motion to Compel Discovery

[1] Practice Tip

If your motion to compel is granted and the requested information is still not produced, you should consider moving
for dismissal. If the judge will not move to dismiss the matter, he or she can still exclude evidence under Mass. R.
Crim. P. 14(c). Therefore, if you fail to have the entire case dismissed, you should still make an attempt to exclude
the evidence.

Pursuant to Mass. R. Crim. P. 14(c)(1), [defendant] requests that the Court compel the Commonwealth to comply
with its discovery obligations and provide to [defendant] the following information and documents:

 [Description of materials sought.]

Notably, the Commonwealth agreed to provide the information and documents listed above by [compliance
deadline]. That deadline has passed. To date, [defendant] has not received the requested information and
documents. In support of the instant motion, [defendant] is submitting concurrently here the affidavit of counsel.

WHEREFORE, [defendant] requests that the Court allow his motion to compel discovery and order the
Commonwealth to produce the discovery materials identified above forthwith.

Respectfully submitted,

By [Defendant]
