entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law Form MOL 15.01

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Forms Appendix

Form MOL 15.01 Motion for Required Finding of Not Guilty

[1] Practice Tip

Issues not raised in a motion for required findings may be waived. It is important to file such a motion at the close of
the prosecutor’s case and again at the close of all evidence.

[2] Form

COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS
 [COUNTY], SS.: TRIAL COURT FOR
 THE
 COMMONWEALTH
 OF
 MASSACHUSETTS
 DOCKET NO.
 ____________

 COMMONWEALTH
 v.

 [DEFENDANT]

 MOTION FOR REQUIRED FINDING OF NOT GUILTY

Pursuant to Mass. R. Crim. P. 25, [defendant] hereby moves for required findings of not guilty on the grounds that
the evidence presented is insufficient as a matter of law to sustain a conviction of the charge of operating under the
influence of intoxicating liquor. In support of the motion, [defendant] states as follows:
 1. Under Commonwealth v. Leonard, 401 Mass. 470 (1988), the Court held that the “defendant’s
 uncorroborated statements that he operated the vehicle were insufficient to sustain conviction for operating
 a motor vehicle while under the influence of intoxicating liquor.” Citing the case of Commonwealth v. Forde,
 392 Mass. 453, 457 (1984), the Court stated “as to an extrajudicial confession, that we would adopt the
 majority rule of this nation that an uncorroborated confession is “insufficient to prove guilt.” We indicated
 our view that “the majority rule has much to commend it, in that it precludes the possibility of conviction of
 crime based solely on statements made by a person suffering a mental or emotional disturbance or some
 other aberration.” Commonwealth v. Forde, 392 Mass. 453, 457 (1984).
 2. The case at bar is no different. This court should require some evidence besides the alleged statement that
 the criminal act was committed by the defendant. In the instant case, there is no other evidence to suggest
 that the [defendant] was operating the motor vehicle, except the unsigned and undated State Police Report
 containing an alleged statement made to Trooper X, which was introduced into evidence without any date
 or signature Trooper X.

 Rafael Faria

 Form MOL 15.01 Motion for Required Finding of Not Guilty

 3. Because the evidence is insufficient as a matter of law to satisfy a rational trier of fact on each of the
 elements of the offense charged, the Court should enter findings of not guilty and dismiss the charges
 against [defendant].

Respectfully submitted,

By [Defendant]
____________________________________________
[ATTORNEY NAME]
[ATTORNEY ADDRESS]
Dated: ______________________
LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law Form MOL 15.04

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Forms Appendix

Form MOL 15.04 Motion for New Trial

[1] Practice Tip

A motion for a new trial is commonly used when a defendant is facing a subsequent OUI charge to try to eliminate
prior offenses. It is filed in the prior case, and not the new case.

If a motion for a new trial is granted, the Commonwealth may try to re-prove the case. Often, this is impossible to
do, as evidence has been lost or destroyed or necessary police witnesses have retired. If a motion is granted and
the Commonwealth re-proves the case, it may seek to impose a harsher sentence than the one the defendant
already served. The defendant should be advised of this possibility to make an informed choice prior to the filing of
such a motion.

[2] Form

COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS
 [COUNTY], SS.: TRIAL COURT FOR
 THE
 COMMONWEALTH
 OF
 MASSACHUSETTS
 DOCKET NO.
 ____________

 COMMONWEALTH
 v.

 [DEFENDANT]

 MOTION FOR NEW TRIAL

Pursuant to Massachusetts Rule of Criminal Procedure 30, [defendant] respectfully requests that the Court dismiss,
strike or set aside his prior conviction entered in the above captioned matter.

As detailed the in the attached memorandum of law and affidavit of [defendant], [defendant’s] prior conviction is
constitutionally invalid because the record does not reflect that he made a knowing and intelligent waiver of his
constitutional rights.

Respectfully submitted,

By [Defendant]
____________________________________________

 Rafael Faria

 Form MOL 15.04 Motion for New Trial

[ATTORNEY NAME]
[ATTORNEY ADDRESS]

entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law Form MOL 15.05

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Forms Appendix

Form MOL 15.05 Memorandum of Law in Support of Motion for New Trial

[1] Practice Tip

A motion for a new trial is commonly used when a defendant is facing a subsequent OUI charge to try to eliminate
prior offenses.

[2] Form

COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS
 [COUNTY], SS.: TRIAL COURT FOR
 THE
 COMMONWEALTH
 OF
 MASSACHUSETTS
 DOCKET NO.
 ____________

 COMMONWEALTH
 v.

 [DEFENDANT]

 MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF MOTION FOR NEW TRIAL

Pursuant to Mass. R. Cr. P. 30, [defendant] moves for a new trial on the grounds that his plea was not entered into
knowingly, intelligently, or voluntarily.

 PRIOR PROCEEDINGS & STATEMENT OF FACTS

On [date], [defendant] was charged with operating under the influence of intoxicating liquor. See Docket Sheet at p.
____________.

On [date], the case was removed to Waltham District Court for trial. Before trial, [defendant] entered a plea on the
advice of counsel. As a result of the plea, [defendant] received [describe sentence]. The clerk’s file contains only a
copy of the docket sheet. There is no indication that [defendant] was properly advised of his right to a jury trial or,
likewise, his right to counsel at the plea colloquy.

 ARGUMENT

The [defendant] moves pursuant to Mass. R. Crim. P. 30(b) that he be granted a new trial on the above entitled
matter as it is in the interests of justice. Commonwealth v. Correa, 43 Mass. App. Ct. 714 (1997).

 Rafael Faria

 Form MOL 15.05 Memorandum of Law in Support of Motion for New Trial

As reasons therefor, the guilty plea of [defendant] was not valid as it was not knowingly, intelligently and voluntarily
made and it appears as though it was not in conformance with Mass. R. Crim. P. 12(c). See Attached Affidavit of
[defendant].

An attack of a guilty plea can be granted on two grounds: (1) if it appears that justice might not have been done; or,
(2) if there has been newly discovered evidence. Mass. R. Crim. P. 30(b); Commonwealth v. Huot, 380 Mass. 403,
406 (1980).

A judge may grant a motion for a new trial “at any time if it appears justice may not have been done.” Mass. R.
Crim. P. 30(b). “If, however, the original criminal proceeding was infected with prejudicial constitutional error, the
motion judge has no discretion to deny a motion for a new trial.” Commonwealth v. Sullivan, 385 Mass. 497, 503
(1982). A judge hearing a motion for a new trial has discretion as to the manner in which the motion is heard, by
affidavits or by taking oral testimony. Fogarty v. Commonwealth, 406 Mass. 103, 110–111 (1989). But “where a
substantial issue is supported by substantial evidentiary showing, the judge should hold an evidentiary hearing.”
Commonwealth v. Stewart, 383 Mass. 253, 260 (1981); Commonwealth v. Meggs, 30 Mass. App. Ct. 111, 114
(1991). Given the circumstances of this case, the Court should convene an evidentiary hearing and allow
defendant’s motion.

I. [Defendant’s] Plea Was Not Entered Into Knowingly, Intelligently, Or Voluntarily

A plea of guilty “must be later set aside, unless the record shows affirmatively that the defendant entered the plea
freely and understandingly.” Commonwealth v. Foster, 368 Mass. 100, 102 (1975) (emphasis added) (finding that
the affirmative showing must be made and recorded at the time the judge accepts the plea). At a minimum, a
pleading defendant must be informed that they are waiving (1) the right to a jury trial; (2) the right to confront
witnesses; and, (3) the privilege against self-incrimination. See Commonwealth v. Dummer, 47 Mass. App. Ct. 926,
927 (1999) (holding that a failure to inform a defendant of the waiver of these rights requires the withdrawal of the
plea).

The Supreme Judicial Court has held that the term “record” is not limited to a tape recording or transcript of a
judicial proceeding, but includes a docket sheet on which a box has been checked indicating that an advisement
was or was not given. See Commonwealth v. Rzepphiewski, 431 Mass. 48, 52 (2000); Commonwealth v. Morel, 74
Mass. App. Ct. 1125 (2009) (denying motion where docket sheet affirmatively indicated the defendant waived his
right to jury trial); Commonwealth v. Wilkerson, 54 Mass. App. Ct. 1114 (2002) (denying motion for new trial where
docket sheet explicitly indicates defendant was made aware of his right to a jury trial).

When a defendant does, indeed, plan to plead guilty he or she necessarily waives several federal Constitutional
rights. See Malloy v. Hogan, 378 U.S. 1 (1964). These rights include the right to a jury trial. See Commonwealth v.
Fernandes, 390 Mass. 714, 715–16 (1984) (finding a defendant did not act voluntarily where the colloquy lacked an
inquiry regarding consultation with counsel or wrongful inducement). Because a plea involves these Constitutional
rights it is only valid if the defendant offers it voluntarily, with awareness of the consequences. See Id. For these
conditions to be met, it must be shown affirmatively on the record. See Boykin v. Alabama, 395 U.S. 238, 242–44
(1969).

In this case, [defendant’s] plea was not entered into voluntarily, intelligently or knowingly when he waived his right
to a jury trial. Additionally, his waiver has not been shown affirmatively on the record. The docket sheet does not
mention the waiver of jury trial, nor does it indicate that [defendant] was made aware of the consequences of his
plea. Failing to affirmatively advise [defendant] of the rights he was waiving requires the Court to withdraw the plea.
See Dummer, 47 Mass. App. Ct. at 927. Moreover, Boykin requires that the defendant waive this right on the
record. 395 U.S. at 244. The record is void of any indication that Mr. Patti waived these rights knowingly and
intelligently. A blanket statement of “waived” is not enough. See Id; Dummer, 47 Mass. App. Ct. at 927.

Therefore, since the only record available, the docket sheet, does not indicate [defendant’s] rights were waived after
a proper plea colloquy, it cannot be said that the right to jury trial was waived voluntarily, knowingly, intelligently and
affirmatively on the record.

 Form MOL 15.05 Memorandum of Law in Support of Motion for New Trial

Accordingly, [defendant’s] motion to withdraw the plea should be granted.

 CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reason, the Court should grant the motion for a new trial.

Respectfully submitted,

By [Defendant]
____________________________________________
[ATTORNEY NAME]
[ATTORNEY ADDRESS]
Dated: ______________________
LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

Form MOL 15.06 Motion for Stay of Execution of Sentence

[1] Practice Tip

Sentences are often imposed at the time the conviction is entered, particularly in District Court. Defendants should
be prepared for this possibility prior to the start of trial.

[2] Form

COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS
 [COUNTY], SS.: TRIAL COURT FOR
 THE
 COMMONWEALTH
 OF
 MASSACHUSETTS
 DOCKET NO.
 ____________

 COMMONWEALTH
 v.

 [DEFENDANT]

 MOTION FOR STAY OF EXECUTION OF SENTENCE

Pursuant to Mass. R. Crim. P. 31(a) and M.G.L. c. 279, § 4, [defendant] requests that the Court stay further
execution of the sentence entered on [date] and admit him to the prior bail pending the final determination of his
appeal to the Massachusetts Appeals Court. In support of the instant motion, [defendant] states as follows:
 1. [defendant] appeal presents “an issue which is worthy of presentation to an appellate court, one which
 offers some reasonable possibility of a successful decision in the appeal.” Commonwealth v. Hodge, 380
 Mass. 851, 855 (1980), quoting Commonwealth v. Allen, 378 Mass. 489, 498 (1979), quoting
 Commonwealth v. Levin, 7 Mass. App. Ct. 501, 504 (1979).
 2. [State the appeal issues].
 3. Lastly, defendant is not a security risk, nor would the Commonwealth be prejudiced or harmed if this court
 allows [defendant’s] motion.

[Defendant] is submitting concurrently herewith a Memorandum of Law in support of his motion to stay further
execution of the sentence entered on [date].

Respectfully submitted,

By [Defendant]

 Rafael Faria

 Form MOL 15.06 Motion for Stay of Execution of Sentence

[ATTORNEY NAME]
[ATTORNEY ADDRESS]

1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law Form MOL 15.07

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Forms Appendix

Form MOL 15.07 Motion to Restore Driver’s License

[1] Practice Tip

A motion to restore driver’s license should be filed immediately after a not guilty finding at trial. Include in your
motion proposed written findings of fact and a proposed order that the judge can sign concurrently with his or her
restoration order.

[2] Form

COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS
 [COUNTY], SS.: TRIAL COURT FOR
 THE
 COMMONWEALTH
 OF
 MASSACHUSETTS
 DOCKET NO.
 ____________

 COMMONWEALTH
 v.

 [DEFENDANT]

 MOTION TO RESTORE DRIVER’S LICENSE

Pursuant to M.G.L. c. 90, § 24(f)(1)(iii), [Defendant] respectfully requests that the Court order the Massachusetts
Registry of Motor Vehicles to restore his Massachusetts driver’s license which was suspended for a period of 120
days for refusal to take a breathalyzer test. In support here, [defendant] states the following:
 1. On [date], the charge against [defendant] for operating under the influence of intoxicating liquor was
 dismissed by the Commonwealth.
 2. Pursuant to M.G.L. c. 90, § 24(f)(1)(iii), there is “rebuttable presumption that said license be restored unless
 the Commonwealth shall establish, by a fair preponderance of the evidence, that restoration of said license
 would likely endanger the public safety. In all such instances, the Court shall issue written findings of fact
 with its decision.”

Respectfully submitted,

By [Defendant]
____________________________________________
[ATTORNEY NAME]

 Rafael Faria

 Form MOL 15.07 Motion to Restore Driver’s License

[ATTORNEY ADDRESS]
Dated: ______________________

1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law Form MOL 15.08

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Forms Appendix

Form MOL 15.08 Proposed Findings of Fact to Restore Driver’s License

[1] Practice Tip

A motion to restore driver’s license should be filed immediately after a not guilty finding at trial. Include in your
motion proposed written findings of fact and a proposed order that the judge can sign concurrently with his or her
restoration order.

[2] Form

COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS
 [COUNTY], SS.: TRIAL COURT FOR
 THE
 COMMONWEALTH
 OF
 MASSACHUSETTS
 DOCKET NO.
 ____________

 COMMONWEALTH
 v.

 [DEFENDANT]

 [PROPOSED] FINDINGS OF FACT TO RESTORE DRIVER’S LICENSE

Upon motion of the [defendant] pursuant to M.G.L. c. 90, § 24(f)(1)(iii) requesting an order to the Registrar of Motor
Vehicles to restore his driver’s license, I make the following Findings of Fact:
 1. On [date], [defendant] was arrested and charged with operating under the influence of an intoxicating
 liquor.
 2. On the same date, [defendant] exercised his right to refuse to submit to a Breathalyzer test.
 3. Subsequently, [defendant] was notified by the Registrar of Motor Vehicles that his license was being
 suspended effective [date] pursuant to G.L. c. 90, § 24 for failure to submit to a Breathalyzer test, for a
 period of 120 days until [date].
 4. On [date], [defendant] appeared for trial on the charge of operating under the influence of intoxicating
 liquor. After trial, [defendant] was found not guilty of operating under the influence of intoxicating liquor.
 5. The Commonwealth presented no evidence in the trial to establish that [defendant] was guilty of the charge
 of operating under the influence of intoxicating liquor. Furthermore, The Commonwealth presented no
 evidence that would suggest that restoration of [defendant’s] license would be likely to endanger the public
 safety.

 Rafael Faria

 Form MOL 15.08 Proposed Findings of Fact to Restore Driver’s License

THEREFORE, it is hereby ordered that the Registrar of Motor Vehicles restore the right to operate a motor vehicle
to [defendant] by issuing a Massachusetts Driver’s License, effective immediately.

____________________________________________
[JUDGE NAME]
Dated: ______________________

1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law Form MOL 6.01

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Forms Appendix

Form MOL 6.01 Motion to Dismiss Under Mass. G.L. c. 90C

[1] Practice Tip

Motions to dismiss are typically heard on the first or second hearing date after arraignment. If there is time, it is best
to file a motion to dismiss prior to arraignment. If the motion is successful, the defendant will not be arraigned, and
no criminal record will result from the arrest.

If there are good grounds for a motion to dismiss, but defense counsel is not retained until immediately before the
arraignment, defense counsel can ask to continue the arraignment until the motion can be filed and heard.

[2] Form
 COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS
 [COUNTY], SS.: TRIAL COURT FOR
 THE
 COMMONWEALTH
 OF
 MASSACHUSETTS
 DOCKET NO.
 ____________

 COMMONWEALTH
 v.

 [DEFENDANT]

 MOTION TO DISMISS UNDER MASS. GEN. LAW CH. 90C

[Defendant], through counsel, moves to dismiss the citation issued against her pursuant to Mass. Gen. Law ch.
90C, sec. 2 because [defendant] was not given a copy of the citation at issue for [time period] after she was
stopped.
 FACTS

On [date], Trooper X stopped [defendant] at [location of stop]. Application for Criminal Complaint at 1. After
conducting field sobriety tests, Trooper X arrested [defendant] and brought her to the police Barracks. Id. at 2.
[Defendant] submitted to a Breath Test and the results were .061 for both of her tests. Id. Trooper X released
[defendant] after the Breath Test results and informed her that no charges would issue. Id.; [Defendant] Aff. ¶ 2-3.
Trooper X then drove [defendant] to her home. Application for Criminal Complaint at 2. [Defendant] first learned of
the charges at issue now when she received a copy of a summons charging her with [operating under the influence
of liquor, marked lanes violation, and failure to use care in starting] in the mail. [Defendant] Aff. at 5. The envelope
in which the citation arrived was postmarked on [date]. Exhibit C attached [Defendant] Aff. at 5. The Application for
Criminal Complaint does not indicate that Trooper X needed to conduct any further investigation at the time he

 Rafael Faria

 Form MOL 6.01 Motion to Dismiss Under Mass. G.L. c. 90C

released [defendant] without issuing her a citation or that any work regarding this matter was actually conducted
after her release. Application of Criminal Complaint at 2.
 ARGUMENT

Mass. Gen. Law ch. 90C, section 2 governs the issuance of citations for “the occurrence of automobile law
violations … .” The police officer must fill out the citation completely and provide a copy to the violator for all motor
vehicle offenses. Mass. Gen. Law ch. 90C, sec. 2. As the law provides:

 A failure to give a copy of the citation to the violator at the time and place of the violation shall constitute a
 defense in any court proceeding for such violation, except where the violator could not have been stopped or
 where additional time was reasonably necessary to determine the nature of the violation or the identity of the
 violator, or where the court finds that a circumstance, not inconsistent with the purpose of this section to create
 a uniform, simplified and non-criminal method for disposing of automobile law violations, justifies the failure.

Massachusetts courts have consistently dismissed citations issued after the time and place of the violation. See,
e.g., Commonwealth v. Carapellucci, 429 Mass. 579, 582 (1999); Commonwealth v. Mullins, 367 Mass. 733, 735–
36 (1975); Commonwealth v. Ryan, 22 Mass. App. Ct. 970, 971 (1986). If the citation is not delivered at the time
and place of the violation, the burden is on the Commonwealth to show that one of the exceptions applies. Mullins,
367 Mass. at 734–35. The defendant is not required to show any prejudice. Id. at 735.

Here, [defendant’s] citation should be dismissed. [Defendant] was not issued the citation at the time of her stop or
while she was at the police station. Although she was arrested, she was told at the end of booking that no charges
would issue. As a result, she did not receive notice of the charges that would have allowed her to conduct an
investigation until more than [one week] after the stop. There was no reason for the delay in the issuance of the
citation, as the police had all the information currently used to charge [defendant] at the time she was released from
the police station without receiving a citation. Because of the failure to comply with Mass. Gen. Law. Ch. 90C, sec.
2, the citation against [defendant] should be dismissed. Carapellucci, 429 Mass. at 582; Mullins, 367 Mass. at 735–
36; Ryan, 22 Mass. App. Ct. at 971.

Respectfully submitted,

By [Defendant]
____________________________________________
[ATTORNEY NAME]
[ATTORNEY ADDRESS]
Dated: ______________________

LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Forms Appendix

Form MOL 6.02 Affidavit in Support of Motion to Dismiss Under Mass. G.L. c.
90C

[1] Practice Tip

Affidavits must accompany your motion to dismiss. Typically, your client will sign the affidavit unless there is
another witness who can provide the relevant information. An attorney can sign the affidavit if the motion is based
on the insufficiency of the complaint or indictment and the affidavit is simply certifying documents received from the
prosecution.

[2] Form
 COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS
 [COUNTY], SS.: TRIAL COURT FOR
 THE
 COMMONWEALTH
 OF
 MASSACHUSETTS
 DOCKET NO.
 ____________

 COMMONWEALTH
 v.

 [DEFENDANT]

 AFFIDAVIT

I, [Defendant], swear under the pains and penalty of perjury that the following is true and correct:

1. I was stopped by the Massachusetts State Police in the early morning hours of [date] in [location].

2. I was then taken to the Police Barracks after the motor vehicle stop. Approximately an hour after I arrived at the
barracks, the Trooper who stopped me told me that I would not be charged with a crime and that I was to be
released.

3. The Trooper then provided me a ride home. He did not provide me with a citation or any other documents
indicating that I would be charged with any motor vehicle infraction.

4. On December [date], I returned to the Police Barracks to receive a copy of the police report to confirm what I was
told. Attached as Exhibit A is a true and correct copy of the police report that I received at that time. I was told that
no other police reports existed at that time.

 Rafael Faria

 Form MOL 6.02 Affidavit in Support of Motion to Dismiss Under Mass. G.L. c. 90C

5. Later, I received a citation in the mail. Although the citation is dated [date], the envelope in which the citation
arrived was postmarked on [date]. I received the citation at some point after [date]. This was the first that I learned
that I would be charged with any motor vehicle infractions. A true and correct copy of the citation is attached as
Exhibit B and a true and correct copy of the envelope in which the citation arrived is attached as Exhibit C.

SIGNED UNDER THE PAINS AND PENALTIES OF PERJURY.

____________________________________________
[Defendant]
Dated: ______________________

1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law Form MOL 6.03

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Forms Appendix

Form MOL 6.03 Motion to Dismiss for Failure of Police to Follow OUI
Procedures

[1] Practice Tip

Police not following certain procedures could lead to a dismissal. Sometimes, an issue that involves a breath test is
best saved for trial, as the prosecution must prove compliance with procedures to introduce the breath test results.
If the case can be dismissed earlier, though, it is typically advantageous to try to end the case.

[2] Form
 COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS
 [COUNTY], SS.: TRIAL COURT FOR
 THE
 COMMONWEALTH
 OF
 MASSACHUSETTS
 DOCKET NO.
 ____________

 COMMONWEALTH
 v.

 [DEFENDANT]

 MOTION TO DISMISS COMPLAINT

Now comes [defendant], in the above-captioned matter and moves this Honorable Court to dismiss the charge of
operating a motor vehicle while under the influence of intoxicating liquor (“OUI”) currently pending in this court.

The Defendant gives his reasons therefor the following:
 1) The official in charge of the Marlborough State Police Barracks or his designee failed to inform him of his
 right to be examined by a physician of his own choosing pursuant to G.L. c. 263, § 5(a). Moreover, they
 failed to inform him of the penalties related to refusing a Breathalyzer test. Therefore, [defendant] was
 prejudiced since he was denied potentially exculpatory evidence that could have been gathered from an
 independent medical examination.
 2) The Commonwealth’s failure to inform [defendant] of his rights under M.G.L. c. 263, § 5(a) constitutes a
 denial of due process and equal protection under the law pursuant to the Constitution of the United States.
 As stated in Commonwealth v. Andrade, 389 Mass. 874 (1983), dismissal is the proper remedy.
 3) See the attached Affidavit of [defendant] filed contemporaneously and incorporated by reference.

WHEREFORE, [defendant] requests that the OUI charge be dismissed.

 Rafael Faria

 Form MOL 6.03 Motion to Dismiss for Failure of Police to Follow OUI Procedures

Respectfully submitted,
[DEFENDANT],
By his attorney,
____________________________________________
[ATTORNEY NAME]
[ATTORNEY ADDRESS]
Date: ______________________

1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law Form MOL 6.04

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Forms Appendix

Form MOL 6.04 Memorandum of Law in Support of Motion to Dismiss for
Failure of Police to Follow OUI Procedures

[1] Practice Tip

The police report may indicate whether the police provided the defendant the right to a medical exam. If not,
discovery the prosecutor provides after arraignment will reveal whether the police provided your client with this
right.

[2] Form
 COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS
 [COUNTY], SS.: TRIAL COURT FOR
 THE
 COMMONWEALTH
 OF
 MASSACHUSETTS
 DOCKET NO.
 ____________

 COMMONWEALTH
 v.

 [DEFENDANT]

DEFENDANT’S MEMORANDUM OF LAW IN SUPPORT OF HIS MOTION TO DISMISS THE COMPLAINT FOR
 FAILURE TO ADVISE THE DEFENDANT OF HIS RIGHT TO AN INDEPENDENT MEDICAL EXAMINE
 STATEMENT OF THE CASE

On or about [date], at approximately [time], Officer [name] of [town] arrested [defendant] for operating a motor
vehicle while under the influence of alcohol (“OUI”). [Defendant] was transported to the [town] Police Station and
booked by Officer [name]. [Defendant] was advised of his right to make a telephone call. [Defendant] was asked
whether he would submit to a breathalyzer test. He said no.

Moreover, [defendant] states that the police department failed to advise him of his rights pursuant to M.G.L. c. 263,
§ 5(a) to wit, that he had a right to an independent medical examination.

[Defendant] also files with this Memorandum of Law, a Motion to Dismiss the complaint for OUI and his Affidavit in
support of that motion.

 I. The Defendant’s Rights Under M.G.L. c. 263, § 5(a) Were Violated by the [Name] Police Department, and
 the Related Charges Should be Dismissed.

 Rafael Faria

 Form MOL 6.04 Memorandum of Law in Support of Motion to Dismiss for Failure of Police to Follow OUI
 Procedures

The [name] Police Department’s failure to inform [defendant] of his right to an independent medical examination,
verbally or in writing, warrants a dismissal of the charges against him for OUI.

M.G.L. c. 263, § 5(A) provides in pertinent part:

 A person held in custody at a police station or other place of detention, charged with operating a motor vehicle
 while under the influence of intoxicating liquor, shall have the right, at his request and at his expense, to be
 examined immediately by a physician selected by him. The police official in charge of such station or place of
 detention, or his designee, shall inform him of such right immediately upon being booked and shall afford him a
 reasonable opportunity to exercise it. [emphasis added].

[Defendant]’s Affidavit states that at no time did any police officer, nor a “police official in charge of such station …
or his designee,” make an attempt to advise him of his right under M.G.L. c. 263, § 5(A) to request an independent
medical examination at his own expense.

Moreover, if the [name] Police Department complied with the statute by posting a copy of the M.G.L. c. 263, § 5(A)
rights in the police department, the officers did not direct [defendant]’s attention to the posting. See Commonwealth
v. Andrade, 389 Mass. 874, 876 (1983) (finding defendant’s statutory rights violated when police failed to bring
posted rights to attention of defendant).
 II. Exigent Circumstances Did Not Exist to Justify a Police Officer’s Failure to Communicate the
 Defendant’s Rights to Him.

The Supreme Judicial Court (“SJC”) found justification for a police officer’s failure to advise a defendant of his rights
under the below circumstances: (1) There is evidence that the defendant was so inebriated that an attempt at
compliance would have been futile. See Andrade, 389 Mass. at 874. (finding that absent substantial evidence of
guilt, dismissal of complaint is suitable remedy for violation of defendant’s rights under M.G.L. c. 263, § 5(A)); 2)
Exigent circumstances existed at the time. See Commonwealth v. Atencio, 12 Mass. App. Ct. 747, 750 (1981)
(finding that a failure by police to inform defendant of right to independent medical examination did not require
suppression of evidence obtained by police because defendant was injured in auto accident and brought to
hospital); or 3) Police report indicating that defendant was so belligerent or uncooperative that attempts at
compliance would have been futile. See Commonwealth v. Andrade, 389 Mass. 874 (1983).

In the instant case, exigent circumstances did not exist. [Defendant] was not injured and the police report does not
indicate any basis for concluding that [defendant] was so intoxicated that an attempt to comply would have been
futile. See Exhibit A. Nor does the report reference any difficult or uncooperative behavior by [defendant]. See
Exhibit A. See also Commonwealth v. Andrade, 389 Mass. 874, 879 (1983). Failing to comply with G.L. c. 263, § 54
not substantiated (finding that absent a showing of exigent circumstances, evidence of extreme inebriation,
belligerence or uncooperativeness).

The Andrade Court reviewed the remedies sufficient under M.G.L. c. 263, § 5(a) violations and stated that “if the
defendant had made any admissions, confessed, or disclosed a lead to the discovery of favorable evidence,
exclusion of such evidence might be an appropriate remedy.” See also Commonwealth v. Andrade, 389 Mass. at
881 (quoting Commonwealth v. Bouchard, 347 Mass. 418, 421 (1964)). The Andrade Court also stated that
suppression of evidence in operating under the influence offenses may not be an appropriate remedy since
violations of Section 5(A) rights “may actually prevent exculpatory evidence from being revealed.” Andrade, 389
Mass. at 881.

In this case, like in Andrade, a breath test was not conducted. Accordingly, there is no unfavorable evidence to
suppress. In Andrade, the SJC reasoned that the dismissal of the charge may be appropriate under these
circumstances because unfair prejudice may have arisen when the violation of the defendant’s Section 5A rights
occurred, since had an independent examination been conducted, evidence which exculpated him or her may have
emerged. See Andrade, 389 Mass. at 881.

 Form MOL 6.04 Memorandum of Law in Support of Motion to Dismiss for Failure of Police to Follow OUI
 Procedures

III. The Likelihood Of The Defendant Being Prejudiced by The Officer’s Non-Compliance With M.G.L. c. 263,
 § 5(A) Demands Dismissal of The Complaint.

As in Andrade, no chemical test was ever performed on [defendant] and the only evidence the Commonwealth has
on the issue of lack of sobriety is the testimony of the police officers. See Commonwealth v. Andrade, 389 Mass. at
879. Therefore the likelihood that [defendant] may have been prejudiced by the police officer’s failure to comply with
G.L. c. 263, § 5(A) is high.
 IV. Conclusion

The [name] Police Department’s failure to inform the [defendant] of his M.G.L. c. 263, § 5(A) rights mandates
dismissal of the complaint. Accordingly, the complaint against the Defendant must be dismissed.

Respectfully submitted,
[DEFENDANT]
By his attorney,
Dated: ______________________
____________________________________________
[ATTORNEY NAME]
[ATTORNEY ADDRESS]

LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

Form MOL 6.05 Motion to Dismiss for Unlawful Stop

[1] Practice Tip

A challenge to the basis for a stop can sometimes be raised during a motion to dismiss. It can also be a ground
raised during a motion to suppress.

[2] Form
 COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS
 [COUNTY], SS.: TRIAL COURT FOR
 THE
 COMMONWEALTH
 OF
 MASSACHUSETTS
 DOCKET NO.
 ____________

 COMMONWEALTH
 v.

 [DEFENDANT]

 MOTION TO DISMISS FOR AN UNLAWFUL STOP

Pursuant to Massachusetts Rule of Criminal Procedure 13, [Defendant], moves to dismiss the above referenced
matter. In support thereof, [Defendant] states as follows:
 1. On [date], [defendant] was stopped by Trooper X at [dated and time].
 2. Trooper X lacked probable cause to stop [defendant], question him and/or search his motor vehicle.
 3. Trooper X’s stop of [defendant’s] motor vehicle was unjustified.
 4. Indeed, [defendant] did not and was not committing any traffic violation at the time that Trooper X stopped
 him.
 5. As such, the Trooper X’s stop of [defendant] violated the 4th Amendment to United States Constitution,
 Article 14 and Article 12 of the Massachusetts Declaration of Rights, and M.G.L. c. 90, as well as
 Commonwealth v. Canavan, 40 Mass. App. Ct. 642 (1996) ; Commonwealth v. Lubiejewski, 49 Mass. App.
 Ct. 212, 214 (2000); Terry v. Ohio, 392 U.S. 1 (1968).
 6. [Defendant] has submitted an affidavit in support of the instant motion.

Respectfully submitted,

By [Defendant]

 Rafael Faria

[ATTORNEY NAME]
[ATTORNEY ADDRESS]

1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law Form MOL 6.06

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Forms Appendix

Form MOL 6.06 Affidavit in Support of Motion to Dismiss for Unlawful Stop

[1] Practice Tip

The affidavit in support of a motion to dismiss for an unlawful stop will typically need to be signed by your client. The
prosecution cannot use the affidavit against your client except if the client testifies, which could happen at a motion
hearing or at trial.

[2] Form
 COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS
 [COUNTY], SS.: TRIAL COURT FOR
 THE
 COMMONWEALTH
 OF
 MASSACHUSETTS
 DOCKET NO.
 ____________

 COMMONWEALTH
 v.

 [DEFENDANT]

 AFFIDAVIT

I, [Defendant], swear under the pains and penalty of perjury that the following is true and correct:

1. On [date and time], I was stopped by the Massachusetts State Police in the [location].

2. At the time of stop, I was pulling my car into the breakdown lane because my motor vehicle had suffered a flat
tire.

3. I was not speeding and was abiding by all of the rules of the road. I stopped my vehicle at a safe location.

4. After I had stopped, Trooper X approached my motor vehicle. Trooper X ordered me to get out of motor vehicle
and asked me several questions. I answered every questions and complied with any requested Trooper X made
upon me.

5. Trooper X then handcuffed me and placed me under arrest. I was placed in the back of the police car.

6. At the time I had stopped, I had committed no traffic violation.

7. I had not committed, was committing or was about to commit a crime before I was stopped.

 Rafael Faria

 Form MOL 6.06 Affidavit in Support of Motion to Dismiss for Unlawful Stop

8. I was only advised of my Miranda rights after I was handcuffed, arrested and transported to the State Police
Barracks.

SIGNED UNDER THE PAINS AND PENALTIES OF PERJURY.

____________________________________________

By [Defendant]

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Forms Appendix

Form MOL 6.08 Motion to Dismiss for Lost or Destroyed Evidence

[1] Practice Tip

Lost or destroyed evidence needs to be significant for a defense in order for a motion to dismiss on this basis to
succeed.

[2] Form
 COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS
 [COUNTY], SS.: TRIAL COURT FOR
 THE
 COMMONWEALTH
 OF
 MASSACHUSETTS
 DOCKET NO.
 ____________

 COMMONWEALTH
 v.

 [DEFENDANT]

 MOTION TO DISMISS DUE TO LOST OR DESTROYED EVIDENCE

[Defendant] hereby moves this Honorable Court pursuant to Mass. R. Crim. P. 13, Article 12 of the Massachusetts
Declaration of Rights, and the Due Process Clause of the United States Constitution, to dismiss the above-
captioned matter due to the Commonwealth’s loss and/or destruction of evidence, thus denying the Defendant his
right to a fair trial. See Commonwealth v. Olszewski, 401 Mass. 749 (1988); Commonwealth v. Troy, 405 Mass. 253
(1989); Commonwealth v. Willie, 400 Mass. 427 (1987).

In the alternative, the [defendant] moves “that all testimony and evidence relating to the lost or destroyed evidence
be excluded from trial.” Olszewski, 401 Mass. at 753. In other words, all observations of [defendant]’s speech and
dexterity should be excluded from evidence at trial.

The Defendant has attached an affidavit and memorandum of law in support of this motion.

Respectfully submitted,
[DEFENDANT]
By his attorney,
____________________________________________
[ATTORNEY NAME]

 Rafael Faria

1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law Form MOL 6.09

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Forms Appendix

Form MOL 6.09 Memorandum of Law in Support of Motion to Dismiss for
Lost or Destroyed Evidence

[1] Practice Tip

A memorandum of law is required for some motions (although not motions to dismiss). It can be helpful to use a
motion to highlight the main issue and then the memorandum of law to provide all the analysis and supporting
authority even when it is not required.

[2] Form
 COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS
 [COUNTY], SS.: TRIAL COURT FOR
 THE
 COMMONWEALTH
 OF
 MASSACHUSETTS
 DOCKET NO.
 ____________

 COMMONWEALTH
 v.

 [DEFENDANT]

 MEMORANDUM OF LAW IN SUPPORT OF MOTION TO DISMISS FOR DESTRUCTION OF EVIDENCE
 FACTS

The Defendant has moved this Honorable Court to dismiss the above-complaint due to the lost or destroyed
booking video in this matter. This video would have produced evidence favorable to the Defendant’s case and thus
this matter should be dismissed in accordance with principles of the Due Process Clause as well as Article 12 of the
Massachusetts Declaration of Rights.
 ARGUMENT

I. A BALANCING TEST SHOULD BE APPLIED IN THIS CASE

The Supreme Judicial Court (“SJC”), in Commonwealth v. Olszewski, 401 Mass. 749 (1988), detailed the relevant
law with respect to lost and/or destroyed evidence. The Court reasoned that in Commonwealth v. Redding, 382
Mass. 154, 157 (1980), “the prosecutor should make every effort to disclose to the defendant exculpatory evidence
which is available to the prosecution.” Redding made this observation while simultaneously citing, Commonwealth
v. St. Germain, 381 Mass. 256 (1980), noting that the “police are part of the prosecution and that the
Commonwealth is to be held responsible for nondisclosure by them.” Olszewski, 401 Mass. at 753. Likewise, in

 Rafael Faria

 Form MOL 6.09 Memorandum of Law in Support of Motion to Dismiss for Lost or Destroyed Evidence

Commonwealth v. Lam Hue To, 391 Mass. 301, 311 (1984) , the Court defined prosecutorial misconduct to include
“the inept and bungling performance of the police, which is attributed to the prosecutor.”

The SJC, in Commonwealth v. Gallarelli, 399 Mass. 17, 20 n. 4 (1987) , held the prosecutor responsible for the
police loss of evidence despite the fact that he was unaware of it.

The SJC determined that where possibly exculpatory evidence is lost or destroyed, the defendant must establish a
“ ‘reasonable possibility, based on concrete evidence rather than fertile imagination,’ that access to the [evidence]
would have produced evidence favorable to his cause.” Id. at 12. Specifically, the SJC has held that “evidence
tending to impeach the credibility of a key prosecution witness is ‘clearly exculpatory.’ ” Commonwealth v. Collins,
386 Mass. 1, 8 (1982). Once this “reasonable possibility” has been established, a balancing test is employed “to
determine the appropriateness and extent of remedial action.” Commonwealth v. Willie, 400 Mass. 427, 432 (1987).
See also, Commonwealth v. Harwood, 432 Mass. 290, 295 (2000) (“Negligence and inadvertence are considered
culpable for this weighing”); Commonwealth v. Gilday, 382 Mass. 166, 177–78 (1980) (holding that distinctions are
drawn between the standard of materiality to be applied where the prosecution fails to supply evidence specifically
requested by the defendant).

Here, [defendant] was charged with OUI. See Exhibit C. [Defendant]’s arrest was based only on observations made
by the arresting officers. Indeed, no field sobriety tests or breathalyzer tests were performed. See Exhibit C.
[Defendant] was booked at the [town] Police Department on or about [date] regarding this matter. See Exhibit C.
The [town] Police Department, on this date, maintained a booking room video recorder to electronically record
defendants and officers as they underwent the booking process. Regarding this case, on or about [date], a
recording was made of [defendant] after his arrest for OUI.

After learning of the existence of a booking room video by the Commonwealth, requests were made by counsel to
receive a copy. See Exhibit A. On or about [date], defense counsel was informed by Officer [name], of the [town]
Police Department, that the booking video in this matter was missing. See Exhibit A. Defense counsel never had
the opportunity to view the video in this matter.

There is a reasonable possibility that this video would have produced evidence favorable to the Defendant’s case.
See Neal, 392 Mass. at 12. The Commonwealth is only seeking to introduce the arresting officers’ observations into
evidence, without the use of field sobriety tests or a breathalyzer test, and this video could possibly refute such
observations thereby producing some of the only evidence favorable to the Defendant’s case. See Commonwealth
v. Collins, 386 Mass. 1 (1982) (“evidence tending to impeach the credibility of a key prosecution witness is clearly
exculpatory”). Thus, the Defendant has met his burden that this evidence was exculpatory and it was reasonably
possible to be favorable to his case therefore warranting that the balancing test should be applied.

II. EVIDENCE RELATED TO THE BOOKING VIDEO SHOULD BE EXCLUDED

The Commonwealth is culpable as the evidence was in their sole possession and defense counsel was never
afforded the opportunity to view the video. Granted, there is nothing to suggest at this point whether the evidence
was lost by willful misconduct on the part of the Commonwealth or by mere negligence. See Commonwealth v.
Cinelli, 389 Mass. 197, 210 (1983) (holding that “absent egregious misconduct or at least a serious threat of
prejudice, the remedy of dismissal infringes too severely on the public interest in bringing guilty persons to justice”).
However, as the [town] Police Department presumably has adequate procedures for safeguarding videotapes it can
be inferred that since this tape is unavailable, losing evidence in light of these procedures rises above the level of
mere negligence and can be more aptly described as “egregious misconduct” warranting a dismissal of the
complaint. See Cinelli, 389 Mass. at 197.

Second, the lost evidence is material as it may directly refute the evidence the Commonwealth seeks to enter into
evidence at any trial regarding this matter. As mentioned, the only inculpatory evidence to be presented in this case
will be the testimony of the arresting officers. This testimony will be limited to their observations of the Defendant’s
demeanor, speech, and body control as no field sobriety tests or breathalyzer tests were performed in this matter.

 Form MOL 6.09 Memorandum of Law in Support of Motion to Dismiss for Lost or Destroyed Evidence

Lastly, the potential for prejudice in this matter is too great not to allow the remedy of dismissal. See Cinelli, 389
Mass. at 197. As stated above, this video could display the Defendant’s sobriety and, therefore, the officers’
exaggeration in their respective descriptions. The loss of the video effectively deprives the Defendant of almost all
possible defenses in this matter and is thus substantially prejudicial to him. See Commonwealth v. Cameron, 25
Mass. Appt. Ct. 538, 548 (1988) (emphasis added).

Alternatively, the Defendant moves “that all testimony and evidence relating to the lost or destroyed evidence be
excluded from trial.” Olszewski, 401 Mass. at 753. As the Defendant is without the aid of the booking video, he
requests that Officer [name] and Officer [name] be estopped from testifying with regard to any alleged observations
of [defendant]’s speech and dexterity with regard to any of the events related to the charges in this matter. This
would include, but is not limited to, testimony regarding the Defendant’s physical appearance, unsteadiness, and
slow, slurred, or deliberate speech.
CONCLUSION

Again, by weighing the culpability of the Commonwealth, the prejudice to the Defendant, and the materiality of the
evidence such observations should be excluded from evidence as the booking video could have possibly refuted
such observations. By allowing the officers to testify to such observations, while at the same time failing to produce
potentially exculpatory evidence that is related to such observations, the Defendant’s Due Process and Article 12
rights are violated. As such, the Defendant respectfully requests that all testimony and evidence of his speech and
dexterity from the initial stop until the end of the booking process be excluded from evidence.

Respectfully submitted,
[DEFENDANT]
By his attorney,
____________________________________________
[ATTORNEY NAME]
[ATTORNEY ADDRESS]

LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

 End of Document

Form MOL 6.10 Affidavit in Support of Motion to Dismiss for Lost or
Destroyed Evidence

[1] Practice Tip

A motion to suppress should be filed well in advance of trial or the issue could be waived. Mass. R. Crim. P. 13(e).
If your client makes any incriminating statements to the police, you must determine if you have grounds to suppress
those statements.

[2] Form
 COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS
 [COUNTY], SS.: TRIAL COURT FOR
 THE
 COMMONWEALTH
 OF
 MASSACHUSETTS
 DOCKET NO.
 ____________

 COMMONWEALTH
 v.

 [DEFENDANT]

 AFFIDAVIT IN SUPPORT OF MOTION TO DISMISS

Under oath, I depose and state that:
 1. I, [attorney], am the attorney of record for the above-captioned Defendant, [name]. [Defendant] is charged
 with Operating under the Influence (“OUI”) stemming from circumstances that the Commonwealth allege
 occur which arose on or about [date].
 2. I was informed by the Commonwealth that the [town] Police Department secured certain physical evidence,
 to wit, a booking video of [defendant] on or about [date], i.e., the date of his arrest. I was also told that this
 video is in the possession of the [town] police department.
 3. On or about [date], my office sent a request for the booking video in question. See Exhibit A. On or about
 [date], after many attempts by this office to discover the location of the video, Officer [name] of the [town]
 Police Department contacted my office and informed us that the booking video of [defendant] was lost and
 could not be found. See Exhibit B. This booking video continues to be missing and has not, at any time,
 been produced in this case.
 4. This case involves a charge of OUI to which [defendant]. At the scene of the stop, the defendant did not
 perform any Field Sobriety or Breathalyzer tests.

 Rafael Faria

 Form MOL 6.10 Affidavit in Support of Motion to Dismiss for Lost or Destroyed Evidence

 5. The booking video could have provided exculpatory evidence directly contradicting the observations of the
 arresting officers. Indeed, it was my intention to examine this video but have been unable to do so.
 6. Due to the disappearance of this key piece of evidence, the Defendant is deprived of evidence favorable to
 his cause.

Signed Under the Pains and Penalties of Perjury:
____________________________________________
[DEFENDANT]
Date: ______________________

Form MOL 7.01 Motion to Suppress Statements Based on Illegal Stop

[1] Practice Tip

A motion to suppress should be filed well in advance of trial or the issue could be waived. Mass. R. Crim. P. 13(e).
If your client makes any incriminating statements to the police, you must determine if you have grounds to suppress
those statements.

[2] Form
 COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS
 [COUNTY], SS.: TRIAL COURT FOR
 THE
 COMMONWEALTH
 OF
 MASSACHUSETTS
 DOCKET NO.
 ____________

 COMMONWEALTH
 v.

 [DEFENDANT]

 MOTION TO SUPPRESS STATEMENTS BECAUSE OF AN ILLEGAL STOP

Pursuant to Massachusetts Rule of Criminal Procedure 13, [defendant], moves to suppress evidence seized from
his motor vehicle on [date and time] at [location] when he was arrested for operating under to influence of alcohol.
In support thereof, [defendant} states as follows:
 1. Trooper X did not possess probable cause to stop [defendant’s] motor vehicle, question him or to search
 the [defendant’s] motor vehicle.
 2. Trooper X’s stop of [defendant’s] motor vehicle was not justified.
 3. Trooper X’s stop of [defendant’s] motor vehicle was not lawful because [defendant] did not commit and was
 not committing a traffic violation at the time.
 4. As such, Trooper X’s stop of [defendant] violated [defendant’s] rights under the 4th Amendment to United
 States Constitution, Article 14 and Article 12 of the Massachusetts Declaration of Rights, and M.G.L. c. 90,
 as well as Commonwealth v. Canavan, 40 Mass. App. Ct. 642 (1996); Commonwealth v. Lubiejewski, 49
 Mass. App. Ct. 212, 214 (2000); Terry v. Ohio, 392 U.S. 1 (1968).
 5. [Defendant] has submitted an affidavit in support of the instant motion.

Respectfully submitted,

 Rafael Faria

 Form MOL 7.01 Motion to Suppress Statements Based on Illegal Stop

By [Defendant]
____________________________________________
[ATTORNEY NAME]
[ATTORNEY ADDRESS]
Dated: ______________________

Form MOL 7.02 Affidavit in Support of Motion to Suppress Based on Illegal
Stop

[1] Practice Tip

All motions to suppress must be accompanied by an affidavit. The defendant typically is the only person on the
defense side who can provide the necessary information for the motion. The prosecution cannot use an affidavit
signed by the defendant against the defendant in the case unless he or she testifies.

[2] Form
 COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS
 [COUNTY], SS.: TRIAL COURT FOR
 THE
 COMMONWEALTH
 OF
 MASSACHUSETTS
 DOCKET NO.
 ____________

 COMMONWEALTH
 v.

 [DEFENDANT]

 AFFIDAVIT IN SUPPORT OF MOTION TO SUPPRESS STATEMENTS

Now comes [defendant] and in support of his Motion to Suppress, states the following:

1. My name is [defendant], and I am the Defendant in the above-captioned matter. On the evening of [date], I was
operating my motor vehicle on [street], in the town of [town], Massachusetts.

2. At [time], I was stopped by Officer [name] of the [name] Police Department. The Officer asked me many
questions. Some of these questions were in regard to how many drinks I had consumed. Additionally, I was asked
to perform field sobriety tests including a leg raise while counting to 20 test, nine-step walk-and-turn test and finger-
to-nose test. After I complied with these tests and the Officer’s other requests, I was told that I was under arrest.

3. At no time prior to being questioned by the officer and/or asked to count out loud to 20, did the officer advise me
of my right to remain silent and/or that anything I said could be used against me. Additionally, I was not advised that
any statements I made could be used against me.

4. I was never advised of my right to not incriminate myself until after I was placed in handcuffs.

Signed this ________________ day of ____________, 20____________, under the pains and penalties of perjury.

 Rafael Faria

 Form MOL 7.02 Affidavit in Support of Motion to Suppress Based on Illegal Stop

____________________________________________
[DEFENDANT]
Dated: ______________________

1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law Form MOL 7.06

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Forms Appendix

Form MOL 7.06 Memorandum of Law in Support of Motion to Suppress
Breathalyzer Results

[1] Practice Tip

The breathalyzer results often provide the Commonwealth’s strongest evidence. Defense counsel should make
sure that all the procedures set forth in 501 Code Mass. Regs. were followed. If not, a motion to suppress should be
filed.

[2] Form
 COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS
 [COUNTY], SS.: TRIAL COURT FOR
 THE
 COMMONWEALTH
 OF
 MASSACHUSETTS
 DOCKET NO.
 ____________

 COMMONWEALTH
 v.

 [DEFENDANT]

 DEFENDANT’S MEMORANDUM OF LAW IN SUPPORT OF MOTION TO SUPPRESS BREATHALYZER TEST

Now comes the Defendant and respectfully submits his brief in support of his motion to suppress his alleged
statements and breathalyzer test results.

I. FACTS

At approximately [time] on [date], [police officer] arrested [defendant] for Operating under the Influence. [Police
officer] transported [defendant] to the [name] Police Station. Once back at the police station, Officer [name] brought
[defendant] to the booking room, where he was booked, read his Miranda rights, and read the Statutory Rights and
Consent Form. [Defendant] then allegedly voluntarily elected to take the breathalyzer test. [Police officer]
administered the breathalyzer test, however, [state officer’s failure to properly administer the breathalyzer test, e.g.,
he/she failed to observe [defendant] for at least 15 minutes before beginning the test].

II. ARGUMENT

 ANY BREATHALYZER TEST RESULTS ATTRIBUTED TO [DEFENDANT] SHOULD BE SUPPRESSED
 BECAUSE [OFFICER NAME] DID NOT OBSERVE [DEFENDANT] FOR 15 MINUTES PRIOR TO THE TEST

 Rafael Faria

 Form MOL 7.06 Memorandum of Law in Support of Motion to Suppress Breathalyzer Results

The breathalyzer test results for a person charged with Operating Under the Influence of Intoxicating Liquor shall
not be considered valid unless the test was performed in compliance with methods approved by the secretary of
public safety. M.G.L. c. 90, § 24K. According to these methods, the breath test operator (“BTO”) must observe the
test subject for at least 15 minutes prior to initiating the test. 501 C.M.R. § 2.13(3). A failure to satisfy this
requirement requires suppression of the breathalyzer test results. See Commonwealth v. Pierre, 72 Mass. App. Ct.
230, 235, 890 N.E.2d 152 (2008). In this case, [Police officer] administered the breathalyzer test, however, he/she
failed to continuously observe [defendant] for 15 minutes prior to initiating the test. Because [police officer] failed to
meet the observation period requirement set forth in 501 C.M.R. § 2.13(3), any results of the breathalyzer test
attributed to [defendant] must be suppressed. Pierre, 72 Mass. App. Ct. at 235.

 III. CONCLUSION

For all the foregoing reasons, the Defendant respectfully requests that this Court suppress the breathalyzer test
results attributed to him.

Respectfully submitted,

By [DEFENDANT]
By his attorney,
____________________________________________
[ATTORNEY NAME]
[ATTORNEY ADDRESS]
Dated: ______________________

1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law Form MOL 9.01

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Forms Appendix

Form MOL 9.01 Motion in Limine Regarding Horizontal Gaze Nystagmus
(HGN)

[1] Practice Tip

It is rare that the police officer has the medical training necessary to administer the HGN test. Typically, this field
sobriety test will not be admissible at trial. Sometimes, the prosecutor may be allowed to introduce some
observations of the officer that were made during the test, even if the prosecutor and police cannot refer to the test
itself.

[2] Form
 COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS
 [COUNTY], SS.: TRIAL COURT FOR
 THE
 COMMONWEALTH
 OF
 MASSACHUSETTS
 DOCKET NO.
 ____________

 COMMONWEALTH
 v.

 [DEFENDANT]

 Motion in Limine To Preclude Results of Horizontal Gaze Nystagmus (HGN) Field Sobriety Test

[Defendant] is charged with operating a motor vehicle while under the influence of intoxicating liquor (“OUI”) in
violation of G.L. c. 90, § 24. Therefore, he moves to preclude the Commonwealth from introducing evidence or
making reference to results of the Horizontal Gaze Nystagmus (“HGN”) test administered to the Defendant by the
arresting officer.

The Defendant states as reasons therefor:
 1. The HGN test has a scientific basis that is not within the common knowledge of a lay person and therefore
 requires expert testimony.
 2. The Commonwealth cannot lay the proper foundation to demonstrate that the HGN field sobriety test is of
 assistance to the fact finder and that the underlying scientific theory or process can be shown to be a
 reliable indicator of the correlation between the consumption of alcohol and the onset of nystagmus.
 3. The arresting officer is not qualified to testify as an expert witness as to the scientific basis, reliability and
 general acceptance of the HGN test in the scientific community as he is neither a medical expert nor a
 scientist.

 Rafael Faria

 Form MOL 9.01 Motion in Limine Regarding Horizontal Gaze Nystagmus (HGN)

WHEREFORE, Defendant, through counsel, requests that this Honorable Court preclude the Commonwealth from
introducing evidence or from making reference to the results any HGN test administered to the Defendant.

Respectfully submitted,
[DEFENDANT]
By is attorney,
____________________________________________
[ATTORNEY NAME]
[ATTORNEY ADDRESS]
Dated: ______________________

entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law Form MOL 9.02

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Forms Appendix

Form MOL 9.02 Memorandum of Law in Support of Motion in Limine
Regarding Horizontal Gaze Nystagmus (HGN)

[1] Practice Tip

It is rare that the police officer has the medical training necessary to administer the HGN test. As a result, this field
sobriety test typically will not be admissible at trial.

[2] Form
 COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS
 [COUNTY], SS.: TRIAL COURT FOR
 THE
 COMMONWEALTH
 OF
 MASSACHUSETTS
 DOCKET NO.
 ____________

 COMMONWEALTH
 v.

 [DEFENDANT]

MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF DEFENDANT’S MOTION IN LIMINE TO PRECLUDE EVIDENCE RELATING
 TO HORIZONTAL GAZE NYSTAGMUS

 FACTS

On [date], [defendant], was arrested and charged with operating a motor vehicle while under the influence of
intoxicating liquor (“OUI”). At the time of the arrest, the arresting officer, Trooper [name] of the Massachusetts State
Police Department, administered a field sobriety test, the so-called Horizontal Gaze Nystagmus (“HGN”), to the
Defendant.

Allegedly, there is a correlation between bio-psychological responses and the consumption of alcohol, as it relates
to vision and the central nervous system. Taken as true, such a conclusion clearly requires scientific evidence
beyond the expertise of the arresting officer.
 ARGUMENT

I. THE HGN FIELD SOBRIETY TEST IS SCIENTIFIC EVIDENCE REQUIRING EXPERT TESTIMONY FROM
A PROFESSIONAL IN THE MEDICAL COMMUNITY.

 Rafael Faria

 Form MOL 9.02 Memorandum of Law in Support of Motion in Limine Regarding Horizontal Gaze Nystagmus
 (HGN)

The HGN test is distinguishable from other field sobriety tests because certain reactions to alcohol are so common
that courts often take judicial notice of them, e.g., odor of breath, flushed appearance, lack of muscular
coordination, etc. That is not the case with HGN, however. Indeed, the HGN test draws “its convincing force from a
scientific principle that consumption of alcohol causes nystagmus.” See State v. Reed, 732 P.2d 66, 68 (Or. App.
1987).

Apparently, there is a bio-psychological basis for the HGN that draws a correlation between the consumption of
alcohol and certain central nervous system and visual responses. The reliability of the HGN test cannot be
determined without the use of expert testimony. See Commonwealth v. Lanigan, 419 Mass. 15 (1994);
Commonwealth v. Sands, 424 Mass. 184, 187–88 (1997).

It is anticipated that the Commonwealth will be unable to show that the HGN Field Sobriety Test is a reliable
indicator of intoxication or that the proffered evidence will be of assistance to the fact finder, as no experts in the
field appear to be listed as witnesses.

II. THE ARRESTING OFFICER CANNOT BE QUALIFIED AS AN EXPERT WITNESS AS BECAUSE HE IS
NOT A MEDICAL PROFESSIONAL

In People v. Loomis, 156 Cal. App. 3d Supp. 1, 203 Cal. Rptr. 767 (Super. Ct. 1984) , the Appellate Department of
the Superior Court for San Diego County held that an arresting officer was not entitled to testify as either a lay
witness or as an expert witness and give his opinion of a blood alcohol content of the defendant based on a gaze
nystagmus test which the officer administered.

In Loomis, the arresting officer testified that he had been a police officer for over five years and had received
between 300 and 400 hours of training in the detection of drunk drivers. See id. The officer had also been working
for a special drinking and driving detail for the police department in his town for about the last three years. See id.
Additionally, he testified that he had stopped over 2,500 people suspected of drinking and driving and had used the
HGN test every single one of those stops. See id.

At trial, the officer testified that his opinion, based on the HGN test, was that the defendant had a HGN reaction at
less than 20 degrees and estimated that the defendant’s blood alcohol content was between .15 and .16 percent.
See id.

The defendant’s attorney objected to this opinion testimony of the officer with respect to the blood alcohol content
based on the HGN test. At trial, the judge ruled in favor of the prosecution, due to the aforementioned factors. See
id at 769. The Appellate Division reversed the trial finding that the officer was, in fact, a lay witness and was not
qualified to give his opinion of the blood alcohol content of the defendant based on the HGN test. See id. at 770.

The Appellate court found that, the trial judge erred in ruling that the officer was not testifying as an expert but could
give an opinion of blood alcohol content based on his training, experience and the number of times he had given
the HGN test. See id. at 769. The Appellate Division ruled, however, that even if the officer’s testimony had been
offered as an expert opinion, it would have been error to allow it as the officer’s credential did not qualify him to
testify as an expert. See id. at 770.

In its decision, the Loomis court cited People v. Kelly, 17 Cal. 3d 24, 130 Cal. Rptr. 144, 549 P.2d 1240 (1976)
(holding there was no showing of that the HGN test was generally accepted in the scientific community).

Here, the Court should follow Loomis. In this case, evidence of approximate blood alcohol levels allegedly
determined by the HGN test is going to be given great weight by the trier of fact. Further, the Commonwealth will be
unable to show the reliability of the HGN test or its validity because they have not proffered a medical expert and
will not be able to who should be allowed to testify with regard to their opinion in this matter.
 CONCLUSION

 Form MOL 9.02 Memorandum of Law in Support of Motion in Limine Regarding Horizontal Gaze Nystagmus
 (HGN)

Therefore, the standard proffered by the Court in Lanigan and in light of the holding in Loomis has not been met.
Since neither the reliability of the HGN field sobriety test nor the qualification of the witness (i.e., arresting officer)
can be established. Therefore, due to the foregoing, the evidence should be excluded.

Respectfully submitted,
[DEFENDANT]
By his attorney,
____________________________________________
[ATTORNEY NAME]
[ATTORNEY ADDRESS]
Dated: ______________________

LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law Form MOL 9.03

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Forms Appendix

Form MOL 9.03 Motion in Limine to Exclude Breath Test Results

[1] Practice Tip

Excluding breath test results can often be the difference between a guilty verdict and a not guilty verdict. Defense
counsel must explore all opportunities to exclude such results by a motion in limine. This motion can also be filed as
a motion to suppress earlier in the case.

[2] Form
 COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS
 [COUNTY], SS.: TRIAL COURT FOR
 THE
 COMMONWEALTH
 OF
 MASSACHUSETTS
 DOCKET NO.
 ____________

 COMMONWEALTH
 v.

 [DEFENDANT]

 MOTION IN LIMINE TO EXCLUDE BREATH TEST RESULTS

Now comes the defendant in the above-captioned matter and requests this Honorable Court to exclude any results
of any breath test administered to the above-named defendant.

In support thereof, the defendant states that the results of said test are not admissible until the Commonwealth
establishes the following evidentiary foundations:

1. The simulator solution used in the defendant’s breath test was properly certified, tested and replaced, pursuant to
501 C.M.R. 2.12.

2. The simulator was properly certified, pursuant to 501 C.M.R. 2.06.

3. The alleged business records of the Office of Alcohol Testing (“OAT”), in particular, the test results in the instant
case, do not qualify as business records pursuant to G.L. c. 233 sec. 78 as they were not made before the action
was commenced and were prepared in anticipation of litigation.

4. The test was administered on a properly certified instrument, pursuant to 501 C.M.R. 2.06.

 Rafael Faria

 Form MOL 9.03 Motion in Limine to Exclude Breath Test Results

5. The results of the breath test were reported and recorded in the maintenance and the use log pursuant to 501
C.M.R. 2.13-15.

6. The reading on the calibration standard analysis check performed at the time of the defendant’s breath test was
either a .14%, .15% .16% regarding, pursuant to 501 C.M.R. 2.14.

7. The test was performed by a certified breath test operator, as defined in 501C.M.R.2.07.

8. The alleged business records of the Office of Alcohol Testing are not properly certified as required by G.L. c. 233
sec. 76 (“genuineness of the signature of such officer shall be attested by the secretary of the commonwealth under
its seal”).

9. The defendant was not observed for a period of at least fifteen (15) minutes, prior to the administration of the test
pursuant to 501 C.M.R. 2.13

Respectfully submitted,
[DEFENDANT]
By his attorney,
____________________________________________
[ATTORNEY NAME]
[ATTORNEY ADDRESS]
Dated: ______________________

LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Forms Appendix

Form MOL 9.04 Motion in Limine to Exclude Reference to Objects Found in
Defendant’s Vehicle

[1] Practice Tip

The introduction of evidence of the presence of alcoholic bottles or cans (whether open or closed) can be highly
prejudicial for the defense. If the prosecution has such evidence, the defense should also evaluate if the evidence
can be excluded with a motion to suppress.

[2] Form
 COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS
 [COUNTY], SS.: TRIAL COURT FOR
 THE
 COMMONWEALTH
 OF
 MASSACHUSETTS
 DOCKET NO.
 ____________

 COMMONWEALTH
 v.

 [DEFENDANT]

 MOTION IN LIMINE TO EXCLUDE REFERENCE TO OBJECTS FOUND IN DEFENDANT’S MOTOR VEHICLE

Now comes [defendant], in the above-captioned case and moves this Honorable Court to exclude in limine the
prosecution from noting observations and/or seizures of [alcohol, cans, bottles, etc.] and states reasons therefor:
 (1) The [alcohol] seized had been in the vehicle for approximately one week. Two of the cans were frozen.
 See Exhibits A, B;
 (2) The police have no other evidence to indicate that the defendant was drinking in his motor vehicle, other
 than said cans of alcohol, at the time he was stopped;
 (3) The arresting officers knew or should have known that the condition of the cans involved and the bottle that
 the defendant had not been drinking from any of them prior to his being stopped and arrested; and,
 (4) Therefore, the evidence is highly prejudicial and outweighs any probative value based on relevancy as to
 whether or not the defendant was under the influence at the time he was placed under arrest.

Respectfully submitted,
[DEFENDANT]
By his attorney,

 Rafael Faria

 Form MOL 9.04 Motion in Limine to Exclude Reference to Objects Found in Defendant’s Vehicle

1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law Form MOL 9.05

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Forms Appendix

Form MOL 9.05 Motion in Limine to Exclude Breathalyzer Results Regarding
Per Se Charge

[1] Practice Tip

Excluding breath test results can often be the difference between a guilty verdict and a not guilty verdict. Defense
counsel must explore all opportunities to exclude such results by a motion in limine. This motion can also be filed as
a motion to suppress earlier in the case.

[2] Form
 COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS
 [COUNTY], SS.: TRIAL COURT FOR
 THE
 COMMONWEALTH
 OF
 MASSACHUSETTS
 DOCKET NO.
 ____________

 COMMONWEALTH
 v.

 [DEFENDANT]

 DEFENDANT’S MOTION IN LIMINE TO EXCLUDE EVIDENCE OF THE RESULTS OF THE BREATHALYZER
 TEST PURSUANT TO A PER SE CHARGE

[Defendant] respectfully moves this Honorable Court to preclude the Commonwealth from introducing results of the
[defendant]’s Breathalyzer test taken on [date] or from referring to any test that was given.

As reasons therefor, [defendant] states the Commonwealth possesses no admissible evidence to document the
defendant’s blood alcohol content at the time of the alleged offense, M.G.L. c. 90, § 24(e), “In any prosecution for a
violation of paragraph (a), evidence of the percentage, by weight, of alcohol in the defendant’s blood at the time of
the alleged offense, as shown by chemical test of analysis of his blood or is indicated by a chemical test or analysis
of his breath, shall be admissible and deemed relevant to the determination of the question of whether such
defendant was at such time under the influence of intoxicating liquor.”

Indeed, the Commonwealth does not possess any evidence at this time to demonstrate the defendant’s blood
alcohol content “at the time of the alleged offense”.

The alleged breath test was administered over one (1) hour after the arrest. Therefore, the test is inadmissible
pursuant to the specific language of the statute. Furthermore, the Commonwealth has not provided the Defendant

 Rafael Faria

 Form MOL 9.05 Motion in Limine to Exclude Breathalyzer Results Regarding Per Se Charge

of notice of any expert witness it intends to call to testify pursuant to a theory of retrograde extrapolation to
determine the defendant’s blood alcohol content at the time of the alleged offense pursuant to Commonwealth v.
Senior, 433 Mass. 453 (2001).

Therefore, the Commonwealth is unable to present reliable evidence as to the Defendant’s blood alcohol content
(“BAC”) at the time of the offense pursuant to M.G.L. c. 90, § 24(e) and the result from that test should be excluded.

Whereas, the [defendant] respectfully requests that the Commonwealth be precluded from introducing evidence at
trial of any information related to a breath test the Defendant submitted to at the [name] Police Station.

Respectfully submitted,
[DEFENDANT]
By his attorney,
____________________________________________
[ATTORNEY NAME]
[ATTORNEY ADDRESS]

entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 15-17 and Form Appendix

entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law Form MOL 9.06

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Forms Appendix

Form MOL 9.06 Motion to Exclude Opinion Testimony from Lay Witness

[1] Practice Tip

For any expert testimony the prosecutor introduces, make sure the expert testimony is explanatory, and not
presented in conclusory form, in terms of whether the defendant did or did not commit a particular offense. Such
testimony is not admissible, as it infringes on the jury. A motion in limine regarding expert testimony can be helpful
to require the prosecutor to specify on the record the precise testimony to be elicited.

[2] Form
 COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS
 [COUNTY], SS.: TRIAL COURT FOR
 THE
 COMMONWEALTH
 OF
 MASSACHUSETTS
 DOCKET NO.
 ____________

 COMMONWEALTH
 v.

 [DEFENDANT]

 MOTION IN LIMINE TO EXCLUDE EXPERT OPINION FROM A LAY WITNESS

Now comes the Defendant in the above captioned complaint and moves this Honorable Court to exclude evidence,
including testimony, concerning opinion evidence and testimony of Officer [name]. The defense anticipates that he
or she will be called as an “expert” to opine on medical issues including, but limited to his or her opinion to Mr. or
Ms. XXXXXX’s impairment and whether the impairment relates to drug use or a medical condition. The officer’s
education history does not include any evidence that the officer is a licensed medical doctor or received a degree
related to the practice of medicine (See Exhibit A).

I. The Court Should Exclude The Officer’s Testimony

[Defendant] moves the Court for an order prior to trial to exclude the testimony of Officer [name], on the grounds
that his testimony is unreliable. Officer [name] is not qualified to testify in the areas medicine and his methodology is
not reliable. His testimony does not meet the minimum standards for expert testimony as outlined in Daubert v.
Merrell Dow Pharmaceuticals, Inc., 509 U.S. 579 (1993) and Kumho Tire Co. v. Carmichael, 119 S. Ct. 1167
(1999), and adopted by the Commonwealth of Massachusetts in Commonwealth v. Lanigan, 419 Mass. 15 (1994),
and Hicks v. Brox Industries, Inc., 47 Mass. App. Ct. 103 (1999) . Accordingly, Officer [name]’s testimony should be
excluded.

 Rafael Faria

 Form MOL 9.06 Motion to Exclude Opinion Testimony from Lay Witness

II. The Court Must Conduct A Daubert Hearing

In the alternative, the [defendant] moves for a hearing to determine whether 1) the theory underlying the opinion of
Officer [name] has been tested; 2) the theories and techniques utilized have been subject to peer review and
publication; 3) the rate of error of such testing is known and whether the said error rate can be applied accurately;
4) whether standards exist to control this form of testing and whether the standards were applied here; and 5) what
is the degree of acceptance of such testing within the relevant community. See Daubert v. Merrell Dow
Pharmaceuticals, Inc., 509 U.S. 579 (1993); Commonwealth v. Lanigan, 419 Mass. 15 (1994); Frye v. United
States, 293 F. 1013 (D.C. Cir. 1923); Commonwealth v. Curnin, 409 Mass. 218 (1991). Daubert requires an inquiry
into both relevance and reliability, applies not only to “scientific” testimony, but to all expert testimony. Kumho Tire
Co., Ltd. V. Carmichael, 526 U.S. 137 (1999).

As reason therefor, the defendant states that such evidence is misleading, confusing, unreliable, not probative,
highly prejudicial and is not relevant, and therefore if introduced into evidence would violate the defendant’s rights
to a fair trial, due process and to confront witnesses, said rights guaranteed under the Fifth, Sixth, and Fourteenth
Amendments to the United States Constitution and Articles 1 and 12 of the Massachusetts Declaration of Rights.

Respectfully submitted,
____________________________________________
[DEFENDANT]
By his attorney,
____________________________________________
[ATTORNEY NAME]
[ATTORNEY ADDRESS]

LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law Form MOL 9.07

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Forms Appendix

Form MOL 9.07 Motion in Limine to Exclude Evidence of Refusal to Perform
Field Sobriety Tests

[1] Practice Tip

Introducing a defendant’s refusal to submit to field sobriety tests would infringe on the defendant’s constitutional
right. If there is a refusal, make sure that the prosecutor is precluded from introducing evidence regarding the
refusal at trial.

[2] Form
 COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS
 [COUNTY], SS.: TRIAL COURT FOR
 THE
 COMMONWEALTH
 OF
 MASSACHUSETTS
 DOCKET NO.
 ____________

 COMMONWEALTH
 v.

 [DEFENDANT]

 MOTION IN LIMINE TO PRECLUDE REFUSAL OF FIELD SOBRIETY TESTS

[Defendant] hereby moves in limine to preclude introduction by the Commonwealth of his statements and actions
with respect to his refusal to submit to field sobriety testing. Specifically, [defendant] moves to preclude the
Commonwealth from introducing or making reference to the following:

[Defendant]’s statements to Trooper X after being requested to submit to field sobriety testing.

In support of his motion in limine, [defendant] states as follows:
 1. [Defendant] was stopped by Trooper X on [date and time] at [location]. At the time, Trooper X ordered
 [defendant] from his motor vehicle to conduct field sobriety testing.
 2. Defendant refused to submit to the field sobriety tests. In connection with his refusal to submit to field
 sobriety tests, [defendant] made statements to Trooper X.
 3. Trooper X arrested [defendant] and charged him with operating under the influence of alcohol.
 4. Trooper X’s questioning of [defendant] and his responses thereto are inadmissible. See Commonwealth v.
 Blais, 428 Mass. 294, 701 N.E.2d 314 (1998); Commonwealth v. Ranieri, 65 Mass. App. Ct. 366 (2006).

 Rafael Faria

 Form MOL 9.07 Motion in Limine to Exclude Evidence of Refusal to Perform Field Sobriety Tests

 5. Accordingly, [defendant] requests that the Commonwealth be precluded from introducing and/or
 referencing any statements made by [defendant] in exercising his right to refuse to submit to field sobriety
 testing.

Respectfully submitted,
By [Defendant]
____________________________________________
[ATTORNEY NAME]
[ATTORNEY ADDRESS]
Dated: ______________________

Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.
