1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law Form MOL 9.08

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Forms Appendix

Form MOL 9.08 Motion in Limine to Exclude Evidence of Refusal to Take
Breath Test and Election Regarding Jury Instruction

[1] Practice Tip

Introducing a defendant’s refusal to submit to a breath test infringes on the defendant’s constitutional right. If there
is a refusal, make sure that the prosecutor is precluded from introducing evidence regarding the refusal at trial.

[2] Form
 COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS
 [COUNTY], SS.: TRIAL COURT FOR
 THE
 COMMONWEALTH
 OF
 MASSACHUSETTS
 DOCKET NO.
 ____________

 COMMONWEALTH
 v.

 [DEFENDANT]

 MOTION IN LIMINE TO PRECLUDE REFUSAL OF FIELD SOBRIETY TESTS

[Defendant] hereby moves in limine to preclude introduction by the Commonwealth of his statements and actions
with respect to his refusal to submit to the breath test and elects that jury [should] [should not] be instructed to
disregard the refusal. Specifically, [defendant] moves to preclude the Commonwealth from introducing or making
reference to the following:

[Defendant]’s statements to Trooper X after being requested to submit to field sobriety testing.

In support of his motion in limine, [defendant] states as follows:
 1. [Defendant] was arrested by Trooper X on [date and time] at [location] for operating under the influence.
 2. During the booking process, Trooper X offered the Defendant the opportunity to take a breathalyzer test.
 3. The Defendant refused the offer and did not take the breathalyzer test.
 4. Trooper X’s questioning of [defendant] and his responses thereto are inadmissible. See Commonwealth v.
 Wolfe, 478 Mass. 142, 149, 83 N.E.3d 811, 817 (2017).

 Rafael Faria

 Form MOL 9.08 Motion in Limine to Exclude Evidence of Refusal to Take Breath Test and Election Regarding
 Jury Instruction

 5. Accordingly, [defendant] requests that the Commonwealth be precluded from introducing and/or
 referencing any statements made by [defendant] in exercising his right to refuse to submit to the
 breathalyzer test.
 6. Moreover, the Defendant elects [does not elect] for the Court to read an instruction to the jury explaining to
 the jurors that they are not to consider the absence of breath test evidence, as approved in Commonwealth
 v. Downs, 53 Mass. App. Ct. 195, 199–200, 758 N.E.2d 1062, 1065 (2001) , The election is the Defendant’s
 to make. Commonwealth v. Wolfe, 478 Mass. 142, 149, 83 N.E.3d 811, 817 (2017).

Respectfully submitted,
By [Defendant]

entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law Form MOL 9.09

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Forms Appendix

Form MOL 9.09 Motion in Limine to Exclude Prior Convictions

[1] Practice Tip

The Commonwealth is not permitted to introduce prior convictions that are similar to the underlying charge. In an
OUI case, the Commonwealth cannot introduce evidence of or refer to prior OUI convictions.

[2] Form
 COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS
 [COUNTY], SS.: TRIAL COURT FOR
 THE
 COMMONWEALTH
 OF
 MASSACHUSETTS
 DOCKET NO.
 ____________

 COMMONWEALTH
 v.

 [DEFENDANT]

 MOTION IN LIMINE TO PRECLUDE PRIOR CONVICTIONS

[Defendant] hereby moves in limine to preclude introduction of his prior OUI conviction(s) as evidence at trial by the
Commonwealth. Specifically, [defendant] moves to preclude the Commonwealth from introducing or making
reference to the following:
 1. Evidence or reference to any prior bad act of the [defendant] for any crime or act similar to the offense with
 which he has been charged including, without limitation, any prior OUI conviction(s).
 2. The probative value of any such evidence to the Commonwealth is substantially outweighed by the danger
 of unfair prejudice to [defendant]. Indeed, it is black letter law that evidence of prior bad acts cannot be
 used by the Commonwealth to establish bad character. Commonwealth v. Helfant, 398 Mass. 214, 224
 (1986). Rather, evidence of prior bad acts may only be used to establish intent, motive, identity, pattern of
 conduct, or common scheme-none of which are relevant here.
 3. As such, the Commonwealth should be precluded from introducing and/or referencing any prior bad acts of
 the defendant.

Respectfully submitted,
By [Defendant]
____________________________________________

 Rafael Faria

 Form MOL 9.09 Motion in Limine to Exclude Prior Convictions

[ATTORNEY NAME]
[ATTORNEY ADDRESS]
Dated: ______________________

1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law Form MOL 9.10

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Forms Appendix

Form MOL 9.10 Motion in Limine to Exclude Portable Breathalyzer Results

[1] Practice Tip

Portable breathalyzer results are not admissible at trial in Massachusetts because the results are not sufficiently
reliable. The police often use portable breathalyzer results during arrests. If there is a portable breathalyzer result,
make sure to move to exclude its introduction at trial.

[2] Form
 COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS
 [COUNTY], SS.: TRIAL COURT FOR
 THE
 COMMONWEALTH
 OF
 MASSACHUSETTS
 DOCKET NO.
 ____________

 COMMONWEALTH
 v.

 [DEFENDANT]

 MOTION IN LIMINE TO PRECLUDE RESULTS OF PORTABLE BREATHALYZER TEST

Now comes [defendant] who is charged with operating a motor vehicle while under the influence of intoxicating
liquor (“OUI”). See M.G.L. c. 90, § 24. [Defendant] moves to prevent the Commonwealth from introducing evidence
of or making reference to the results of a Portable Breathalyzer Test (PBT) as a test administered to [defendant] by
the arresting officer.
[Defendant] gives as his reasons therefor:
 1. The PBT test has a scientific basis, which is not within the common knowledge of a lay person and
 requires expert testimony.
 2. The arresting officer is not qualified to testify as an expert witness as to the scientific basis, reliability and
 general acceptance of the PBT test in the scientific community.
 3. The Commonwealth cannot present evidence demonstrating that the PBT test is generally accepted in the
 scientific community as a reliable indicator of the correlation between the consumption of alcohol and the
 results of the test.
 4. The PBT does not comply with the Massachusetts CMRs or the Massachusetts General Laws, regarding
 the administration of Breathalyzer Tests in the Commonwealth.

 Rafael Faria

 Form MOL 9.10 Motion in Limine to Exclude Portable Breathalyzer Results

WHEREFORE, [defendant] respectfully requests that the Commonwealth be precluded from introducing evidence
of or making reference to the administration of or the results of the PBT administered to [defendant] by the arresting
officer.

Respectfully submitted,
[DEFENDANT]
By his attorney,
____________________________________________
[ATTORNEY NAME]
[ATTORNEY ADDRESS]
Dated: ______________________

1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law Form MOL 9.19

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Forms Appendix

Form MOL 9.19 Request for Voir Dire Questions

[1] Practice Tip

The Court will always ask standard voir dire questions of potential jurors. Make sure that if you want a question
considered, you propose the question in advance of trial.

[2] Form
 COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS
 [COUNTY], SS.: TRIAL COURT FOR
 THE
 COMMONWEALTH
 OF
 MASSACHUSETTS
 DOCKET NO.
 ____________

 COMMONWEALTH
 v.

 [DEFENDANT]

 VOIR DIRE QUESTIONS

1. [Defendant] is charged with operating a motor vehicle under the influence of intoxicating liquors. Does that
charge make it difficult for you to remain impartial or interfere with your ability to decide the case?

2. Are you or any of your relatives or friends members of Mothers Against Drunk Driving (MADD), Fathers Against
Drunk Driving, or any other similar-type organization?

3. Some of the witnesses are police officers. If one of these police officers were to say that a certain thing
happened would you tend to believe the police officer more than the defendant due to his status as a police officer?

4. Are you or someone you know a member of Alcoholics Anonymous, Alateen, or Alanon, or a related group? If
so, would this affect your ability to be impartial in a case involving alcohol?

5. Do you think a person should be punished because he was drinking and driving even though he was not
intoxicated?

6. Do you feel that a person who drinks alcohol and then drives a car has violated the law, regardless of the effect
on him?

Respectfully Submitted,

 Rafael Faria

[DEFENDANT]
By his/her attorney,

entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law Form MOL 9.20

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Forms Appendix

Form MOL 9.20 Motion to Bifurcate

[1] Practice Tip

The prejudice is significant when a defendant must face an operating under the influence charge as well as any
charge in which the Commonwealth will be required to prove a prior operating under the influence conviction at trial.
A motion to bifurcate should be filed in such circumstances.

[2] Form
 COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS
 MIDDLESEX, SS.: TRIAL COURT FOR
 THE
 COMMONWEALTH
 OF
 MASSACHUSETTS

 COMMONWEALTH
 v.

 [DEFENDANT]

 MOTION TO BIFURCATE

Now comes [defendant] in the above-captioned case and moves this Honorable Court to bifurcate the charges in
this case to be tried separately and states reasons therefor:

(1) The defendant is charged with operating under the influence of alcohol as well as operating after a suspended
license for operating under the influence;

(2) The prosecution intends to try these charges together, which means that the jury will hear evidence that the
defendant was previously convicted of operating under the influence while deciding if the defendant was operating
under the influence on [date of offense];

(3) In Commonwealth v. Beaulieu, 79 Mass. App. Ct. 100, 944 N.E.2d 1057 (2011), the Massachusetts Court
Appeals affirmed a trial court’s decision to allow these charges to be tried at the same time and for the jury to hear
evidence for both as long as the trial judge properly instructed the jury. In Commonwealth v. Lopes, 85 Mass. App.
Ct. 341, 10 N.E.3d 146 (2014), the Appeals Court affirmed this practice, but cautioned, “Beaulieu should not be
understood to discourage bifurcation as a means to prevent potential prejudice in cases of this nature.”;

(4) The potential prejudice to the defendant is great and the charges should be tried separately.

Respectfully Submitted,
[DEFENDANT]

 Rafael Faria

 Form MOL 9.20 Motion to Bifurcate

By his attorney,
____________________________________________
[ATTORNEY NAME]
[ATTORNEY ADDRESS]
Dated: ______________________

Chapter 15 POST-TRIAL MOTIONS AND APPEALS

 PART I: STRATEGY

 § 15.01 Scope

entries.title: Motions for Required Findings (Rule 25)
entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 15-17 and Form Appendix
entries.sourceFile: __15.04 Motions for Required Findings (Rule 25).pdf
entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 15.04

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 15 POST-TRIAL MOTIONS AND
APPEALS > PART II: PREPARING POST-TRIAL MOTIONS AND APPEALS

§ 15.04 Motions for Required Findings (Rule 25)

Regardless of whether it is a bench or jury trial, Massachusetts Rule of Criminal Procedure 25 (Rule 25) governs a
motion for required findings of not guilty. Rule 25 allows a motion to be filed at the close of the prosecutor’s case as
well as at the close of all evidence.

The standard for deciding a motion for required findings of not guilty is “whether, after viewing the evidence in the
light most favorable to the prosecution, any rational trier of fact could have found the essential elements of the
crime beyond a reasonable doubt.” Commonwealth v. Shabo, 47 Mass. App. Ct. 923, 924, 715 N.E.2d 475 (1999) ;
Commonwealth v. Carter, 423 Mass. 506, 669 N.E.2d 203 (1996). Rule 25(a) requires the court to rule on a motion
for required findings of not guilty immediately when made at the end of the prosecutor’s case.

Rule 25(b)(1) and (2) allows the court to reserve ruling on a motion for required findings of not guilty made at the
close of all evidence until: (1) before or after the jury returns; and (2) after discharge of the jury without delivering
the verdict. Lastly, Rule 25(b)(2) grants the judge discretion to find the defendant guilty of a lesser included crime,
set aside a guilty verdict and order a new trial, and enter a finding of not guilty notwithstanding the verdict.

 Warning:

 Issues not raised in a motion for required findings may be waived, so it is important to file such a motion at
 the close of the prosecutor’s case and the close of all evidence.

LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

 End of Document

 Rafael Faria

1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 15.05

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 15 POST-TRIAL MOTIONS AND
APPEALS > PART II: PREPARING POST-TRIAL MOTIONS AND APPEALS

§ 15.05 Use of Caretaker Statute to Prevent Incarceration

Massachusetts now has a the caretaker statute, G.L. c. 279, § 6B(b) that provides: “Unless a sentence of
incarceration is required by law, the court may, upon conviction, consider the defendant’s status as a primary
caretaker of a dependent child before imposing a sentence.” The Court has to consider this statute if applicable
prior to sentencing a defendant to incarceration and make written findings regarding the Court’s decision.
Commonwealth v. Martin, 98 Mass. App. Ct. 727, 729–30, 159 N.E.3d 722, 725–26 (2020) (reversing trial court’s
decision rejecting statute as unconstitutional).

entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 15-17 and Form Appendix

entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 15.06

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 15 POST-TRIAL MOTIONS AND
APPEALS > PART II: PREPARING POST-TRIAL MOTIONS AND APPEALS

§ 15.06 Motions to Revise and Revoke (Rule 29)

Massachusetts Rule of Criminal Procedure 29 (Rule 29) governs motions to revise or revoke a previous sentence.
Indeed, a previous sentence may be revised/revoked at any time if it appears that justice may not have been done.
These motions must be filed within 60 days after the imposition of a sentence or after an appeal is affirmed or
denied. The Court has no discretion to alter this deadline. Commonwealth v. Burrone, 347 Mass. 451, 198 N.E.2d
407 (1964).

A motion to revoke or revise a sentence must be accompanied by an affidavit establishing grounds as to why the
motion should be allowed. Reasons to revoke or revise include hardships (medical or otherwise), as well as
disparate sentences given to codefendants.

Importantly, you should weigh the risk versus the reward in filing such a motion, as the court has the authority to
also increase a sentence. Commonwealth v. Carver, 33 Mass. App. Ct. 378, 600 N.E.2d 588 (1992).

The Commonwealth may use Rule 29 to revise a sentence if a continuance without a finding was imposed and it
was not an authorized sentence. Commonwealth v. Beverly, 485 Mass. 1, 6, 147 N.E.3d 426, 431 (2020).

LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

 End of Document

 Rafael Faria

entries.title: Motion for New Trial (Rule 30)
entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 15-17 and Form Appendix
entries.sourceFile: __15.07 Motion for New Trial (Rule 30).pdf
entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 15.07

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 15 POST-TRIAL MOTIONS AND
APPEALS > PART II: PREPARING POST-TRIAL MOTIONS AND APPEALS

§ 15.07 Motion for New Trial (Rule 30)

Massachusetts Rule of Criminal Procedure 30 (Rule 30) governs motions for a new trial. A motion for a new trial
must be submitted to the trial judge or the judge who took the defendant’s plea. Pursuant to Rule 30(c)(3), the party
moving for a new trial must submit an affidavit supporting its position. A judge may grant a motion for a new trial “at
any time if it appears justice may not have been done.” Mass. R. Crim. P. 30(b). Three common bases for filing a
motion for a new trial include circumstances surrounding the conduct of the trial, newly discovered evidence, and
pleas that were not freely and knowingly entered. There is no time limit on filing a motion for a new trial.

Examples of a motion for a new trial based on the conduct of the trial include: improper jury instructions,
Commonwealth v. Francis, 411 Mass. 579, 583 N.E.2d 849 (1992) ; the Commonwealth’s failure to disclose
exculpatory evidence, Commonwealth v. Schand, 420 Mass. 783, 653 N.E.2d 566 (1995); and juror misconduct,
Commonwealth v. Fidler, 377 Mass. 192, 204, 385 N.E.2d 513, 520 (1979) (reversing denial of motion for new trial
based on allegations of jury misconduct) (reversed on other grounds by Mass R. Prof. Conduct 3.5(c)). A juror who
slept through the trial could require a new trial if the Court took no action to remedy the situation. “ ‘[A] judicial
observation that a juror is asleep, or a judge’s receipt of reliable information to that effect, requires prompt judicial
intervention.’ ” Commonwealth v. Faircloth, 96 Mass. App. Ct. 1102, 134 N.E.3d 1150, review denied, 483 Mass.
1105, 137 N.E.3d 1066 (2019) (quoting Commonwealth v. Beneche, 458 Mass. 61, 78, 933 N.E.2d 951 (2010)).

For defendants who pled guilty and their case involved a breath test during the period when breath test results
could not be used, the defendant will not automatically receive a new trial. Instead, they must “demonstrate a
reasonable probability that he … would not have pleaded guilty had he … known of OAT's misconduct.”
Commonwealth v. Hallinan, 491 Mass 730, 750 (2023); Commonwealth v. D.H., 261 N.E.3d 903 (Mass. App. Ct.
2025) (unpublished decision).

To succeed on a motion for a new trial based on newly discovered evidence, the defendant must establish that the
new evidence could not have been discovered through reasonable pretrial diligence, it casts doubt on the justice of
the conviction, it is material, it is credible, and it “carr[ies] a measure of strength in support of the defendant’s
position.” Commonwealth v. Scanlon, 412 Mass. 664, 680, 592 N.E.2d 1279 (1992).

“[T]he standard for prejudice with respect to an ineffective assistance of counsel claim is an objective one.”
Commonwealth v. Tompkins, 101 Mass. App. Ct. 1102, 185 N.E.3d 954 (2022) (unpublished). “The question is not
whether the judge, subjectively, concludes that he would have found the defendant not guilty had the evidence
been presented. The question is what, objectively, the impact of the error would have been on a reasonable finder
of fact coming freshly to the case.” Tompkins, 101 Mass. App. Ct. 1102.

Lastly, a motion for a new trial may be filed if you believe your client did not enter a plea freely and knowingly. A
plea of guilty “must be later set aside, unless the record shows affirmatively that the defendant entered the plea
freely and understandingly.” Commonwealth v. Foster, 368 Mass. 100, 102, 330 N.E.2d 155, 157 (1975) (emphasis
added) (finding that the affirmative showing must be made and recorded at the time the judge accepts the plea).
When a defendant does, indeed, plan to plead guilty, he or she necessarily waives several federal constitutional
rights. See Malloy v. Hogan, 378 U.S. 1, 84 S. Ct. 1489, 12 L. Ed. 2d 653 (1964) . These rights include the right to a
jury trial. See Commonwealth v. Fernandes, 390 Mass. 714, 715–716, 459 N.E.2d 787, 788–789 (1984) (finding a

 Rafael Faria

 § 15.07 Motion for New Trial (Rule 30)

defendant did not act voluntarily when the colloquy lacked an inquiry regarding consultation with counsel or
wrongful inducement). Because a plea involves these Constitutional rights, it is only valid if the defendant offers it
voluntarily, with awareness of the consequences. For these conditions to be met, it must be shown affirmatively on
the record. See Boykin v. Alabama, 395 U.S. 238, 242–244, 89 S. Ct. 1709, 23 L. Ed. 2d 274 (1969).

At a minimum, a pleading defendant must be informed that he or she is waiving: (1) the right to a jury trial, (2) the
right to confront witnesses, and (3) the privilege against self-incrimination. See Commonwealth v. Dummer, 47
Mass. App. Ct. 926, 927, 716 N.E.2d 166, 168 (1999) (holding that a failure to inform a defendant of the waiver of
these rights requires the withdrawal of the plea). To the extent your client was not advised that he or she was
waiving these rights, you may consider filing a motion for a new trial on those grounds.

 Strategic Point:

 A motion for a new trial is commonly used when a defendant is facing a subsequent OUI charge to try to
 eliminate prior offenses.

 Warning:

 If a motion for a new trial is granted, the Commonwealth may try to re-prove the case. Often, this is
 impossible to do, as evidence has been lost or destroyed or necessary officer witnesses have retired. If a
 motion is granted and the Commonwealth re-proves the case, it may seek to impose a harsher sentence
 than the one the defendant already served. The defendant should be advised of this possibility to make an
 informed choice prior to the filing of such a motion.

LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

 End of Document

entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 15-17 and Form Appendix

entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 15.08

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 15 POST-TRIAL MOTIONS AND
APPEALS > PART II: PREPARING POST-TRIAL MOTIONS AND APPEALS

§ 15.08 Stay of Execution of Sentence (Rule 31)

Massachusetts Rule of Criminal Procedure 31 (Rule 31) governs motions to stay an execution of sentence pending
appeal as well as to stay a term of probation or suspended sentence. Such a motion must be made to the
sentencing judge or, if not practicable to do so, to a single justice of the Supreme Judicial Court. Such a motion may
include a request to stay payment of fines and costs, as long as the defendant demonstrates that he or she has
perfected and is diligently pursuing an appeal.

Factors considered by the court in deciding whether to allow such a motion include security considerations, as
enumerated by Mass. G.L. c. 276, § 58, as well as whether such an appeal has merit. Commonwealth v. Hodge,
380 Mass. 851, 856 (1980); Commonwealth v. Allen, 378 Mass. 489, 498, 392 N.E.2d 1027, 1032–33 (1979);
Stranad v. Commonwealth, 366 Mass. 847, 318 N.E.2d 617 (1974) . As such, any such motion filed should address
these two factors in great detail.

LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

 End of Document

entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 15-17 and Form Appendix

entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 15.09

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 15 POST-TRIAL MOTIONS AND
APPEALS > PART II: PREPARING POST-TRIAL MOTIONS AND APPEALS

§ 15.09 Motion to Restore License After Not Guilty Finding

If your client is found not guilty of the OUI charge and has no other alcohol-related charges pending against him or
her, you should immediately file a motion to have your client’s license restored. Mass. G.L. c. 90, § 24(1)(f)(1)(iii).

 Strategic Point:

 You should include proposed written findings of fact that the judge can sign concurrently with his or her
 restoration order.

 Warning:

 The motion to restore the license needs to be made “immediately” upon the finding of not guilty. Otherwise,
 the defendant will lose the right to have the license restored. Commonwealth v. Richards, 480 Mass. 413,
 421–22, 105 N.E.3d 1168, 1174–75 (2018) (reversing restoration of license made after a later filed motion).

Notably, unless the Commonwealth establishes by a preponderance of the evidence that the restoration of your
client’s licenses endangers public safety, the presumption is that his or her license should be restored.

LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

 End of Document

 Rafael Faria

entries.title: Appeals
entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 15-17 and Form Appendix
entries.sourceFile: __15.10 Appeals.pdf
entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 15.10

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 15 POST-TRIAL MOTIONS AND
APPEALS > PART II: PREPARING POST-TRIAL MOTIONS AND APPEALS

§ 15.10 Appeals

Your notice of appeal must be filed within 30 days of either the verdict or sentence, whichever date is later. The
notice of appeal should state the date and actions/rulings that are being appealed. Additional time, which must be
sought from the trial court, may be granted for excusable neglect. Carelessness of counsel in missing the deadline
does not constitute excusable neglect. Notably, counsel can toll the initial 30-day period for filing a notice of appeal
by filing a timely motion for a new trial. Specifically, the motion for a new trial must be “filed in the lower court within
thirty days after the verdict or finding of guilt or within thirty days after imposition of sentence and the full time fixed
by this rule shall commence to run and shall be computed from the date of entry of an order denying such motion.”
Mass. R. App. P. 4(b).

 Warning:

 A notice of appeal contains a one-sentence description of what is being appealed. There is little substance
 to it. Defense counsel may consider filing the notice immediately upon losing a jury verdict to preserve all the
 defendant’s rights.

 Warning:

 After you file a notice of appeal, you must request the preparation of the record. You will need the hearing
 transcript from the trial and any relevant pretrial hearing, such as a motion to suppress or motion to dismiss
 hearing. Indeed, the failure to request the relevant hearing transcript can be the basis to deny the appeal.
 Commonwealth v. McCarthy, 103 Mass. App. Ct. 1120, 225 N.E.3d 844 (2024) (“To the extent the defendant
 challenges the denial of her motion to suppress her admission, she has waived that claim by not providing
 us with a copy of the hearing transcript and by not supporting the claim with adequate appellate argument.”).

LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

 End of Document

 Rafael Faria

entries.title: Motion to Reconsider
entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 15-17 and Form Appendix
entries.sourceFile: __15.11 Motion to Reconsider.pdf
entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 15.11

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 15 POST-TRIAL MOTIONS AND
APPEALS > PART II: PREPARING POST-TRIAL MOTIONS AND APPEALS

§ 15.11 Motion to Reconsider

If the judge makes an error of law or fact with respect to a decision, the defendant may move the court to reconsider
the decision. This can serve as a quicker and lower cost means to correct an error than an appeal. Motions to
reconsider are authorized by Mass. R. Crim. P. 13(a)(5).

 Warning:

 Judges typically do not appreciate parties asking them to decide again something that they just decided and
 motions for reconsideration are typically heard by the original motion judge. For these reasons, motions to
 reconsider should only be used sparingly.

LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

 End of Document

§ 16.03 CHECKLIST: Suspensions Prior to Conviction

 • An operator’s motor vehicle license may be suspended prior to conviction for failing or refusing a breath
 test.

 Discussion:

 Forms:

 • Failing a breath test with a 0.08 or above results in a 30-day suspension.

 Mass. G.L. c. 90, § 24(1).

 • Refusing a breath test results in a 180-day loss of license.

 § 16.03 CHECKLIST: Suspensions Prior to Conviction

 Mass. G.L. c. 90, § 24(1)(f)(1).

 Forms:

 • An individual who is under 21 can incur a youth alcohol program suspension.

 Discussion:

REVOCATION > PART II: SUSPENSIONS PRIOR TO CONVICTION

§ 16.05 Failure of Breath Test

If an individual over the age of 21 takes a breath test and has a result of 0.08 or above, there is a 30-day
suspension of license. Mass. G.L. c. 90, § 24(1). If an individual under the age of 21 takes a breath test and blows
0.02 or above, there is a 30-day suspension of license and the individual must complete a youth alcohol program.
Additionally, there is a $500 reinstatement fee after the suspension terminates.

entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 16.06

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 16 LICENSE SUSPENSION AND
REVOCATION > PART II: SUSPENSIONS PRIOR TO CONVICTION

§ 16.06 Refusal of Breath Test

Under Mass. G.L. c. 90, § 24(1)(f)(1), if an individual refuses to take a breath test (also known as chemical test
refusal, or “CTR”), his or her license will be suspended for a period of at least 180 days. The length of a CTR
suspension is determined by the individual’s prior history of OUIs, if any. Set forth below is a chart detailing various
suspension periods:

 Age Prior Convictions Length of Suspension
 21 or older 0 180 Days
 1 3 Years
 2 5 Years
 3 or more Lifetime
 Under 21 0 3 Years
 1 3 Years
 2 5 Years
 3 or more Lifetime

A defendant can have two different suspensions running at the same time. Commonwealth v. Moore, 97 Mass. App.
Ct. 1115, 145 N.E.3d 895, review denied, 485 Mass. 1104, 150 N.E.3d 1127 (2020) (unpublished) (lifetime
suspensions for breath test refusal and OUI conviction running at the same time).

Additionally, if an individual who refuses a breath test has a prior OUI involving serious bodily injury, then a 10-year
suspension is imposed. Lastly, if any individual refuses a breath test and has a prior OUI conviction in which a
vehicular homicide occurred, a lifetime suspension is imposed.

The penalty is different for the charge of OUI while boating. For that charge, the maximum penalty for refusing a
chemical test is 120 days. Commonwealth v. Thompson, 87 Mass. App. Ct. 572, 32 N.E.3d 1273 (2015).

Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 16.11

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 16 LICENSE SUSPENSION AND
REVOCATION > PART III: SUSPENSIONS AFTER CONVICTION OR PLEA

§ 16.11 OUI While Operating After Suspension

An individual may be charged under Mass. G.L. c. 90, §§ 24(1)(a), 24D, 24E, 24G, 24L, and 24N for operating a
vehicle with a suspended license for a prior OUI conviction or admission to sufficient facts. Indeed, the driver may
be charged for both an OUI and OUI with a suspended license under these circumstances. In addition to a one-year
suspension of his or her license, the individual will be subject to a minimum one-year jail sentence. Notably,
pursuant to Melanie’s Law, 2005 Mass. Acts c. 122, a suspension under the statutes above will start to run after the
OUI suspension for the prior offense; they do not run concurrently.

 Exception:

 The charge of operating a vehicle after having a license suspended for OUI only covers suspensions for OUI
 dispositions, and not suspensions regarding breath test refusals or failures.

 Exception:

 Individuals cannot be charged with both Operating with a Suspended License and Operating with a
 Suspended License for OUI, as the two are duplicative. Commonwealth v. Bishop, 99 Mass. App. Ct. 1126,
 170 N.E.3d 347, review denied, 488 Mass. 1101, 172 N.E.3d 716 (2021); Commonwealth v. Phuon, 486
 Mass. 35, 40 (2020).

entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 16.13

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 16 LICENSE SUSPENSION AND
REVOCATION > PART III: SUSPENSIONS AFTER CONVICTION OR PLEA

§ 16.13 Cahill Disposition

An individual who has been convicted of an OUI and has only one previous conviction for an OUI that is 10 or more
years prior may be eligible for a “Cahill disposition.” In Commonwealth v. Cahill, 442 Mass. 127, 810 N.E.2d 1196
(2004), the Supreme Judicial Court held that an individual charged with a second OUI, who had a previous
conviction more than 10 years earlier, was subject to a loss of license of not more than 90 days, regardless of
certain other statutory provisions prescribing heightened penalties for second-time offenders. To calculate the 10-
year period in determining whether an individual may receive a Cahill disposition, the time period between the
original OUI disposition date and the new offense date is considered.

If there is, in fact, a 10-year period of time that elapsed between OUI convictions, an individual given a Cahill
disposition may qualify for many of the benefits afforded to a first offender disposition under Mass. G.L. c. 90, §
24D. Importantly, a Cahill disposition counts as a second offense with regard to any future OUI convictions. Mass.
G.L. c. 90, § 24D.

LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

 End of Document

entries.title: Boating Under the Influence
entries.collectionLabel: OUI Practice Guide: Ch. 15-17 and Form Appendix
entries.sourceFile: __16.14 Boating Under the Influence.pdf
entries.text:
1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 16.14

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 16 LICENSE SUSPENSION AND
REVOCATION > PART III: SUSPENSIONS AFTER CONVICTION OR PLEA

§ 16.14 Boating Under the Influence

Massachusetts has one of the strongest boating under the influence laws in the nation. Indeed, an operator’s motor
vehicle license may be revoked for boating under the influence. Mass. G.L. c. 90, § 8. If a boating under the
influence suspect refuses to submit to a breath test, his or her motor vehicle license is revoked for 120 days. Similar
to an OUI disposition regarding motor vehicles, a boating under the influence conviction results in a loss of license
for the defendant’s motor vehicle. The license loss period depends on whether the defendant has prior convictions
for OUI (whether involving a motor vehicle or a boat). The period ranges from 45 days for a first OUI charge to 15
years for a fourth or greater subsequent OUI charge. There is only a 10-year look-back period for boating under the
influence subsequent offenses, unlike the lifetime look-back period for motor vehicle offenses. In addition, the boat
registration (called a “certificate of number”) may also be suspended.

 Practice Tip:

 The license loss for refusing a chemical test in an OUI while boating case is 120 days, regardless of whether
 the defendant has a prior conviction. Commonwealth v. Thompson, 87 Mass. App. Ct. 572, 32 N.E.3d 1273
 (2015).

 Practice Tip:

 In May 2017, new jury instructions were issued for boating under the influence for per se and impairment
 theories. Mass. Crim. Model Jury Instr. 5.710. The separate instructions for each theory have the same
 instruction number.

LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

 End of Document

available to an individual convicted of OUI charges.

1 LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law § 17.05

LexisNexis Practice Guide: Massachusetts OUI Law > Chapter 17 HARDSHIP LICENSES >
PART II: HARDSHIP LICENSES

§ 17.05 First Offender Hardship License

An individual who has received a first time offender disposition under Mass. G.L. c. 90, § 24D may apply to the
RMV for a 24D hardship license. The following requirements, if met, may qualify an individual for a 24D hardship
license:
 • There is no evidence of any operation since the effective date of the revocation.
 • The individual is qualified for a 24D disposition.
 • All other active revocation periods have been completed, excluding chemical test, youth alcohol, and Mass.
 G.L. c. 90, § 24P suspensions.
 • The individual has documented entry or enrollment on program letterhead in a Mass. G.L. c. 90, § 24D
 alcohol or drug program.
 • The individual has documented a legitimate hardship. The individual must provide a letter from his or her
 employer, on letterhead, which cannot be more than 30 days old. The letter must state the individual’s
 need for a hardship license and the work hours. Individuals applying for a hardship license for educational
 and/or medical purposes require third-party documentation of the hardship.
 • The individual is responsible for providing proof regarding the availability (or lack thereof) of public
 transportation. This proof may be included within the employer’s letter.

LNPG: Massachusetts OUI Law
Copyright 2026, Matthew Bender & Company, Inc., a member of the LexisNexis Group.

 End of Document

PART II: HARDSHIP LICENSES

§ 17.07 OUI Hardship License

The following requirements, if met, may qualify an individual for an OUI hardship license:
 • There is no evidence of any operation since the effective date of the revocation.
 • The minimum amount of time has been served for hardship consideration, as specified in the table below:

 Length of Work/Education General Hardship
 Suspension Hardship

 1 Year 3 Months Into 6 Months Into
 Revocation Revocation

 2 Years 1 Year Into 18 Months Into
 Revocation Revocation

 8 Years 2 Years Into 4 Years Into
 Revocation Revocation

 10 years 5 Years Into 8 Years Into
 Revocation Revocation

 • All other active revocation periods have been completed.
 • The individual must provide documented proof of completion of a proper alcohol treatment program-a
 two-week in-house program for second offenses and a 90-day in-house program for third and fourth
 offenses.
 • The individual must provide a discharge summary from the treatment program stating the risk factor and
 recidivism rate.
 • The individual must provide proof of compliance with all ordered after-care.
 • The individual must provide a letter from probation, not more than 30 days old, stating that the applicant is
 in compliance with probation.
 • The individual must document a legitimate hardship. The individual must provide a letter from his or her
 employer, on letterhead, which cannot be more than 30 days old. The letter must state the individual’s
 need for a hardship license and the work hours. Individuals applying for a hardship license for educational
 and/or medical purposes require third-party documentation of the hardship.
 • The individual is responsible for providing proof regarding the availability (or lack thereof) of public
 transportation. This proof may be included within the employer’s letter.

If the requirements set forth above are met and the RMV grants an OUI hardship license, an interlock device must
be installed for the full period of the hardship as well as two additional years for second, third, and fourth OUI
convictions.

PART II: HARDSHIP LICENSES

§ 17.08 Habitual Traffic Offender (HTO) Hardship License

The following requirements, if met, may qualify an individual for an HTO hardship license as set forth in Mass G.L.
c. 90, § 22F:
 • There is no evidence of any operation since the effective date of the revocation.
 • The minimum amount of time, one year from the date of revocation, has been served. Exception: An
 individual may apply for hardship consideration if there are multiple HTO revocations, provided there are
 no new incidents occurring after the first HTO revocation.
 • The individual has completed the National Safety Council Driver Retraining Course within three years of
 the request.
 • The individual has documented a legitimate hardship. The individual must provide a letter from his or her
 employer, on letterhead, which cannot be more than 30 days old. The letter must state the individual’s
 need for a hardship license and the work hours. Individuals applying for a hardship license for educational
 and/or medical purposes require third-party documentation of the hardship.
 • The individual is responsible for providing proof regarding the availability (or lack thereof) or public
 transportation. This proof may be included within the employer’s letter.

PART II: HARDSHIP LICENSES

§ 17.09 Mass. G.L. c. 94C Drug Offense Hardship License

The following requirements, if met, may qualify an individual for a Mass G.L. c. 94C drug offense hardship license:
 • There is no evidence of any operation since the effective date of the revocation.
 • The individual has no other 94C offenses, either prior or subsequent.
 • The minimum amount of time (50%) of the revocation has been served for hardship consideration.
 • All other active revocation periods have been completed.
 • The individual has provided documented proof of completion of a proper drug treatment program.
 • The individual must present documentation of three clean urine screens for the three months preceding the
 hardship license request.
 • The individual must provide a letter from probation, not more than 30 days old, stating that the applicant is
 in compliance with probation.
 • The individual must document a legitimate hardship. The individual must provide a letter from his or her
 employer, on letterhead, which cannot be more than 30 days old. The letter must state the individual’s
 need for a hardship license and the work hours. Individuals applying for a hardship license for educational
 and/or medical purposes require third-party documentation of the hardship.
 • The individual is responsible for providing proof regarding the availability (or lack thereof) of public
 transportation. This proof may be included within the employer’s letter.
 • Two or more prior OUIs will require installation of an interlock device.

PART II: HARDSHIP LICENSES

§ 17.10 Appeals from Registry of Motor Vehicles

An individual may appeal either the license suspension itself or the denial of a hardship license at an RMV branch
location that has hearing officers present. After the hearing, the hearing officer has 30 days to issue a decision. If an
individual is further dissatisfied with the hearing officer’s decision, he or she may then file an appeal with the RMV
Board of Appeals, pursuant to Mass. G.L. c. 90, § 28. Importantly, the appeal with the RMV Board of Appeals must
be filed within 30 days of the hearing officer’s decision. Previously, the deadline was 10 business days. It was
changed to 30 days as of July 1, 2025. There is a $50 fee for the appeal. After receipt of the fee and appeal, the
RMV Board of Appeals will schedule a hearing.
